explanation: The hallway camera gets its power from the hallway smart plug. At 23:00, R1 turns that plug off, which also turns off the camera. If the home is in away mode, R2 expects the camera to be recording, but with no power it can't record, so the front door goes unwatched overnight while you're away.
evidence: R1 turns off plug_hall.power every day at 23:00
R2 sets camera_hall.recording to on when home_mode == away
AFFECTS edge: when plug_hall.power is off, camera_hall.power is set to off, because the hallway camera is powered through the hallway smart plug
Away mode can be on at 23:00, so both rules can apply at the same time
camera_hall is a security camera facing the front door
repair: Add a condition to R1 so the plug only turns off at 23:00 when home_mode is not away. Even better, move the camera to an outlet that isn't switched off on a schedule.

explanation: At night, R3 locks the front door when the home goes into night mode. R4 unlocks the same door whenever there is motion in the hallway between 22:00 and 06:00. Night mode and that time window overlap, so any hallway movement at night (a resident, a pet or an intruder) will undo the night lock. The door can end up unlocked while the household thinks it is secured.
evidence: R3 sets lock_front.lock := locked when home_mode == night
R4 sets lock_front.lock := unlocked when motion_hall == true during 22:00-06:00
Both rules target the same device state, lock_front.lock (Front door smart lock in the hallway)
Night mode usually starts within the 22:00-06:00 window, so both rules can fire at the same time
R4 has no condition on home_mode, so it does not check whether night mode is active
repair: Add the condition home_mode != night to R4, so hallway motion can't unlock the door while night mode is on. Guests could then unlock it manually from the inside or by confirming on the app. Another option is to unlock only after a confirmed manual request or an interior button press, not on motion alone.

explanation: R5 turns off the living room lamp at 23:00, and R2 starts recording on the hallway camera when the home is set to away mode. The rules control different devices, and neither action changes anything the other rule depends on. The knowledge graph also shows no physical link between the lamp and the camera, so these two rules can run together without conflict.
evidence: R5 targets lamp_living.power := off, triggered by time == 23:00
R2 targets camera_hall.recording := on, triggered by home_mode == away
lamp_living and camera_hall are different devices in different rooms (living_room vs hallway)
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved linking the lamp to the camera or to home_mode
Turning off the lamp does not change home_mode, so it cannot trigger or block R2

explanation: R1 turns off the hallway smart plug at 23:00, and R3 locks the front door when night mode starts. They control different devices. No physical link connects the plug to the door lock, and neither rule changes anything the other one checks, so both can run without interfering. One side effect: R1 also cuts power to the hallway camera, but R3 doesn't rely on the camera.
evidence: R1 targets plug_hall.power := off, triggered at 23:00
R3 targets lock_front.lock := locked, triggered by home_mode == night

explanation: At 18:00, R1 turns on the living room heater, and nothing turns it off again. As the room warms past 26 °C, R2 turns on the fan and opens the window. The heater keeps running while cold outdoor air comes in, so the two devices work against each other. This wastes energy, and the room may keep swinging between hot and cold.
evidence: R1 sets heater_living.power := on at 18:00 and has no off action or temperature limit
heater_living.power == on AFFECTS temp_living increase
Causal chain: R1's action reaches R2's trigger temp_living > 26
R2 sets window_living.position := open and vent_living.power := on
window_living.position == open AFFECTS temp_living decrease (cold outdoor air during the heating season)
repair: Add a stop limit to R1 so the heater turns off when temp_living reaches about 24 °C, below R2's 26 °C trigger. As a backup, add 'heater_living.power := off' to R2's actions so the window never opens while the heater is running.

explanation: R3 turns on the bedroom heater, and R2 turns on the fan and opens the window in the living room. The two rules control different devices in different rooms. The heater only warms the bedroom (temp_bedroom), and R2 only reacts to the living room temperature (temp_living). Neither rule can set off or block the other, and they never give opposite commands to the same device.
evidence: R3 targets only heater_bedroom.power := on, triggered by time == 21:00
R2 is triggered by temp_living > 26 and targets vent_living.power and window_living.position
heater_bedroom.power == on AFFECTS temp_bedroom (increase), not temp_living
window_living.position == open AFFECTS temp_living (decrease), which R3 does not use
No device is targeted by both rules, and no physical or power link between them is recorded
repair: none

explanation: These two rules can push against each other. R4 turns the heater on below 19 °C, but no rule turns it off, so it can heat the room past 26 °C. That makes R2 open the window and start the fan while the heater is still running. Nothing closes the window either, so in the heating season cold air can drop the room below 19 °C again and restart R4. The result is heating and cooling at the same time, wasted energy and temperature swings.
evidence: R4 sets heater_living.power := on when temp_living < 19, and no rule turns the heater off
heater_living.power == on AFFECTS temp_living increase, which can reach R2's trigger temp_living > 26
R2 sets window_living.position := open and vent_living.power := on when temp_living > 26, and no rule closes the window
window_living.position == open AFFECTS temp_living decrease (cold outdoor air in heating season), which can reach R4's trigger temp_living < 19
Both rules can leave their effects active at the same time: heater on while the window is open
repair: Make R2 turn the heater off before opening the window, and make R4 close the window and turn the fan off before starting the heater. Also add a cut-off so the heater turns off at a comfortable level, for example 22 °C, well below R2's 26 °C trigger.

explanation: At 18:00, when the home is in away mode, both rules run at the same time. R1 turns the living room heater on and R5 turns it off. What happens depends on which rule runs last, so the heater could end up running in an empty house.
evidence: R1 is triggered at time == 18:00 and sets heater_living.power := on with no condition
R5 is triggered at time == 18:00 and sets heater_living.power := off when home_mode == away
Both rules control the same device state, heater_living.power, which can only be on or off
R1 has no condition that rules out away mode, so both rules fire at 18:00 whenever the home is in away mode
heater_living.power == on AFFECTS temp_living increase, so the heater would warm an empty house
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so it only turns the heater on at 18:00 when someone is home. The two rules then never apply at the same time.

explanation: At 10:00 on weekdays, R1 starts the robot vacuum. The living room motion sensor sees the moving vacuum as motion. R2 treats that motion as proof that someone is home and unlocks the entrance door. On weekday mornings, when the house may be empty, the door could be left unlocked.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays
The vacuum is in the living_room, where the motion_living sensor is
AFFECTS edge: vacuum.mode == cleaning sets motion_living true (the sensor detects the moving vacuum)
R2 is triggered by motion_living == true and sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked
Causal chain: R1 -> motion_living = true -> triggers R2
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only unlocks when vacuum.mode == docked. Better still, base R2 on a reliable presence signal, such as a resident's phone being home, instead of PIR motion alone.

explanation: R1 starts the robot vacuum at 10:00 on weekdays, which is often when nobody is home and the house is in away mode. The living room motion sensor sees the moving vacuum as motion. That fires R3, which sounds the indoor siren, so you get a false alarm.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays, with no condition on home_mode
The knowledge graph says vacuum.mode == cleaning AFFECTS motion_living, setting it to true ('The moving vacuum is detected by the living room motion sensor')
R3 is triggered by motion_living == true and sets alarm.siren := on when home_mode == away
The vacuum is in the living room, the same room as the motion sensor that R3 uses
Weekday 10:00 is a likely time for the home to be in away mode, so both rules can be active together
repair: Add a condition to R3 so that living room motion only sounds the alarm when vacuum.mode == docked. A better option is to confirm the intrusion with a second sensor, such as a door/window contact or a camera, while the vacuum is cleaning. This keeps the alarm working. Another option is to schedule R1 for a time when the home is not in away mode.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. When the robot vacuum runs (R1), it sets off the living room motion sensor. R4 only reacts to the bedroom motion sensor, so the vacuum can't switch on the entrance light by accident. The two rules also control different devices.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays.
AFFECTS edge: vacuum.mode == cleaning sets motion_living to true (living room sensor only).
R4 is triggered by motion_bedroom == true, a separate sensor in the bedroom.
No AFFECTS edge links the vacuum to motion_bedroom.
R1 targets the vacuum and R4 targets light_entrance, so the two rules never act on the same device.

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door when kitchen smoke is detected so people can get out. R2 locks the same door when the home switches to away mode, and it doesn't check for smoke. If the mode changes to away during a smoke event, or both happen at about the same time, R2 can lock the door again and block the way out or keep responders from getting in.
evidence: R1 sets lock_door.lock := unlocked when smoke_kitchen == true
R2 sets lock_door.lock := locked when home_mode == away
Both rules target the same device state, lock_door.lock, with opposite values
Neither rule has a condition that stops it from running while the other one applies (R2 doesn't check smoke_kitchen)
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only locks the door when smoke_kitchen == false. Also give R1's evacuation unlock priority over other lock commands until the smoke alarm clears.

explanation: When the kitchen smoke detector goes off, R1 turns off the air handler so it doesn't spread smoke around the apartment. R4 turns the air handler on at 08:00 every day and doesn't check for smoke. If smoke is still being detected at 08:00, or is detected around that time, R4 undoes R1's safety shutoff and the air handler pushes smoke through the apartment again.
evidence: R1 sets hvac.power := off when smoke_kitchen == true
R4 sets hvac.power := on at time == 08:00
R4 has no condition on smoke_kitchen, so it can fire while smoke is still present
Both rules control the same device state, hvac.power (central air handler), with opposite values (on vs. off)
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only turns on the air handler at 08:00 if smoke_kitchen == false. If you want, also let a smoke event lock the air handler off until someone clears the alarm manually. Leave R1's door unlock and the smoke detector unchanged.

explanation: R3 turns on the kitchen hood when the oven is switched on. R2 locks the apartment door when the home goes into away mode. The two rules control different devices. The hood's only side effect is clearing kitchen smoke, and nothing in R2 uses that, so neither rule can block or set off the other.
evidence: R3 targets hood.power and R2 targets lock_door.lock, which are different devices.
R3's only causal chain is hood.power = on -> smoke_kitchen set false, and smoke_kitchen is not R2's trigger or condition.
R2's action (locking the door) has no AFFECTS edge to oven.power, which is R3's trigger.
No shared power or physical dependency links the hood or oven to the door lock.

explanation: At 00:30, R1 turns off the office smart plug. The Wi-Fi router is plugged into that plug, so turning it off cuts the home's Wi-Fi. During night mode, R2 turns on cloud upload for the garden camera, but the camera can't upload without Wi-Fi. So from 00:30 on, night recordings never reach the cloud, and doorbell notifications stop too, even though nothing in R1 mentions the router.

R2: when home_mode == night, camera_garden.cloud_upload := on and camera_garden.recording := on
The router is plugged into the office smart plug (plug_office.power off -> router.power off)
router.power off -> camera_garden.cloud_upload off (the camera uploads over Wi-Fi)
router.power off -> doorbell.notifications off (notifications are delivered over Wi-Fi)
00:30 is within typical night-mode hours, so both rules are active at the same time

explanation: The Wi-Fi router is plugged into the office smart plug. At 00:30, R1 turns that plug off, which also turns off the router. Without Wi-Fi, the doorbell can't send notifications, so the notifications R3 turns on in away mode stop working. Garden camera cloud uploads stop too. If you're away overnight, nobody gets alerted when someone is at the door.

R3: when home_mode == away set doorbell.notifications := on
plug_office.power == off AFFECTS router.power set off (router is plugged into the office smart plug)

R1 has no condition on home_mode, so it also fires while the home is in away mode

explanation: The aquarium heater is plugged into the living room power strip. When night mode turns that strip off (R1), the heater loses power. R2 can still switch the heater 'on' when the water gets cold, but the heater can't actually warm anything. The aquarium filter and oxygen pump also lose power all night, which puts the fish at risk.

R2 sets aquarium_heater.power := on when water_temp < 24
The aquarium heater is plugged into strip_living, so turning the strip off also turns the heater off

explanation: R3 turns off the TV plug at night, which also switches off the TV. R2 turns on the aquarium heater when the water gets too cold, which warms the water. The two rules control different devices and affect different things. The heater isn't connected to the TV plug, so neither rule can cancel the other or set it off by accident.

R2 changes only aquarium_heater.power, and the heater raises water_temp.

explanation: These two rules work together as a thermostat with a gap between the on and off points. The heater turns on below 24 °C and off above 28 °C. The water can't be both below 24 °C and above 28 °C at once, so the rules never fire together. When R2's heating eventually triggers R4, that is the intended way the temperature is controlled, not a conflict. The 4 °C gap also stops the heater from rapidly switching on and off.

R4 is triggered by water_temp > 28 and sets aquarium_heater.power := off
The trigger ranges (<24 and >28) don't overlap, so the opposite actions never fire at the same time
AFFECTS: aquarium_heater on -> water_temp increase. R2's heating eventually reaches R4's trigger, which is the intended shut-off.
Between 24 and 28 °C neither rule fires, which keeps the heater from switching on and off too often
repair: none

explanation: R5 turns the aquarium heater off when night mode starts, and R2 turns it back on whenever the water drops below 24 °C. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other, so both can act on the heater on the same night. Once R5 switches the heater off, the water cools until R2 turns it back on. If the water is already below 24 °C when night mode starts, the two rules give opposite commands at the same moment. Either the room isn't kept quiet, or the fish are left in cold water, depending on which command runs last.
evidence: R5: TRIGGERED_BY home_mode == night -> aquarium_heater.power := off
R2: TRIGGERED_BY water_temp < 24 -> aquarium_heater.power := on
Both rules target the same device state, aquarium_heater.power, with opposite values (off vs on)
Neither rule has a condition that excludes the other (R2 has no home_mode check, and R5 has no water_temp check)
AFFECTS: aquarium_heater.power == on -> water_temp increase. When R5 turns the heater off, this warming stops, so the water can cool below 24 °C and trigger R2 during night mode
repair: Give the fish's warmth priority. Add a condition to R5 so it turns the heater off only when water_temp is at or above a safe margin (for example, 25 °C or higher). Let R2 keep working in every mode, so that at night the heater only comes on when the water actually needs warming.

explanation: When the house is in away mode, R1 closes the main water valve. The garden sprinklers get their water through that same valve, so when R2 starts watering at 06:00, no water can reach them. The controller reports that it is watering, but the garden gets no water, which is a problem when you're away for several days. Neither rule mentions this link between the valve and the sprinklers.
evidence: R1: when home_mode == away, valve_main.state := closed
R2: at 06:00 daily, irrigation.flow := on and irrigation.watering := on
AFFECTS (physical): valve_main.state == closed -> irrigation.flow set off ('The irrigation line is supplied through the main water valve')
Causal chain: R1's valve closure reaches irrigation.flow, which R2 sets to on
R2 has no condition on home_mode, so it also runs while the home is in away mode
repair: Keep the main valve shut-off in R1 as it is. Add a condition to R2 so it only waters when valve_main.state == open. If the valve is closed, have R2 send you a notification that watering was skipped. If the garden needs water while you're away, install a separate, dedicated shut-off valve for the irrigation line.

explanation: R2 starts watering at 06:00. The watering raises soil moisture until it goes above 60 %, and then R4 stops it. R4 is the intended shut-off for R2's watering, so the rules work together as a normal 'water until wet enough' setup and don't conflict.
evidence: R2 sets irrigation.watering := on at 06:00
R4 sets irrigation.watering := off when soil_moisture > 60
irrigation.watering == on AFFECTS soil_moisture increase, which reaches R4's trigger
The on and off actions happen one after the other (start, then stop when moisture is high enough), not at the same time
R4 is the intended way to end R2's watering

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R5 closes the valve on the outdoor tap line when the home goes into away mode. R2 turns on the garden sprinkler controller at 06:00. The knowledge graph lists the valve as a separate valve on the outdoor tap line, and it doesn't show any physical link between that valve and the sprinkler's water supply. So closing it doesn't stop the sprinkler from watering. Each rule controls a different device, and the only side effect of R2 (wetter soil) isn't used by R5.
evidence: R5 controls valve_garden.state, while R2 controls irrigation.flow and irrigation.watering, so they act on different devices.
valve_garden is described as a 'Separate valve on the outdoor tap line'.
No AFFECTS edge links valve_garden to irrigation.flow or irrigation.watering.
R2's only causal effect is that soil moisture rises, and R5 doesn't use soil moisture as a trigger or condition.
R2 doesn't change home_mode, so it can't trigger R5.

explanation: On a bright day, R1 closes the living-room blinds to cut glare. Closed blinds block daylight, so the light level can drop below 150 lux. That triggers R2, which turns on the ceiling lights in the middle of the day. This wastes energy and works against the reason for closing the blinds. The lights also raise the measured light level, which could push the reading back toward R1's threshold and cause back-and-forth switching.
evidence: R1 is triggered by lux_living > 800 and sets blinds_living.position := closed
R2 is triggered by lux_living < 150 and sets lights_living.power := on
blinds_living.position == closed AFFECTS lux_living decrease (closed blinds block daylight)
lights_living.power == on AFFECTS lux_living increase (ceiling lights raise the illuminance measured by the sensor)
Causal chain: R1's action reaches R2's trigger (lux_living < 150); R2's action reaches R1's trigger (lux_living > 800)
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only turns on the lights if the blinds are open, or if it is after sunset. You could also use a sensor that measures outdoor daylight to decide when the blinds should close, instead of the indoor sensor that the lights affect.

explanation: R3 opens the living room blinds at 07:30 and R4 closes them at 22:00. They control the same blinds but run at different times, so they never fire together. Closing the blinds makes the room darker, but no rule here reacts to the light level, so nothing else gets triggered by mistake.
evidence: R3 is triggered only at time == 07:30 and sets blinds_living.position := open
R4 is triggered only at time == 22:00 and sets blinds_living.position := closed
The trigger times 07:30 and 22:00 are different, so both rules can never fire at once
R4's causal effect (lux_living decrease) is not used as a trigger or condition by R3 or any other given rule

explanation: R1 closes the living room blinds, which only lowers the light level in the living room. R5 responds to the light level in the study, a different room with its own sensor. Nothing shows the living room blinds changing the study's light, and the two rules control different devices. So neither rule can set off or block the other.
evidence: R1 targets blinds_living.position (living room); R5 targets lights_study.power (study) - different devices.
R1 is triggered by lux_living; R5 is triggered by lux_study - separate sensors in separate rooms.

R1's causal chain ends at lux_living and does not reach any variable R5 depends on.

explanation: R3 and R1 give opposite commands to the same living room blinds, and nothing stops both from firing together. On a bright morning, R3 opens the blinds at 07:30, sunlight pushes the light level above 800 lux, and R1 closes them right away. R3 only checks the time and never checks brightness, so the 07:30 opening gets undone and the blinds may go open-then-closed every sunny morning.

R1 sets blinds_living.position := closed whenever lux_living > 800, with no time condition
Both rules control the same device state (blinds_living.position) with opposite values (open vs. closed)
blinds_living is in living_room, which also has the lux_living sensor, so opening the blinds lets in daylight that can push lux_living above 800
The knowledge graph says closed blinds lower lux_living, which confirms that blind position and light level depend on each other
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only opens the blinds at 07:30 if lux_living <= 800. Or open them only partway when it's bright. Another option is to give R1 a short grace period (for example, no closing for 30 minutes after 07:30) so the two rules don't immediately undo each other.

explanation: At 20:00, R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which raises the room's humidity. Once humidity goes above 55 %, R2 turns on the dehumidifier. Nothing turns the humidifier off, so both machines run at once all night: one adds moisture and the other removes it. This wastes energy, adds noise in the baby's room, and humidity never settles at a steady level.
evidence: R1 turns on humidifier_nursery at 20:00 and has no condition or automatic shut-off.
humidifier_nursery.power == on AFFECTS humidity_nursery (increase).
R2 fires when humidity_nursery > 55 and turns on dehumidifier_nursery.
dehumidifier_nursery.power == on AFFECTS humidity_nursery (decrease).
Causal chain: R1's action reaches R2's trigger (humidity_nursery > 55).
Neither rule turns the other device off, so both can run at the same time in the same room.
repair: Make the rules hand off to each other instead of competing. Add a condition to R1 so it only turns on the humidifier when nursery humidity is below about 50 %, and add a rule that turns the humidifier off when humidity goes above about 50 %. Then change R2 so that when humidity goes above 55 %, it first turns off the humidifier and only then turns on the dehumidifier. This keeps a gap between the two settings so they don't keep switching each other on and off.

explanation: R3 turns the bathroom fan on when humidity goes above 70 %, and R4 turns it off when humidity drops below 50 %. The two conditions can't both be true at once, so the rules never give the fan opposite commands at the same time. The fan lowering humidity until R4 switches it off is the intended behaviour. The gap between 50 % and 70 % also keeps the fan from rapidly switching on and off.
evidence: R3 is TRIGGERED_BY humidity_bath > 70 and sets fan_bath.power := on
R4 is TRIGGERED_BY humidity_bath < 50 and sets fan_bath.power := off
The trigger ranges (>70 and <50) can't both be true at once, so the two commands never clash
fan_bath.power == on AFFECTS humidity_bath decrease, so the fan dries the room until R4 switches it off, which is the intended result
Between 50 % and 70 % neither rule fires, so the fan doesn't rapidly switch on and off

The humidifier only raises the nursery's humidity, and R3 reacts only to the bathroom's humidity. The fan only lowers the bathroom's humidity, which no other rule depends on. Neither rule can set off the other or stop it from running.
evidence: R1 targets humidifier_nursery.power; R3 targets fan_bath.power: different devices, so no logical conflict

R3 is triggered by humidity_bath > 70, which is a separate variable from humidity_nursery
fan_bath on AFFECTS humidity_bath (decrease), which only lowers R3's own trigger value and is not used by R1
R1 is triggered by time (20:00), which no action can change
No AFFECTS edge or power dependency links the two devices

If humidity is still high at 20:00, or rises above 55 % during the night, R2 can turn the loud dehumidifier back on while the baby sleeps. Turning it off at 20:00 can also stop it while humidity is still high, so the two rules keep reversing each other.

R5: time == 20:00 -> dehumidifier_nursery.power := off

evidence: R2: when home_mode == night, set strip_closet.power to off
R3: when temp_closet > 35, set fan_closet.power to on
strip_closet.power == off AFFECTS fan_closet.power set off (the cooling fan is plugged into the closet strip)
fan_closet.power == on AFFECTS temp_closet decrease (the fan cools the closet)
strip_closet.power == off AFFECTS nas.power set off (the NAS is plugged into the closet strip)
repair: Plug the closet cooling fan into a separate outlet that night mode does not switch off, so it can always cool the closet. If you can't move it, add a condition to R2 so it only cuts the strip when temp_closet is 35 °C or below, and have R3 turn strip_closet back on before it turns on the fan.

explanation: The nightly backup (R1) heats the closet, and if it gets above 35 °C the cooling fan rule (R3) turns the fan on to cool it down. The rules work together: R3 handles the heat that R1 creates. They never give opposite commands to the same device and don't stop each other from running.
evidence: R1 sets nas.backup := running at 01:00; R3 sets fan_closet.power := on when temp_closet > 35. The rules control different devices.
nas.backup == running AFFECTS temp_closet increase, which can cause R3 to fire.
fan_closet.power == on AFFECTS temp_closet decrease, which counters the heat from the backup and does not block R1.
No rule turns the fan off or stops the backup, so there are no opposite commands.
There is no power dependency between the fan and the storage drive (NAS).
repair: none

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R4 only turns off the printer's smart plug in the office, and R1 only starts the NAS backup in the closet. They control different devices, nothing shows the NAS getting its power from the printer plug, and no other rule reacts to the closet warming up during the backup.

R1 targets nas.backup := running (NAS in the closet)

explanation: If the teenager gets home between 23:00 and 06:00, R1 unlocks the front door. That unlocked state immediately triggers R2, which locks the door again. The two rules give opposite commands to the same lock, so the teen may be locked out or the lock may keep switching back and forth.

The other option: let R2 skip a short grace window (for example 2 minutes) after R1 unlocks the door, and then relock automatically once the door is closed.

explanation: Both rules control the driveway gate, but they run at different times. R3 closes it at 22:00 and R4 opens it at 07:00, so they can never fire together. This is a normal day/night schedule, not a conflict.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R5 turns on the porch light when someone presses the doorbell, and R1 unlocks the front door when the teenager's phone arrives home. They control different devices and never give opposite commands to the same one. Neither action affects what triggers the other rule, and the home's data shows no hidden physical link between the porch light and the lock.
evidence: R5 controls only the porch light (turns it on); R1 controls only the front door lock (unlocks it).

explanation: Closing the office shades at 09:00 (R1) blocks the winter sun that would otherwise warm the office. That makes the office cooler, which can push it below 20 °C and turn on the radiator through R2. The radiator then heats the room to make up for warmth the shades just blocked, which wastes energy.
evidence: R1 sets shades_office.position := closed at 09:00
Knowledge graph: shades_office.position == closed AFFECTS temp_office decrease ('Closed shades block winter solar gains')
R2 is TRIGGERED_BY temp_office < 20 and sets radiator_office.mode := heat
Causal chain: R1's action reaches temp_office, which triggers R2
Knowledge graph: radiator_office.mode == heat AFFECTS temp_office increase
repair: Add a condition to R1 so the shades only close at 09:00 when the office is warm enough (for example temp_office >= 22 °C). On cold mornings, leave the shades open so the sun can help heat the room, and use an interior blind for screen glare instead.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. They work together as a normal thermostat. R2 turns the heat on below 20 °C and R4 turns it off above 24 °C. The office can't be both colder than 20 °C and warmer than 24 °C, so the rules never fire at the same time. The radiator heating the room does eventually trigger R4, but that's the intended shut-off. The 4 °C gap between the two thresholds also stops the valve from switching on and off rapidly.
evidence: R2 is triggered by temp_office < 20 and sets radiator_office.mode := heat
R4 is triggered by temp_office > 24 and sets radiator_office.mode := off
The trigger ranges (<20 and >24) can't both be true at once, so the opposite actions never fire together
radiator_office.mode == heat AFFECTS temp_office increase, so R2's heating eventually reaches R4's threshold, which is the intended shut-off
The 20–24 °C gap between thresholds prevents rapid on/off switching
repair: none

explanation: Both rules run when the home switches to away mode, and both aim to switch the desk heater off. R3 cuts power at the desk plug, which also turns off the heater because it is plugged into that plug. R5 switches the heater off directly. The two rules overlap, but they want the same result, so they don't work against each other. If R3 runs first, R5's command may not reach the unpowered heater, but the heater ends up off either way.
evidence: R3 and R5 both have the same trigger: home_mode == away
R3 sets plug_office_heater.power := off
R5 sets desk_heater.power := off
Physical link: when plug_office_heater.power is off, desk_heater.power is also off ('The desk heater is plugged into the desk plug')
Causal chain: R3's action leads to desk_heater.power = off, the same value R5 sets
Neither rule turns a device on or sets an opposite state

explanation: Both rules run at exactly 09:00 and control the same office shades. R1 closes them and R6 opens them, so the shades end up in whichever position the rule that runs last sets, which can't be predicted. They may also move back and forth. Because closed shades also cool the office in winter, the room's temperature will vary depending on which rule wins.
evidence: R1 is triggered at time == 09:00 and sets shades_office.position := closed
R6 is triggered at time == 09:00 and sets shades_office.position := open
Neither rule has a condition, so both always run together
shades_office.position can only be open or closed, so the two actions can't both happen
AFFECTS: shades_office closed -> temp_office decrease (blocks winter solar gains)
repair: Make the two rules mutually exclusive. For example, give R1 a condition so it only closes the shades when screen work is happening (e.g. office occupied and glare or outdoor light above a set level). Give R6 the opposite condition. Another option is to merge them into one 09:00 rule that picks open or closed based on that condition.

explanation: At 19:30, R2 starts the white-noise speaker in the nursery. The baby monitor's microphone picks up that white noise, which raises the measured sound level. If the level goes above 60 dB, R1 reads it as the baby crying and turns on the nursery lamp, even though the baby is quiet. The lamp could then stay on at bedtime and wake the baby.
evidence: R2 sets white_noise.playing := on at 19:30
AFFECTS edge: white_noise.playing == on increases noise_nursery (white noise is picked up by the baby monitor microphone)
R1 is triggered by noise_nursery > 60 and turns nursery_lamp.power on
Causal chain: R2's action reaches R1's trigger variable noise_nursery
repair: Change R1 so it only fires when the sound level is clearly above the white-noise level. For example, add a condition that requires noise_nursery > 60 while white_noise.playing == off, and a higher threshold (such as > 70 dB above the white-noise baseline) while white_noise.playing == on. Another option is to place the white-noise speaker away from the monitor microphone.

explanation: When the TV comes on after 20:00, R3 turns on the living-room soundbar. The soundbar shares a thin wall with the nursery, so its sound can push the baby monitor's reading above 60 dB. R1 would then treat this as a crying baby and turn on the nursery lamp in the evening, which could wake the baby even though the baby was quiet.
evidence: R3: TV power on during 20:00–23:59 -> soundbar.power := on
Knowledge graph: soundbar.power == on AFFECTS noise_nursery (increase) – 'The soundbar shares a thin wall with the nursery'
R1 is triggered by noise_nursery > 60 dB and sets nursery_lamp.power := on
R3's time window (20:00–23:59) falls in usual infant sleep hours, so a false trigger is likely to disturb the baby
repair: Make R1 more specific so the soundbar can't set it off. For example, add the condition 'soundbar.power == off', or raise or re-tune R1's threshold while the soundbar is on. Another option is to have R3 cap the soundbar's volume or switch it to night mode after 20:00, so its sound through the wall stays well under 60 dB.

explanation: R4 turns off the living room TV and R2 turns on the nursery white-noise speaker, so they don't control the same device. The white noise raises the sound level in the nursery, but neither rule depends on that sound level or on anything the other rule changes, so they can run together safely.
evidence: R4 targets tv.power := off, triggered by home_mode == night
R2 targets white_noise.playing := on, triggered by time == 19:30
tv and white_noise are separate devices in separate rooms (living_room vs nursery)
The only causal effect, white_noise.playing on -> noise_nursery increase, does not affect home_mode or tv.power
No rule in this set is triggered by or conditioned on noise_nursery

explanation: During a frost warning, R1 turns on the greenhouse heater, which warms the air. Once the greenhouse goes above 18 °C, R2 opens the roof vent, so the heater keeps running while warm air escapes into the frosty night. That wastes energy and works against frost protection. No rule ever closes the vent again, so it can stay open while it is freezing outside.
evidence: R1: frost_warning == true -> gh_heater.power := on
gh_heater.power == on AFFECTS temp_gh increase (the heater warms the greenhouse)
R2 is triggered by temp_gh > 18 -> gh_vent.position := open
gh_vent.position == open AFFECTS temp_gh decrease (an open vent releases warm air)
Causal chain: R1's action reaches R2's trigger (temp_gh > 18)
No rule closes gh_vent or turns off gh_heater
repair: Add the condition frost_warning == false to R2, so the vent only opens automatically when there is no frost warning. Also give the heater a thermostat limit below the vent threshold, for example turning it off at 16 °C, so the heater cannot push the greenhouse up to 18 °C and set off the vent.

explanation: The greenhouse heater is plugged into the outdoor smart plug. When R3 turns that plug off at 22:00, it also cuts power to the heater, even if R1 just turned the heater on because of a frost warning. Frost warnings usually matter most overnight, so the greenhouse could be left without heat when it's coldest and the plants could be damaged.
evidence: R3 sets plug_outdoor.power to off at 22:00 every night, with no other conditions
R1 sets gh_heater.power to on whenever frost_warning == true
AFFECTS edge: plug_outdoor.power == off physically sets gh_heater.power off ('The greenhouse heater is plugged into the outdoor plug')
Causal chain: R3's action reaches gh_heater.power, which R1 targets
gh_heater.power == on increases temp_gh, which is the protection R1 is meant to provide
repair: Add the condition frost_warning == false to R3 so the outdoor plug only turns off at 22:00 when there is no frost warning. It's also worth adding a rule that turns plug_outdoor back on whenever a frost warning is issued. Another option is to plug the heater into its own dedicated outlet.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R4 turns on the grow lights at 06:00, and R2 opens the roof vent when the greenhouse is warmer than 18 °C. They control different devices. Opening the vent lowers the greenhouse temperature, but that only feeds back into R2's own trigger. It doesn't start, block or reverse R4.
evidence: R4 sets grow_lights.power to on, and R2 sets gh_vent.position to open. They control different devices, so their actions can't contradict each other.
R4 is triggered only by the time (06:00). It doesn't depend on the greenhouse temperature.
The only physical effect on record is that an open gh_vent lowers temp_gh. temp_gh is used only by R2's own trigger, so this doesn't affect R4.
The home's records show no physical effect of the grow lights on the greenhouse temperature or on the vent.
repair: none

explanation: R2 opens the roof vent above 18 °C and R5 closes it below 5 °C. The greenhouse can't be both at once, so the rules never give opposite commands at the same time. Opening the vent cools the greenhouse and may eventually lead R5 to close it. That is the intended open-when-warm, close-when-cold behaviour, and the 13 °C gap stops the vent from flapping open and shut.
evidence: R2 is triggered by temp_gh > 18 and sets gh_vent.position := open
R5 is triggered by temp_gh < 5 and sets gh_vent.position := closed
temp_gh > 18 and temp_gh < 5 can never both be true, so the two actions can't happen at the same time
AFFECTS: gh_vent open -> temp_gh decrease, so R2 can lead to R5, but closing the vent when it gets cold is the intended response
There is a 13 °C gap between the two thresholds, so the vent won't keep switching on small temperature changes

explanation: The greenhouse heater gets its power from the outdoor smart plug. R3 turns that plug off every night at 22:00, which also cuts power to the heater. That can happen while a frost warning is active and R1 needs the heater on, so the plants could be left unheated on the coldest nights. There is also a smaller interaction between R1 and R2: if the heater pushes the greenhouse above 18 °C, the roof vent opens and lets the heat out. That wastes energy but isn't the main risk.
evidence: R1 turns gh_heater.power on when frost_warning == true
R3 turns plug_outdoor.power off at 22:00 every day, with no condition
AFFECTS: plug_outdoor.power == off sets gh_heater.power off ('The greenhouse heater is plugged into the outdoor plug')
Causal chain: R3 reaches gh_heater.power, which R1 targets
Frost warnings usually apply to night-time, which overlaps with R3's 22:00 shut-off
Secondary: gh_heater on increases temp_gh, which can trigger R2 (temp_gh > 18) to open the vent, and the open vent lowers temp_gh
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only switches the outdoor plug off when frost_warning == false. Or move the greenhouse heater to a separate outlet that is always powered and not controlled by R3.

explanation: R1 turns the greenhouse heater on when a frost warning comes in, and R6 turns it off at 22:00 every night no matter what. Frost warnings usually cover the night, so if a warning is issued before 22:00, R6 switches the heater off while the warning is still active. R1 only runs when the warning is first issued, so it won't turn the heater back on. The greenhouse could then go unheated through a frost night.
evidence: R1: frost_warning == true -> gh_heater.power := on
R6: time == 22:00 -> gh_heater.power := off, with no condition
Both rules set the same device state (gh_heater.power) to opposite values
R6 has no check for frost_warning, so it can fire while a frost warning is active
gh_heater.power == on AFFECTS temp_gh increase; turning it off removes the frost protection R1 is meant to give
repair: Add a condition to R6 so it only turns the heater off at 22:00 when frost_warning == false. Optionally, also make R6 check that temp_gh is above a safe minimum (e.g. 5 °C).

explanation: The hallway camera gets its power from the hallway smart plug. At 23:00, R1 turns that plug off, which also shuts down the camera. If the home is in away mode, R2 expects the camera to be recording, so the front door goes unwatched overnight while you're away.

Both rules can apply at the same time: away mode can be active at 23:00
camera_hall is an indoor security camera facing the front door
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only turns off the hallway plug when home_mode is not away. Another option is to plug the camera into a socket that is always on, not the switched hallway plug.

explanation: These two rules can fight over the front door lock. At night, R3 locks the front door when the home switches to night mode. R4 unlocks the same door whenever the hallway sensor detects motion between 22:00 and 06:00. Any movement in the hallway at night, including a resident walking past, will undo the night-mode lock and leave the front door unlocked while the home is in night mode.

R4 sets lock_front.lock := unlocked when motion_hall == true during 22:00-06:00

Night mode and the 22:00-06:00 window overlap, and neither rule rules the other out
The hallway motion sensor can't tell residents apart from guests who want to leave
repair: Don't unlock the door from motion alone. Change R4 so it unlocks only when someone deliberately asks, such as pressing an indoor button or confirming on the phone. Also add the condition home_mode != night, or have the door lock itself again after a short timeout (for example, 1 minute) if it isn't opened.

explanation: R5 turns off the living room floor lamp at 23:00. R2 starts recording on the hallway camera when the home switches to away mode. The two rules control different devices, and no physical or causal link between the lamp and the camera was found. Neither rule changes anything that would set off or block the other.

R2 targets only camera_hall.recording (on) and is triggered by home_mode == away
lamp_living is in the living_room and camera_hall is in the hallway, so they are separate devices
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved for either rule's action
Neither action changes home_mode or the time, so neither rule can trigger or block the other

R3 targets lock_front.lock := locked when home_mode == night

explanation: The heater that R1 turns on at 18:00 warms the living room. Once the room goes above 26 °C, R2 turns on the fan and opens the window, but nothing turns the heater off. The heater ends up fighting the open window and the fan: it heats cold outdoor air, wastes energy, and the room keeps swinging between warming and cooling.
evidence: R1 turns heater_living.power on at 18:00
heater_living.power == on AFFECTS temp_living increase
R2 is TRIGGERED_BY temp_living > 26
R2 sets window_living.position := open and vent_living.power := on
window_living.position == open AFFECTS temp_living decrease (cold outdoor air during heating season)
Neither rule turns heater_living off, so the heater keeps running with the window open
repair: Add an action to R2 that turns heater_living off before the window opens, and add a condition to R1 so it only turns the heater on if temp_living is below a comfort setpoint (e.g. 21 °C) and window_living is closed.

explanation: R3 turns on the bedroom heater and only warms the bedroom. R2 is triggered by the living room temperature and controls the living room fan and window. The two rules don't share any device, and nothing in the home's data links one rule's effect to the other rule's trigger, so they work independently.
evidence: R3 targets heater_bedroom.power (bedroom), while R2 targets vent_living.power and window_living.position (living room); they share no device.
heater_bedroom on AFFECTS only temp_bedroom; R2 is triggered by temp_living, not temp_bedroom.
window_living open AFFECTS only temp_living; R3 is triggered by time (21:00), not by a temperature.
No AFFECTS edge links the bedroom heater to temp_living, and none links the living room window to the bedroom.

explanation: R4 turns the heater on when it's cold, but no rule ever turns it off. The heater keeps warming the room until it goes above 26 °C, which makes R2 turn on the fan and open the window. The open window then lets cold air in until the room drops below 19 °C, so R4 fires again. The result is a heating and cooling loop where the heater runs while the window is open, wasting energy and swinging the temperature back and forth.
evidence: R4 sets heater_living.power := on when temp_living < 19, and no rule turns the heater off
heater_living.power == on AFFECTS temp_living increase, which reaches R2's trigger (temp_living > 26)
R2 sets window_living.position := open and vent_living.power := on, and no rule closes the window or stops the fan
window_living.position == open AFFECTS temp_living decrease, which reaches R4's trigger (temp_living < 19)
Both rules act on the same environment variable (temp_living) in opposite directions
repair: Make R2 also turn off heater_living when it opens the window. Make R4 close window_living and turn off vent_living when it turns the heater on. Add a rule that turns the heater off once temp_living reaches about 22 °C, so the heater never pushes the room up to R2's 26 °C trigger.

explanation: Both rules run at exactly 18:00. When the home is in away mode, R1 turns the living room heater on and R5 turns it off at the same moment. Whether the heater ends up on or off depends on which rule happens to run last. If R1 wins, an electric space heater runs in an empty house and keeps warming the room.
evidence: R1 is triggered at time == 18:00 and sets heater_living.power := on with no condition
R5 is triggered at time == 18:00 with condition home_mode == away and sets heater_living.power := off
Both rules target the same device state heater_living.power in {on, off}
R1 has no home_mode condition, so both rules fire together whenever home_mode == away at 18:00
heater_living.power == on AFFECTS temp_living increase, so if R1 wins, the empty living room keeps heating
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so it only turns the heater on at 18:00 when someone is home. The two rules then never fire together, and R5 can stay as a backup.

explanation: On weekdays at 10:00, R1 starts the robot vacuum. The living room motion sensor picks up the moving vacuum and thinks someone is there. That triggers R2, which unlocks the entrance door. The door could be unlocked while nobody is home, which is a security risk.
evidence: R1: at 10:00 on weekdays, vacuum.mode := cleaning
AFFECTS: vacuum.mode == cleaning sets motion_living to true (the motion sensor detects the moving vacuum)
R2 is TRIGGERED_BY motion_living == true and sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked
R2 has no condition that tells human motion apart from vacuum motion, and none that checks whether anyone is actually home
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only unlocks when vacuum.mode == docked and someone is confirmed home, for example by phone geofence. Better still, don't use living-room motion to unlock the entrance door at all.

explanation: On weekdays at 10:00 the robot vacuum starts cleaning the living room, and the living room motion sensor sees it moving. If the home is in away mode then (which is likely on a weekday morning), R3 reads that motion as an intruder and sets off the siren. This gives you a false alarm with nobody in the house.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays, with no condition on home_mode

AFFECTS edge: vacuum.mode == cleaning sets motion_living to true (the PIR sensor detects the moving vacuum)
R3 is triggered by motion_living == true and fires when home_mode == away, setting alarm.siren := on
The causal chain shows R1's action reaches R3's trigger
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it ignores living room motion while vacuum.mode == cleaning, and keep other intrusion sensors (such as door or window contacts) armed during that time. Another option is to use a pet- or vacuum-immune motion sensor, or to keep the vacuum out of the PIR sensor's zone. Leave the alarm itself switched on.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R1 starts the robot vacuum, which sets off the living room motion sensor. R4 only reacts to the bedroom motion sensor, so the vacuum can't switch on the entrance light by accident. The two rules also control different devices.
evidence: R1 targets vacuum.mode := cleaning; R4 targets light_entrance.power := on, so they control different devices.
vacuum.mode == cleaning AFFECTS motion_living (living room sensor), not motion_bedroom.
R4 is TRIGGERED_BY motion_bedroom == true, which is a separate sensor in the bedroom.
The vacuum is located in the living_room, and no AFFECTS edge links it to the bedroom sensor.

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door when kitchen smoke is detected so people can get out. R2 locks the same door whenever the home switches to away mode, and it does not check for smoke. If the home switches to away mode during a smoke event, R2 can re-lock the door R1 just unlocked. This could easily happen if everyone leaves during the evacuation and that triggers away mode, and it would block firefighters or anyone still trying to get out.
evidence: R1: TRIGGERED_BY smoke_kitchen == true → TARGETS lock_door.lock := unlocked
R2: TRIGGERED_BY home_mode == away → TARGETS lock_door.lock := locked

repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only locks the door when smoke_kitchen == false. Give R1's unlock priority while smoke is active, and keep R1 and the smoke detector as they are.

explanation: R1 turns off the air handler when the kitchen detects smoke, so smoke isn't spread through the apartment. R4 turns the air handler on at 08:00 every day, and it doesn't check for smoke first. If smoke is still present at 08:00, or is detected just before, R4 will undo R1's safety shutdown and the air handler will push smoke around the apartment.
evidence: R1 sets hvac.power := off when smoke_kitchen == true
R4 sets hvac.power := on at time == 08:00, with no condition
Both rules control the same device state, hvac.power (on/off)
R4 has no check on smoke_kitchen, so it can fire while smoke is still present
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only turns on the air handler when smoke_kitchen == false. You could also make R1's smoke shutdown take priority until the smoke alarm is cleared and someone manually resets it.

explanation: These two rules control different devices and react to unrelated triggers. R3 turns on the kitchen hood when the oven turns on. R2 locks the door when the home goes into away mode. The hood only affects kitchen smoke, and no rule here reacts to smoke, so neither rule can trigger, block or undo the other.
evidence: R3 is triggered by oven.power == on and only changes hood.power
R2 is triggered by home_mode == away and only changes lock_door.lock
The only causal link is hood.power == on clearing smoke_kitchen (sets it to false), and neither rule reads smoke_kitchen or home_mode as a result of the other
hood and lock_door are different devices, so the two rules never send opposing commands to the same device

explanation: At 00:30, R1 turns off the office smart plug. The Wi-Fi router is plugged into that smart plug, so the router loses power too. R2 turns on cloud upload for the garden camera in night mode, but without Wi-Fi the camera can't upload anything. The doorbell also stops sending notifications, so overnight security coverage is quietly lost.
evidence: R1: at 00:30 turn plug_office.power off

explanation: The rules don't show how the hallway camera gets power. If it's plugged into the hallway smart plug, R1 cuts its power at 23:00 every night. That would stop the recording R2 started for away mode, leaving the hallway unmonitored while you're out. If the camera has its own power supply, there's no conflict. The rules don't control the same device setting, so this isn't a logical conflict.
evidence: R1 sets plug_hall.power to off at 23:00 and has no conditions, so it also runs when the home is in away mode.
R2 sets camera_hall.recording to on when home_mode is away, so the camera is expected to keep recording while the home is in away mode.
Both devices are in the hallway, so the camera could plausibly be powered through plug_hall. This is an assumption: the rules don't show how the camera is powered.
If the camera is powered through plug_hall, turning the plug off also stops the camera from recording.
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1 so the hallway plug stays on while the home is in away mode. Alternatively, power the camera from an outlet that isn't switched. Don't let an energy-saving rule turn off the camera.

explanation: R3 locks the front door when the home goes into night mode. R4 unlocks the same door whenever there is motion in the hallway between 22:00 and 06:00. Night mode and that time window usually overlap. So any hallway movement at night, even a resident walking to the bathroom, will unlock the door that night mode just locked, and it stays unlocked overnight.
evidence: R3 sets lock_front.lock := locked when home_mode == night
R4 sets lock_front.lock := unlocked when motion_hall == True during 22:00–06:00
Both rules act on the same device (lock_front) with opposite states
Night mode normally runs during the 22:00–06:00 window, so both rules can fire in the same period
R4 has no check for home mode, who is home, or whether the door is relocked afterward
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only runs when home_mode != night, and make it relock the door automatically after a short delay (for example 2 minutes). Better still, require an explicit action such as an indoor button press or confirmation before unlocking, instead of unlocking on any motion.

explanation: R5 turns off the living room lamp at 23:00. R2 starts recording on the hallway camera when the home is set to away mode. The two rules control different devices, and neither action changes anything the other rule depends on, so they can run together without interfering.
evidence: R5 only changes lamp_living.power (sets it to off).
R2 only changes camera_hall.recording (sets it to on).
The rules control different devices (living room lamp vs. hallway camera) in different rooms.
R5's trigger (the time) and R2's trigger (home_mode) are not changed by either rule's action.
Turning off a lamp in the living room has no stated effect on the hallway camera, its power or its recording.
repair: none

explanation: R1 turns off the hallway smart plug, and R3 locks the front door. They control different devices, and neither action changes the home mode that R3 depends on. Nothing in the home's description says the door lock, or a hub it needs, gets power from the hallway plug, so these two rules don't interfere with each other.
evidence: R1 only controls plug_hall.power (it turns it off at 23:00).

explanation: R1 turns on the living room heater at 18:00, and nothing turns it off or caps the temperature. As the room heats past 26 °C, R2 turns on the fan and opens the window while the heater keeps running. The two rules end up working against each other: the heater warms the room while the fan and open window cool it, which wastes energy and keeps the room from settling at a steady temperature.
evidence: R1 sets heater_living.power := on at 18:00 with no conditions and no temperature limit.
No rule turns heater_living off.
R2 fires when temp_living > 26, which the running heater can cause.
R2 sets vent_living.power := on and window_living.position := open in the same room, while the heater is still on.
repair: Add heater_living.power := off to R2's actions, so the heater stops before the fan and window cool the room. Also add a condition to R1 so it only turns the heater on if temp_living is below a set point, for example 21 °C, and the window is closed.

explanation: R3 turns on the bedroom heater at 21:00. R2 reacts to the living room temperature by turning on the living room fan and opening the living room window. The two rules control different devices in different rooms. R2 only reacts to the living room sensor, and nothing in this home says the bedroom heater affects that sensor or shares power with the fan or window. So neither rule cancels, blocks or unexpectedly sets off the other.
evidence: R3 only controls heater_bedroom.power (bedroom).
R2 only controls vent_living.power and window_living.position (living room).
R2 is triggered by temp_living, the living room temperature, not the bedroom temperature.
No device is controlled by both rules, so their actions can't contradict each other.
No shared power supply or other physical link between the bedroom heater and the living room devices is given.
repair: none

explanation: The two rules never fire at the same moment because their temperature thresholds don't overlap. But R2 opens the window and turns on the fan, and nothing ever closes or switches them off. If it gets cold outside, the open window can cool the room below 19 °C. R4 then turns on the heater while the window is still open and the fan is still running, so the heater fights the cold air, wastes energy and may never warm the room.
evidence: R2 sets window_living.position := open and vent_living.power := on when temp_living > 26
No rule in the set closes window_living or turns off vent_living
An open window and a running fan lower temp_living, which is the variable that triggers R4
R4 sets heater_living.power := on when temp_living < 19 and has no condition about the window or fan state
So the heater can run while the window is open and the fan is on
repair: Change R4 so it first closes window_living and turns off vent_living, then turns on heater_living. Alternatively, add a condition to R4 that window_living is closed, plus a rule that closes the window and stops the fan once temp_living falls below about 24 °C.

explanation: Both rules run at exactly 18:00 and control the same living room heater. R1 has no conditions, so when the home is in away mode, both rules fire at once. R1 turns the heater on and R5 turns it off. The final state depends on which rule runs last, so the heater could end up heating an empty house.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 18:00, no conditions, action heater_living.power := on
R5 trigger: time == 18:00, condition home_mode == away, action heater_living.power := off
Same device (heater_living.power) and same trigger time, with opposite target values
Whenever home_mode == away at 18:00, both rules fire together
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so it only turns the heater on when someone is home. The two rules then can't both fire at the same time.

explanation: At 10:00 R1 starts the robot vacuum. As it moves through the living room, the motion sensor can pick it up as motion. R2 treats that motion as "someone is home" and unlocks the entrance door. This can leave the house unlocked while nobody is there, which is a security risk.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays, a time when people are often away
A robot vacuum moving through the living room can set off the living-room motion sensor
R2 fires on motion_living == True with no other conditions and sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked
R2 does not check whether anyone is actually home or whether the vacuum is cleaning
repair: Add conditions to R2 so it only unlocks when vacuum.mode != cleaning and a reliable presence check confirms a resident is home (for example, a phone geofence). Better still, unlock only on an authenticated action, not on motion alone.

explanation: The robot vacuum starts at 10:00 on weekdays, when people are often out and the home is in away mode. As it moves around the living room, the motion sensor can pick it up as motion. R3 would then sound the alarm, which is a false alarm caused by your own vacuum.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00, with no condition on home_mode
R3 turns alarm.siren on when motion_living == True and home_mode == away
At 10:00 on a weekday, the home is likely to be in away mode
A moving robot vacuum can set off motion sensors in the living room it cleans
repair: Add a condition to R3 so that it ignores living-room motion while vacuum.mode == cleaning. Alternatively, use a pet-immune or zone-limited motion sensor, or have the alarm check a second sensor (for example a door or window contact) before sounding. Keep the alarm itself active.

explanation: At 10:00 the robot vacuum starts cleaning and moves around the house. If it cleans the bedroom, the bedroom motion sensor can pick it up as motion. R4 then turns on the entrance light even though nobody is there, which wastes energy and makes the motion signal unreliable.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 with no conditions, so a moving device runs inside the house.
R4 runs on motion_bedroom == True with no conditions, so it doesn't check whether the motion came from a person.
A robot vacuum normally cleans every room, including the bedroom, so it can set off the bedroom motion sensor.
R4's action (light_entrance.power := on) doesn't depend on the vacuum's state, so motion caused by the vacuum leads straight to the entrance light turning on.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only fires when vacuum.mode != cleaning. Another option is to also require someone to be home (presence detected) before the entrance light turns on.

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door when kitchen smoke is detected so people can get out, but R2 locks the same door whenever the home switches to away mode. If the mode changes to away during or after a smoke event, for example when residents leave or a geofence or schedule switches the mode, R2 locks the door again. That blocks firefighters or anyone still inside. Neither rule checks the other, so they give the door opposite commands.
evidence: R1 sets lock_door.lock := unlocked when smoke_kitchen == True
R2 sets lock_door.lock := locked when home_mode == away
Both rules control the same device (lock_door.lock) with opposite values
Neither rule has a condition that stops it from firing while the other's trigger is active (R1 has none; R2 has none)
If the home switches to away mode after smoke is detected, R2 locks the door during an active smoke event
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only locks when smoke_kitchen == False (and optionally not until some time after the smoke clears). This keeps the smoke evacuation rule in charge of the door.

explanation: R1 turns off the air handler when there is smoke in the kitchen, so smoke doesn't spread. R4 turns the air handler on at 08:00 every day and doesn't check for smoke. If smoke is still present at 08:00, R4 overrides R1's safety shutdown and could spread smoke through the apartment.
evidence: R1 sets hvac.power := off when smoke_kitchen == True
R4 sets hvac.power := on at time == 08:00 with no conditions
Both rules control the same device state (hvac.power) with opposite values
R4 has no check on smoke_kitchen, so it can fire during an active smoke event
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only turns on the air handler when smoke_kitchen == False. Also keep the HVAC locked off until the smoke alarm has been cleared.

explanation: These two rules control different devices and don't affect each other. R3 turns on the range hood when the oven comes on. R2 locks the apartment door when the home switches to away mode. Neither one changes anything the other rule depends on, and there's no hidden physical link between them.
evidence: R3 is triggered by oven.power and acts only on hood.power.
R2 is triggered by home_mode and acts only on lock_door.lock.
No device is acted on by both rules, so they can't give opposite commands.
Turning on the hood doesn't change home_mode, and locking the door doesn't change oven.power, so neither rule can set off or block the other.
No power or physical link between the hood and the door lock is described.

explanation: When night mode starts, R1 turns off the living room power strip. In a studio flat the aquarium is probably in the living room, so the heater may be plugged into that strip. If it is, the heater gets no power all night: R2 can still send 'on' when the water falls below 24 °C, but nothing heats the tank. This conflict only exists if the heater is powered through that strip.
evidence: R1 sets strip_living.power := off whenever home_mode switches to night, with no conditions.
R2 turns on aquarium_heater.power when water_temp < 24, which can happen at night as the room cools.
The home is a studio flat, so the living room is likely the only room and probably where the aquarium is.
The rules don't say where the heater is plugged in. A hidden power dependency through strip_living is plausible but not confirmed.
repair: Power the aquarium heater (and filter) from an outlet that strip_living doesn't control, such as a wall socket or its own smart plug. Or limit R1 to switching off only named non-essential outlets instead of the whole strip.

explanation: R3 turns off the TV plug at night, and R2 turns on the aquarium heater when the water gets cold. They control different devices, and neither one changes anything the other rule depends on. Nothing in this home says the heater is plugged into the TV plug, so turning the plug off won't cut power to the heater.

R2 acts only on aquarium_heater.power (on) and is triggered by water_temp < 24.
No shared device: plug_tv and aquarium_heater are separate actuators.
Turning off a TV plug does not noticeably affect aquarium water temperature, and turning on the heater does not change home_mode.
No stated power dependency (e.g. heater plugged into plug_tv) exists in the home description.

explanation: The two rules work together as a normal thermostat with a gap between the on and off points. R2 turns the heater on only when the water is below 24 °C, and R4 turns it off only when the water is above 28 °C. The water can't be in both ranges at once, so the rules never fight each other. When R2 warms the water, that eventually triggers R4 to switch the heater off, which is what you want.
evidence: R2 fires only when water_temp < 24 and sets aquarium_heater.power := on
R4 fires only when water_temp > 28 and sets aquarium_heater.power := off
The trigger ranges (<24 and >28) never overlap, so both rules can't fire at the same time
The 24–28 °C gap stops the heater from rapidly switching on and off

explanation: R5 turns the aquarium heater off when night mode starts. R2 turns the same heater on whenever the water drops below 24 °C. These two rules can both fire during the night, so the heater could switch on and off over and over. Turning the heater off also makes the water cool down, which makes R2 more likely to fire. If R5 wins, the fish could be left in water that's too cold.
evidence: R5 sets aquarium_heater.power := off when home_mode == night, with no conditions
R2 sets aquarium_heater.power := on when water_temp < 24, with no conditions
Neither rule excludes the other: night mode and water below 24 °C can be true at the same time
R5 turning the heater off lets the water cool, which leads to the water_temp < 24 trigger in R2
repair: Make R2 take priority so the fish stay safe: add the condition water_temp >= 24 to R5, so it only turns the heater off at night when the water is warm enough. Optionally, give R2 a small buffer (for example, on below 23.5 °C and off above 24.5 °C) so the heater doesn't keep switching on and off.

explanation: The garden irrigation probably gets its water through the main water valve, but neither rule says so. When the home is in away mode, R1 closes that valve. R2 still starts watering at 06:00 every day, so the irrigation system runs with no water. The garden doesn't get watered, and a pump or flow controller could run dry or report a fault.
evidence: R1 sets valve_main.state to closed whenever home_mode is away, and nothing in the rules reopens it.
R2 sets irrigation.watering and irrigation.flow to on at 06:00 every day, with no conditions.
R2 doesn't check home mode or the valve state, so it also fires while the house is in away mode.
In a detached house, garden irrigation is usually supplied by the main water line, so it depends on the main valve being open.
repair: Pick one, depending on how the house is plumbed. Option 1: add a condition to R2 so it only waters when valve_main.state is open, or when home_mode is not away. Option 2: if you want watering to continue while you're away, put the irrigation line on its own valve that stays open in away mode, and keep R1 closing the main house supply as it does now.

explanation: R2 turns watering on at 06:00 every day without checking soil moisture, while R4 turns it off when moisture is above 60 %. On a day when the soil is already wet, the two rules set opposite states. If R4 only reacts when moisture first crosses 60 %, it won't fire again and the garden gets overwatered. R4 also turns off only 'watering' and leaves 'flow' on, so the system can end up in a mismatched state.
evidence: R2 sets irrigation.watering := on at 06:00 with no conditions (soil moisture is not checked).
R4 sets irrigation.watering := off when soil_moisture > 60.
Both rules control the same state, irrigation.watering, with opposite values, and both can apply when the soil is already wet at 06:00.
R2 also sets irrigation.flow := on, but R4 never turns irrigation.flow off.
repair: Add the condition 'soil_moisture <= 60' to R2, and add 'irrigation.flow := off' to R4's actions so stopping the watering also stops the water flow.

explanation: The two rules control different devices, but they probably share the same outdoor water supply. If you set the home to away mode, R5 closes the garden valve. R2 will still switch the irrigation on at 06:00, but no water reaches it, so the garden isn't watered while you're away. Neither rule mentions this dependency, which is why it's a physical conflict. If your irrigation runs on a separate water line, there's no conflict.
evidence: R5 sets valve_garden.state to closed whenever home_mode becomes away, and nothing reopens it.
R2 sets irrigation.watering and irrigation.flow to on at 06:00 every day, with no conditions on home mode or valve state.
Neither rule says whether the irrigation is fed by the outdoor tap valve. In a typical detached-house setup it is, so the closed valve blocks the flow.
Being away and the 06:00 time can overlap, for example on holiday, so R2 can fire while R5's closed valve is still in effect.
repair: Change R2 so that at 06:00 it first opens valve_garden, then starts the irrigation, and when watering finishes it closes the valve again if home_mode is away. This keeps the outdoor tap shut while you're away except during the scheduled watering. If you'd rather not water at all while away, add the condition home_mode != away to R2 instead.

explanation: These rules can conflict. On a sunny day, R1 closes the living-room blinds when it gets brighter than 800 lux. With the blinds closed, the room can drop below 150 lux, which makes R2 turn on the ceiling lights in the middle of the day. That wastes energy and works against the reason for closing the blinds. No rule reopens the blinds, so the lights may stay on until someone steps in.
evidence: R1 action: blinds_living.position := closed when lux_living > 800
R2 trigger: lux_living < 150 turns lights_living.power := on
Closing the blinds lowers lux_living, which R2 reads
Neither rule has a condition such as time of day or blind position that stops R2 from firing after R1
No rule reopens the blinds or turns off the lights afterward
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only turns on the lights when blinds_living.position is open, or when it is after sunset. Alternatively, have R1 tilt or partly close the blinds instead of fully closing them, so the room stays above 150 lux.

explanation: Both rules control the living room blinds, but they fire at different fixed times: R3 opens them at 07:30 and R4 closes them at 22:00. They can never fire at the same moment, so they work together as a normal daily open/close schedule rather than a conflict.
evidence: R3 is triggered only at time == 07:30 and sets blinds_living.position to open.
R4 is triggered only at time == 22:00 and sets blinds_living.position to closed.
The two trigger times are 14.5 hours apart and never overlap.
Neither rule has conditions that depend on environmental variables the other rule changes.

explanation: R1 closes the living room blinds when that room is too bright. R5 turns on the study desk light when the study is too dark. The two rules control different devices in different rooms and use separate light sensors. The rules do not control any of the same devices
Closing the living room blinds changes light in the living room, not the study, and no shared space or link between the rooms is described

explanation: These two rules can fight over the living room blinds. R3 opens them at 07:30 no matter what. R1 closes them whenever the room is brighter than 800 lux. On a sunny morning, opening the blinds lets in light. If that pushes the room over 800 lux, R1 closes the blinds right after R3 opened them, so they open and then quickly close again. If the room is already that bright, the two rules simply undo each other.
evidence: R3 sets blinds_living.position := open at 07:30 with no conditions.
R1 sets blinds_living.position := closed when lux_living > 800, also with no conditions.
Both rules control the same device and set opposite states (open vs. closed).
Opening the blinds raises lux_living, which can cause R1 to fire right after R3.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only opens the blinds if the outdoor or room light is below the glare level (for example, a forecast or outdoor lux below 800). Or have R3 open the blinds only partway instead of fully. Also give R1 a hysteresis or cooldown, such as requiring more than 800 lux for 10 minutes, so the blinds don't keep switching back and forth.

explanation: At 20:00, R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which adds moisture to the air. Once humidity goes above 55%, R2 turns on the dehumidifier in the same room. The two devices then run against each other all night. This wastes energy, and the baby's room may end up too damp or too dry depending on which device is stronger.
evidence: R1 turns humidifier_nursery on at 20:00 with no humidity limit.
R2 turns dehumidifier_nursery on whenever humidity_nursery > 55.
Both devices are in the nursery and change the same variable (humidity_nursery) in opposite directions.
Neither rule turns off the other device or checks whether it is running.
repair: Add a humidity limit to the humidifier: run R1 only while nursery humidity is below 50%, and turn the humidifier off when humidity reaches 55%. Also add a condition to R2 so the dehumidifier starts only when the humidifier is off. This way only one device runs at a time and humidity stays around 50–55%.

Humidity can't be above 70 % and below 50 % at once, so the two rules never fire together. The 50–70 % gap stops the fan from switching on and off rapidly. When the fan dries the room, R4 turns it off, which is the intended result and not a hidden side effect.
evidence: R3 trigger: humidity_bath > 70 → fan_bath.power := on
R4 trigger: humidity_bath < 50 → fan_bath.power := off
The trigger ranges (>70 and <50) don't overlap, so the rules can't fire at the same time
The 50–70 % band leaves the fan in its current state, which prevents rapid on/off switching
The fan lowering humidity until R4 fires is the intended on/off cycle

Neither rule cuts power to, or otherwise physically affects, the device the other rule controls.

R5 turns it off at 20:00 for quiet sleep, but if humidity goes above 55 % after that, R2 turns it back on during the night.
