repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs between 07:00 and 20:00. Add a morning rule that turns the dehumidifier on at 07:00 if humidity_nursery > 55. If the device has a quiet or night mode, R5 could switch to that instead of turning it off, so mould protection keeps running overnight.

explanation: In most homes the bedroom wall switch powers the ceiling light, so a smart bulb there gets its power through that switch. When night mode starts, R1 turns the switch off and the bulb loses power. When the alarm rings in the morning, R2 tries to fade the bulb in to 60%, but an unpowered bulb can't receive the command, so the wake-up light silently fails.
evidence: R1 sets switch_bedroom.power to off when home_mode becomes night.
R2 sets bulb_bedroom.power to on and brightness to 60 when alarm_clock rings.
Both devices are in the bedroom, and a smart bulb is usually wired behind the room's wall switch, so the switch controls its power.
Night mode usually lasts through the night, so the alarm normally rings while the switch is still off.
Neither rule turns the switch back on before the bulb is sent its command.
repair: Change R2 so it first turns on switch_bedroom, waits a few seconds for the bulb to reconnect, and then fades bulb_bedroom in to 60%. Another option is to change R1 so it turns off bulb_bedroom itself and leaves the wall switch on.

explanation: Both rules control the corridor bulb, but at different times. R3 turns it off when the home switches to night mode, usually in the evening. R4 turns it on at 06:30. Together they make a normal off-at-night, on-in-the-morning routine. R3 only runs at the moment night mode starts, so it won't turn the light off again after R4 turns it on.
evidence: R3 fires when home_mode changes to night and sets bulb_corridor.power to off
R4 fires at 06:30 and sets bulb_corridor.power to on
Both rules are one-time events with no conditions, so neither keeps the bulb in a set state
Night mode normally starts in the evening, not at 06:30, so the two triggers would almost never happen at the same moment

explanation: R1 and R4 control two different devices: R1 turns off the bedroom wall switch and R4 turns on the corridor bulb. Nothing says the corridor bulb is wired through the bedroom switch, so turning off the switch shouldn't cut power to the bulb. Neither rule changes anything the other one reacts to, so they can run together without interfering.
evidence: R1 acts only on switch_bedroom.power (off) when home_mode becomes night.
R4 acts only on bulb_corridor.power (on) at 06:30.
The two rules control different devices, so their on/off commands can't clash.
R4 is triggered by a time of day. R1 doesn't change the time, and turning on a bulb doesn't change the home mode that R1 reacts to.
Nothing says the corridor bulb gets its power through the bedroom wall switch.

explanation: Both rules control the same thermostat, and their times overlap. At 18:00, R1 sets heating to 23 °C. If someone arrives home between 17:00 and 19:00, R2 sets eco mode at 19 °C. Depending on which rule runs last, the flat ends up warm or cool, and the thermostat may switch back and forth when someone arrives around 18:00.
evidence: R1 fires at 18:00 and sets thermostat.setpoint := 23 and mode := heat
R2 fires when home_mode becomes home during [17:00, 19:00] and sets thermostat.setpoint := 19 and mode := eco
18:00 falls inside R2's 17:00–19:00 window, so both rules can act on the thermostat in the same period
The setpoint values (23 vs 19) and modes (heat vs eco) don't match, and the result depends on which rule runs last
repair: Make the two time windows separate: limit R2 to 17:00–17:59 so R1's 18:00 heating setting isn't overridden afterward. Alternatively, add the condition 'time < 18:00' to R2.

explanation: R3 cools the living room only when it is above 24 °C, and R4 heats it only when it is below 20 °C. These conditions can never both be true, and the rules control different devices. The 4 °C gap between the thresholds stops the cooling from quickly setting off the heating, or the other way round. One possible issue is that neither rule switches its device off again. If that's a concern, you could add rules that turn each device off once the room is back between 20 and 24 °C.
evidence: R3 fires only when temp_living > 24, and R4 fires only when temp_living < 20. The room can't be in both ranges at once.
R3 controls ac_living.mode and R4 controls thermostat.mode, so they act on different devices.
Between 20 and 24 °C neither rule fires, so the cooling and heating don't keep setting each other off.

explanation: R1 and R5 both control the thermostat mode, but they never run at the same time. R1 runs at 18:00 and turns on heating at 23 °C for the evening. R5 runs at 08:00 and switches to eco mode for the day. Together they make a normal day/evening schedule, and neither rule cancels the other or stops it from running.
evidence: R1 triggers only at time == 18:00 and sets thermostat.setpoint := 23 and thermostat.mode := heat.
R5 triggers only at time == 08:00 and sets thermostat.mode := eco.
The two triggers are separate points in time 10 hours apart, so both rules can never fire together.

explanation: When you're away, R1 turns off the garage circuit breaker. That probably also cuts power to the garage exhaust fan and the garage door opener, and possibly to the CO sensor itself. If carbon monoxide builds up while you're away, R2 will still fire, but its commands can't run: the fan stays off, the door stays shut, and the gas isn't vented. This is a safety-critical conflict because the house is empty when it can happen.
evidence: R1 sets breaker_garage.power to off whenever home_mode switches to away.
R2 depends on fan_garage and garage_door, which are both garage devices and probably powered by the garage circuit.
Neither rule has a condition that stops them from applying at the same time, so CO can be detected while the home is in away mode.
Neither rule mentions that the fan and door opener depend on the garage breaker, so this physical link isn't handled.
repair: Move the garage exhaust fan, the garage door opener and the CO sensor onto a circuit that stays on all the time, or that R1 doesn't switch off. As a backup, change R2 so that it first sets breaker_garage.power to on, then turns on the fan and opens the door.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door to vent carbon monoxide, and R3 closes the same door when the home switches to away mode. Neither rule has a condition that stops it from running while the other is active. For example, if a car runs in the garage while the household leaves, R3 could close the door that R2 just opened. That would trap CO inside, next to the house the family shares with the neighbours.
evidence: R2 sets garage_door.position := open when co_garage == True
R3 sets garage_door.position := closed when home_mode == away
R2 and R3 have no conditions, so they can fire at the same time or one after the other
CO can be present when the mode changes to away, for example from a car started in the garage as people leave
Closing the door during a CO event works against R2's safety ventilation
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only closes the garage door when co_garage == False. Also make R2 take priority: while CO is detected, block any close command for the garage door and send the owner a notification instead.

explanation: R4 starts EV charging when the car is parked in the garage. The charger sits in the garage, so it very likely runs on the garage circuit breaker. R1 turns that breaker off whenever the home goes into away mode. If the car is parked and charging (for example, you leave in another car or travel without it), going away cuts the charger's power. The car then won't charge, and R4 wrongly thinks charging is on.
evidence: R1 action: breaker_garage.power := off when home_mode == away
R4 action: ev_charger.charging := on when car_present == True (car parked in the garage)
The EV charger is in the garage, so it probably gets its power from breaker_garage. Neither rule states this link.
Neither rule has a condition that stops both from applying at once. The car can be parked in the garage while the home is in away mode.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only turns off the garage breaker when car_present == False or ev_charger.charging == off. Another option is to move the EV charger to its own circuit that R1 doesn't switch off.

explanation: Both rules run when the car is parked in the garage, but they control different devices: R4 starts the EV charger and R5 turns on the garage light. Neither rule undoes the other, and neither changes anything the other one checks. Nothing in the rules shows that the two devices share a power supply or depend on each other, so they work together without a conflict.
evidence: R4 and R5 share the same trigger: car_present == True
R4 acts only on ev_charger.charging (set to on)
R5 acts only on light_garage.power (set to on)
No device is set to opposite states by the two rules
Neither action changes car_present, and neither rule has extra conditions that the other could affect
No shared circuit or power limit between the charger and the garage light is given

explanation: These two rules can set each other off. Every day at 12:00, R1 dispenses food, and the cat will usually go to the feeder to eat. evidence: R3 only controls heater_bedroom.power (bedroom).
R2 is triggered by temp_living (living room temperature) and controls vent_living and window_living (living room).
No device is controlled by both rules, so they can't give opposite commands.
The bedroom heater shouldn't change the living room temperature, and the living room fan and window don't affect R3's time-based trigger.
Nothing in the setup shows the rules sharing power or wiring.
repair: none

explanation: The two rules never fire at the same moment, because their temperature limits don't overlap. But neither rule ever turns anything back off, so each one can set off the other. R2 opens the window and starts the fan. If it's cold outside, the room can drop below 19 °C, and then R4 turns the heater on while the window is still open and the fan is still running. The heater is never switched off either, so the room can climb back above 26 °C and set off R2 again while the heater keeps running. This wastes energy and makes the temperature swing back and forth.
evidence: R2 triggers on temp_living > 26 and sets vent_living.power := on and window_living.position := open.
R4 triggers on temp_living < 19 and sets heater_living.power := on.
Neither rule closes the window, turns off the fan, or turns off the heater, so these states persist.
An open window and a running fan lower temp_living, which can reach the R4 trigger (< 19 C) and turn the heater on while ventilation is still active.
A heater left on raises temp_living, which can reach the R2 trigger (> 26 C) and open the window while the heater is still on.
repair: Make each rule undo the other's actions. Have R4 close window_living and turn off vent_living before it turns on heater_living. Have R2 turn off heater_living when it opens the window and starts the fan. You can also add stop rules, for example: when the room reaches about 22 °C, close the window, turn off the fan, and turn off the heater.

explanation: Both rules run at 18:00. If the home is in away mode, R1 turns the living room heater on and R5 turns it off at the same moment. The heater's final state then depends on which rule runs last. If R1 wins, the heater runs in an empty house, which wastes energy and could be a safety risk.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 18:00, no conditions, action heater_living.power := on
R5 trigger: time == 18:00, condition home_mode == away, action heater_living.power := off
Both rules act on the same device state (heater_living.power) with opposite values
When home_mode == away, both rules fire at the same moment
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so the heater only turns on at 18:00 when someone is home. R5 then has no competing rule when the house is in away mode.

explanation: At 10:00 on weekdays the robot vacuum starts cleaning. As it moves through the living room, the motion sensor can register it as motion. R2 treats that motion as a sign that someone is home and unlocks the entrance door. Weekday mornings are often when the house is empty, so the front door could be left unlocked with nobody there.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 (weekdays), when occupants are often away
R2 triggers on motion_living == True with no conditions and sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked
A moving robot vacuum can trip a living-room motion sensor, so motion_living becomes True
R2 has no presence check to tell the vacuum apart from a person
repair: Add conditions to R2 so it only unlocks when vacuum.mode != cleaning and a confirmed occupant presence check (e.g., phone geofence) shows someone is home. Better still, never unlock the entrance door based on motion alone.

explanation: The robot vacuum starts at 10:00 on weekdays, which is often when nobody is home and the house is in away mode. As the vacuum moves through the living room, the motion sensor can pick it up as motion. That makes R3 sound the alarm even though there is no intruder.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 with no condition on home_mode or occupancy.
10:00 on a weekday is a typical time for the home to be empty and in away mode.
R3 sets alarm.siren := on when motion_living == True and home_mode == away.
A moving robot vacuum can trigger the living-room motion sensor, setting motion_living to True.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only sounds the siren when vacuum.mode != cleaning, or have it rely on a second confirming sensor such as a door/window contact or camera person detection. Another option is to use pet-immune motion sensing or exclude the vacuum's cleaning area while it runs. The alarm stays fully active at all other times.

explanation: At 10:00 on weekdays R1 starts the robot vacuum, which moves around the house. If it cleans the bedroom, the bedroom motion sensor can pick it up as motion. That would fire R4 and turn on the entrance light when nobody is there, wasting energy and giving a misleading sign that someone is moving around.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays, so the robot vacuum moves through the home
R4 fires on motion_bedroom == True and has no conditions
R4 has no check for whether the vacuum is running, so movement from the vacuum can trigger it
Robot vacuums usually clean whole homes, including bedrooms, which puts them in range of the bedroom motion sensor
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only runs when vacuum.mode != cleaning. Another option is to set the vacuum's map to skip the bedroom, or to stop the motion sensor from reacting to pets or small low objects.

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door when kitchen smoke is detected so people can get out. R2 locks the same door whenever the home switches to away mode, and it doesn't check for smoke. If away mode starts during or right after a smoke event (for example, a geofence or schedule triggers it), R2 re-locks the door that R1 just unlocked. That could block evacuation or keep firefighters out.
evidence: R1 sets lock_door.lock := unlocked when smoke_kitchen == True
R2 sets lock_door.lock := locked when home_mode == away
R2 has no conditions, so nothing stops it from firing while smoke_kitchen is still True
Both rules control the same device state (lock_door.lock) with opposite values, and the result depends on which rule fires last
repair: Add the condition smoke_kitchen == False to R2, so the door only locks in away mode when no smoke is detected. That way the evacuation unlock from R1 always wins while smoke is present.

explanation: If there is kitchen smoke, R1 turns the air handler off so it won't spread smoke around the apartment. R4 has no conditions, so if smoke is still present at 08:00, it turns the air handler back on. That undoes R1's safety action during a fire.
evidence: R1 sets hvac.power := off when smoke_kitchen == True
R4 sets hvac.power := on at time == 08:00 with no conditions
Nothing stops R4 from firing while smoke is still detected, so the two rules give opposite commands to the same device (hvac.power)
repair: Add the condition smoke_kitchen == False to R4, so the air handler only turns on at 08:00 when no smoke is detected. Also have the smoke-emergency state block any automatic restart of the air handler until a person clears the alarm.

explanation: These two rules control different devices and don't affect each other. R3 turns on the range hood when the oven is turned on, and R2 locks the apartment door when the home switches to away mode. Neither action changes anything that would start or block the other rule, and the rules don't mention any shared power or physical link.
evidence: R3 is triggered by oven.power == on and only sets hood.power := on.
R2 is triggered by home_mode == away and only sets lock_door.lock := locked.
The rules act on different devices: the range hood and the door lock.
Turning on the hood doesn't change home_mode, and locking the door doesn't change oven.power, so neither rule can trigger or block the other.
The rules don't state any power or physical dependency between the hood and the door lock.
repair: none

explanation: R1 turns off the office plug at 00:30, and R2 turns on cloud upload and recording for the garden camera when night mode starts. They control different devices, and neither one changes anything the other rule depends on. A conflict could only happen if something the camera needs, like the router or a camera hub, were plugged into the office plug. Nothing in the setup says that.
evidence: R1 only controls plug_office.power (off at 00:30).
R2 only controls camera_garden.cloud_upload and camera_garden.recording (on when home_mode == night).
No rule controls the same device as another rule.
Neither rule changes home_mode or the time, which are the only things that trigger the rules.
Nothing in the setup says the garden camera, router or network equipment is powered through plug_office.
repair: none

explanation: R1 and R3 don't conflict. R1 turns off the office plug at 00:30, and R3 turns on doorbell notifications when the home switches to away mode. They control different devices, and nothing says the doorbell or its notifications depend on the office plug. Neither action changes a temperature, presence or other setting that would set off or block the other rule.
evidence: R1 only acts on plug_office.power (sets it to off) and is triggered by the time 00:30.
R3 only acts on doorbell.notifications (sets them to on) and is triggered by home_mode == away.
No rule says the doorbell is powered by or connected to the office plug.
Turning off the office plug does not change home_mode, and turning on doorbell notifications does not affect the time trigger.

explanation: R4 turns off the desk lamp plug at 00:30, and R2 turns on cloud upload and recording for the garden camera in night mode. They control different devices, and nothing in the rules shows the garden camera is powered through the desk lamp plug. Turning off a desk lamp doesn't change anything that triggers R2, so neither rule gets in the way of the other.
evidence: R4 only acts on plug_desk_lamp.power (sets it to off at 00:30).
R2 only acts on camera_garden.cloud_upload and camera_garden.recording (sets both to on when home_mode == night).
No device is controlled by both rules, so their actions can't clash.
R2 is triggered by home_mode, which R4's action doesn't change.
The setup doesn't say the garden camera draws power from the desk lamp plug, so there's no hidden physical link.
repair: none

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R4 only turns off the desk lamp plug at 00:30, and R3 only turns on doorbell notifications when the home switches to away mode. They control different devices and don't change any shared setting like light, presence or home mode. Nothing says the doorbell gets its power from the desk lamp plug.
evidence: R4 acts only on plug_desk_lamp.power (sets it to off) at 00:30.
R3 acts only on doorbell.notifications (sets it to on) when home_mode == away.
No rule changes home_mode or time, so neither rule can trigger the other or stop it from running.
Nothing in the home description says the doorbell is plugged into the desk lamp plug.
repair: none

explanation: The rules don't say how the aquarium heater gets power. In a studio flat, the aquarium is probably in the living area and plugged into the living room power strip. If so, R1 cuts power to the strip every night, and R2 can switch the heater 'on' while it still gets no power. The water would then cool overnight and could harm the fish. If the heater is on a different outlet, there's no conflict, but it's worth checking.
evidence: The home is a studio flat, so there is a single main living space where the aquarium is likely located.
R1 switches strip_living.power off whenever home_mode becomes night, with no exceptions.
R2 relies on aquarium_heater.power being able to turn on whenever water_temp < 24 C, including at night.
Neither rule says which outlet or strip powers the aquarium heater, so it may be plugged into the strip.
repair: Plug the aquarium heater into a separate outlet that is always on, not the living room strip, or use a smart strip that lets you exclude the heater's socket from R1's night-mode shut-off. You could also add a condition to R1 so the strip stays on while the heater needs power.

explanation: R3 only turns off the TV plug when night mode starts. R2 only turns on the aquarium heater when the water gets too cold. They control different devices, and neither one changes anything the other rule checks. Nothing says the heater is powered through the TV plug, so turning that plug off shouldn't affect the heater.
evidence: R3 acts only on plug_tv.power (off), triggered by home_mode == night.
R2 acts only on aquarium_heater.power (on), triggered by water_temp < 24.
No rule sets home_mode or affects water_temp in a way that would trigger or block the other rule.
No stated physical dependency (e.g., the aquarium heater drawing power through plug_tv).
repair: none

explanation: R2 and R4 can never fire at the same time because the water can't be below 24 °C and above 28 °C at once. Together they work like a normal thermostat: the heater turns on below 24 °C and off above 28 °C. The 4 °C gap between the two stops the heater from switching on and off too often. When the heater warms the water enough for R4 to turn it off, that's the intended behavior, not a conflict.
evidence: R2 fires only when water_temp < 24 and sets aquarium_heater.power to on
R4 fires only when water_temp > 28 and sets aquarium_heater.power to off
The two triggers can't both be true at once, so the rules can't give opposite commands at the same moment
The 24–28 °C gap means the heater won't keep switching on and off around a single temperature
Neither rule has extra conditions that could make their triggers overlap
repair: none

explanation: R5 and R2 give opposite commands to the same aquarium heater, and both can fire on the same night. Night mode turns the heater off. With no heating, the water cools below 24 °C, and R2 turns the heater back on. The heater may then go back and forth, and whichever rule fired last decides whether the fish are kept warm.
evidence: R5 sets aquarium_heater.power := off when home_mode == night, with no conditions
R2 sets aquarium_heater.power := on when water_temp < 24, with no conditions
Both rules act on the same device (aquarium_heater.power) with opposite values
Night mode can last for hours, and turning the heater off lets the water cool, which makes R2's trigger (water_temp < 24) likely during that time
repair: Add a condition to R5 so it only turns the heater off when water_temp >= 25 (above R2's 24 °C threshold, to leave some margin). Then the water temperature always wins over the quiet-night setting, and the heater stays on whenever the fish need heat.

explanation: The garden irrigation in a detached house is usually fed from the main water line. When you are away, R1 closes the main water valve. R2 still turns on watering at 06:00, but no water can reach the garden. The irrigation system then runs dry, so the garden goes unwatered and the pump or valves may be stressed. Neither rule mentions that the irrigation depends on the main valve.
evidence: R1 sets valve_main.state to closed whenever home_mode switches to away, and nothing reopens it while you are away.
R2 sets irrigation.watering and irrigation.flow to on at 06:00 every day, with no conditions.
In a typical detached house, the irrigation is supplied by the main water line, downstream of the main valve.
Nothing stops a 06:00 trigger from happening while the home is in away mode, so both rules can be active at once.
repair: Add a condition to R2 that only starts watering when valve_main.state is open. If the garden should still be watered while you are away, connect the irrigation to its own supply line or valve that R1 does not close.

explanation: R2 and R4 give opposite commands to the same irrigation watering state. R2 doesn't check soil moisture, so it turns watering on at 06:00 even if the soil is already above 60%. Because R4 only fires when moisture crosses 60%, it may never fire again, and the garden gets overwatered. If it does fire, the two rules toggle the system on and off. R4 also turns off only 'watering' and never 'flow', so water can keep flowing after watering is 'stopped'.
evidence: R2 sets irrigation.watering := on at 06:00 with no conditions
R4 sets irrigation.watering := off when soil_moisture > 60
Both rules act on the same device state (irrigation.watering) with opposite values
R2 has no soil-moisture check, so it can run when moisture is already above 60%
R4 is triggered by a threshold, so it may not fire again if moisture is already above 60% when R2 starts
R2 turns on irrigation.flow, but R4 never turns it off
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when soil_moisture <= 60. Also have R4 set irrigation.flow := off together with irrigation.watering := off.

explanation: When the home is in away mode, R5 closes the outdoor tap valve. In a detached house, the garden irrigation is normally supplied through that valve. R2 has no condition on home mode, so it still starts watering at 06:00 while the valve is closed. The system would then report that it is watering, but no water would reach the garden. Running the pump or flow against a closed valve may also cause dry-running or a pressure fault.
evidence: R5 sets valve_garden.state := closed when home_mode == away.
R2 sets irrigation.watering := on and irrigation.flow := on at 06:00 every day, with no conditions.
R2 does not check home_mode or the valve state, so it can fire while away mode is active and the valve is closed.
Neither rule mentions that the irrigation water comes through the outdoor tap valve (valve_garden), so this dependency is hidden.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only starts watering when valve_garden.state == open. If you want the garden watered while you are away, let R2 open the valve before watering and close it again when watering ends.

explanation: When strong sunlight pushes the living room above 800 lux, R1 closes the blinds. Closing the blinds can drop the room below 150 lux, and R2 then turns on the ceiling lights during a sunny day. That wastes energy and works against what R1 was meant to do. If the lights also push the brightness back up, the two rules could keep firing in response to each other.
evidence: R1 action blinds_living.position := closed lowers the living room's light level (lux_living).
R2 is triggered by lux_living < 150, the same sensor that R1's action affects.
Neither rule has a condition, such as time of day, outdoor light or blind state, that keeps R2 from firing after R1 closes the blinds.
Both rules are in the same room (living room) of the townhouse.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only turns on the lights when it is actually dark outside, for example after sunset or when an outdoor light sensor reads below a threshold. Another option is to skip turning on the lights while the blinds are closed and the outdoor light level is high.

explanation: Both rules control the living room blinds, but at different times. R3 opens them at 07:30 and R4 closes them at 22:00. They can never run at the same moment, so the blinds won't get conflicting commands. Together they make a normal daily open-and-close schedule.
evidence: R3 fires only at time == 07:30 and sets blinds_living.position := open
R4 fires only at time == 22:00 and sets blinds_living.position := closed
The trigger times are different and never overlap, so the two actions can't happen at once
Neither rule has conditions that the other rule's action could change
repair: none

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R1 closes the living room blinds when that room is bright, and R5 turns on the study desk light when the study is dark. They control different devices and read different light sensors. Nothing in the home description says closing the living room blinds changes the study's light level.
evidence: R1 reads lux_living and controls only blinds_living.position.
R5 reads lux_study and controls only lights_study.power.
The two rules never act on the same device, so they can't give opposite commands to one device.
Nothing says the study gets light through the living room blinds, or that the study light affects the living room sensor.
repair: none

explanation: Both rules control the living room blinds and give opposite commands: R3 opens them at 07:30 and R1 closes them when it is brighter than 800 lux. On a sunny morning, opening the blinds lets in enough daylight to push the room over 800 lux, so R1 closes them again soon after. That undoes R3's opening and can make the blinds open and close repeatedly.
evidence: R3 sets blinds_living.position := open at 07:30 with no conditions
R1 sets blinds_living.position := closed whenever lux_living > 800, with no conditions
Both rules act on the same device (blinds_living) with opposite target states
Opening the blinds raises lux_living, which can directly trigger R1 right after R3 runs
Neither rule has a condition or time window that keeps them from firing at the same time
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only closes the blinds if they have been open for at least 30 minutes or the time is after 10:00. Also stop R1 from running again until lux_living drops below a lower value such as 600 lux, so the blinds don't flip back and forth.

explanation: At 20:00, R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which pushes the room's humidity up. Once humidity goes above 55 %, R2 turns on the dehumidifier in the same room. Nothing turns the humidifier off, so both machines end up running against each other all night. This wastes energy, and the baby's room won't stay at either the humidity you want for sleep or the level that prevents mould.
evidence: R1 sets humidifier_nursery.power := on at 20:00, with no conditions and no off action
Running a humidifier raises humidity_nursery
R2 fires when humidity_nursery > 55 and sets dehumidifier_nursery.power := on
Both devices are in the same room (the nursery), and neither rule checks or turns off the other device
repair: Make the two rules work together: add a condition to R1 so it only runs while humidity_nursery < 50 and the dehumidifier is off, and change R2 so it first turns the humidifier off when humidity goes above 55 %. Turn the dehumidifier on only if humidity is still high after that. The gap between 50 % and 55 % stops the devices from switching back and forth.

explanation: R3 and R4 don't conflict. They form a normal on/off pair with a gap between their thresholds. The fan turns on above 70% humidity and off below 50%. Humidity can't be above 70% and below 50% at once, so the two rules never fire together. The fan lowering the humidity until R4 switches it off is the intended behaviour, not a side effect.
evidence: R3 fires only when humidity_bath > 70; R4 fires only when humidity_bath < 50, so the triggers can't both be true at the same time.
The gap between 50% and 70% stops the fan from rapidly switching on and off around a single threshold.
R3's action (the fan running) lowers bathroom humidity, which eventually fires R4. This is the expected cycle and doesn't override or block another rule.
No other rule acts on fan_bath, and no power dependency is stated.
repair: none

explanation: R1 turns on the humidifier in the nursery, and R3 turns on the bathroom fan when the bathroom gets humid. The two rules control different devices in different rooms. The humidifier only adds moisture to the nursery, so it shouldn't push the bathroom sensor over 70 %. Neither rule undoes or blocks the other.
evidence: R1 only controls humidifier_nursery.power and turns it on at 20:00.
R3 only controls fan_bath.power and is triggered by humidity_bath > 70.
The two rules share no device and never set opposite states.
The humidifier is in the nursery and the trigger sensor is in the bathroom, so it is unlikely to affect bathroom humidity.
No shared power supply or other physical link between the devices is stated.
repair: none

explanation: Both rules control the nursery dehumidifier's power, and they can work against each other. At 20:00, R5 turns the dehumidifier off for quiet sleep. But R2 has no time limit, so if nursery humidity goes above 55% during the night, R2 turns it back on and undoes R5. If humidity is already high at 20:00, the device may switch off and then straight back on.
evidence: R2 sets dehumidifier_nursery.power := on whenever humidity_nursery > 55, with no conditions or time window.
R5 sets dehumidifier_nursery.power := off at 20:00, with no conditions.
Both rules act on the same device state (dehumidifier_nursery.power), with opposite values (on vs. off).
Nursery humidity can go above 55% after 20:00, for example from a sleeping child's breathing or a damp ground-floor flat. That would fire R2 during the quiet period R5 is meant to protect.
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs between 07:00 and 20:00. To keep mould under control, also add a daytime rule that runs the dehumidifier before bedtime, for example from 18:00 to 20:00 if humidity is above 50%. If the dehumidifier has a quiet or low-fan night mode, use that at night instead of turning it off completely.

explanation: R1 turns off the bedroom wall switch in night mode, and that switch most likely powers the bedroom smart bulb. When the wake-up alarm rings, R2 tries to turn the bulb on at 60%, but the bulb has no power and can't respond. Neither rule turns the switch back on, so the wake-up light will most likely fail.
evidence: R1 sets switch_bedroom.power := off when home_mode == night
R2 sets bulb_bedroom.power := on and brightness := 60 when alarm_clock == True
The switch and the bulb are in the same room, and a bedroom wall switch usually feeds the ceiling light circuit (a dependency the rules don't state)
Night mode normally lasts until the morning alarm, and no rule turns switch_bedroom back on before R2 fires
repair: Change R2 so it first sets switch_bedroom.power := on, waits a few seconds for the bulb to reconnect, then sets bulb_bedroom.power := on and brightness := 60. Alternatively, have R1 turn off bulb_bedroom instead of cutting power at the wall switch.

explanation: R3 turns the corridor bulb off when the home switches into night mode, and R4 turns it on at 06:30. Both control the same bulb, but they fire at different moments, so together they make a normal 'off at night, on in the morning' routine. They don't keep undoing each other. One thing to check: R4 ignores the home mode, so if the flat is still in night mode at 06:30, the bulb will turn on anyway.
evidence: R3 is triggered by the event home_mode switching to night and sets bulb_corridor.power := off
R4 is triggered by time == 06:30 and sets bulb_corridor.power := on
The two triggers are separate events and won't normally fire at the same moment
Neither rule has conditions that make it fire again or keep forcing the bulb's state
repair: none

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R1 turns off the bedroom wall switch when night mode starts, and R4 turns on the corridor bulb at 06:30. They control different devices, and nothing in this home says the corridor bulb gets its power from the bedroom switch. Neither rule changes anything the other rule depends on.
evidence: R1 acts only on switch_bedroom.power (off).
R4 acts only on bulb_corridor.power (on).
No stated wiring dependency between switch_bedroom and bulb_corridor (corridor bulb is not fed by the bedroom switch).
R1 is triggered by home_mode; R4 is triggered by time; neither action changes the other's trigger.

explanation: Both rules control the same thermostat, and R2's 17:00–19:00 window includes R1's 18:00 trigger. If someone arrives between 17:00 and 18:00, R2 sets eco at 19 °C, and then R1 changes it to heat at 23 °C at 18:00. If someone arrives between 18:00 and 19:00, R2 undoes R1's 23 °C and goes back to 19 °C eco. The thermostat ends up in whichever state the most recent rule set, so the result depends on arrival time.
evidence: R1 sets thermostat.setpoint := 23 and thermostat.mode := heat at 18:00 with no conditions.
R2 sets thermostat.setpoint := 19 and thermostat.mode := eco when home_mode becomes home during 17:00–19:00.
18:00 falls inside R2's window, so both rules can fire on the same evening and set different setpoints and modes.
repair: Make R2's window end before R1 fires, e.g. 17:00–17:59. Also add a condition to R1 so it only runs when home_mode == home. Then the 18:00 comfort setting always wins and arrivals after 18:00 won't drop it back to eco.

explanation: R3 cools only when the living room is above 24 °C, and R4 heats only when it is below 20 °C, so they can never fire at the same time. They also control different devices (the air conditioner vs. the thermostat). The 4 °C gap between 20 °C and 24 °C keeps the system from switching rapidly between heating and cooling.
evidence: R3 trigger: temp_living > 24; R4 trigger: temp_living < 20 — the trigger ranges do not overlap
R3 acts on ac_living.mode, R4 acts on thermostat.mode — different devices, so there are no opposing commands to the same device
Neither rule has conditions that depend on the other rule's action
The 20–24 °C range where neither rule fires prevents immediate back-and-forth switching
repair: none

explanation: Both rules change the thermostat, but at different times: R1 at 18:00 and R5 at 08:00. They can never run at the same moment, and neither one changes anything that would start or block the other. Together they make a normal daily cycle: heat to 23 °C in the evening and eco mode in the morning.
evidence: R1 runs only at 18:00 and sets thermostat.setpoint to 23 and thermostat.mode to heat.
R5 runs only at 08:00 and sets thermostat.mode to eco.
The two trigger times are different, so the actions never happen at the same time.
Neither rule has a condition based on temperature, presence or any other value the other rule changes, so there is no semantic chain.
No power or other physical dependency between devices is involved, since both rules only change the thermostat's own settings.
repair: none

explanation: When the home goes into away mode, R1 switches off the garage circuit breaker. The garage exhaust fan and garage door opener most likely run on that circuit. If carbon monoxide builds up in the garage while you're away, R2 will tell the fan to turn on and the door to open, but neither device will have power. The garage won't be ventilated during a CO emergency.
evidence: R1 sets breaker_garage.power to off whenever home_mode becomes away, with no conditions.
R2 uses fan_garage and garage_door, which are garage devices and probably powered by the garage breaker.
R2 has no conditions, so it can fire in away mode, after R1 has already cut garage power.
Neither rule mentions that the two depend on the same power circuit, so the dependency is hidden.
repair: Move the garage exhaust fan, the garage door opener and the CO sensor to a separate circuit that is always on, so R1 doesn't cut their power. Also add a safety step: if co_garage is True, switch breaker_garage back on before turning on the fan and opening the door, and don't switch the breaker off while CO is detected.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door to let carbon monoxide out, and R3 closes the same door when the home switches to away mode. Neither rule has a condition that stops it from running while the other is active. For example, if you leave while CO is still present, or someone starts a car and leaves, R3 can close the door during a CO event. That traps the gas in the garage and undoes the safety action.
evidence: R2 sets garage_door.position := open when co_garage == True
R3 sets garage_door.position := closed when home_mode == away

explanation: During a frost warning, R1 turns on the greenhouse heater. Once the heater pushes the greenhouse above 18 °C, R2 opens the roof vent. Warm air then escapes into the freezing night, so the heater and vent work against each other. This wastes energy, and the temperature can swing down and back up, which may undermine the frost protection.

R2 is triggered by temp_gh > 18, a value the heater can reach
R2 opens gh_vent with no condition about frost or the heater being on
R1 fires during frost_warning == True, when outside air is near freezing, so an open vent loses heat quickly
repair: Add conditions to R2 so the vent only opens when frost_warning == False and gh_heater.power == off. Another option is to raise R2's threshold above the heater's target temperature while a frost warning is active.

explanation: These two rules can conflict if the greenhouse heater gets its power from the outdoor plug. That's likely on a farmhouse, but the rules don't say so. Even if the plug is off before the warning arrives, R1 will set the heater to on, but it still won't get any power. Either way, your plants are unprotected exactly when you need the heater.

Neither rule checks the other, and nothing turns plug_outdoor back on when a frost warning is active.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only switches off plug_outdoor when frost_warning == False. Also add plug_outdoor.power := on to R1, before it turns the heater on. If the heater isn't actually on the outdoor plug, you can ignore this conflict.

Neither rule cuts power to a device the other rule needs.

Neither rule turns off or cuts power to a device the other rule relies on.

explanation: When the robot vacuum starts at 10:00 on a weekday and moves around the living room, the living-room motion sensor can pick it up. evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode to cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays, a time when people are often away from home.

repair: Add conditions to R2 so it only unlocks the door when vacuum.mode is not 'cleaning' and a trusted presence signal (such as a resident's phone or a person-detection sensor) confirms someone is actually home. Motion alone shouldn't unlock the door.

explanation: R1 starts the robot vacuum at 10:00 on weekdays, when the house is often empty and set to away mode. If the vacuum moves through the living room, the motion sensor may pick it up. R3 would then treat that as an intruder and sound the siren, which is a false alarm.

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door when kitchen smoke is detected so people can get out. R2 locks the same door whenever the home switches to away mode, and it doesn't check for smoke. repair: Add a condition to R2: smoke_kitchen == False. This way, away mode can't lock the door while smoke is detected. As an option, R2 could lock the door only after the smoke has cleared.

explanation: R1 turns off the air handler when there is smoke in the kitchen, so smoke isn't blown through the apartment. R4 turns the air handler back on at 08:00 and checks nothing else first. repair: Add the condition smoke_kitchen == False to R4, so the air handler only turns on at 08:00 when no smoke is detected.

R2 has no soil-moisture check, so at 06:00 it can fire while moisture is already above 60 %
R4 does not reset irrigation.flow, so flow can stay on after watering is switched off
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only starts watering when soil_moisture <= 60, and make R4 also set irrigation.flow := off.

repair: Make the watering rule check the valve. Add a condition to R2: valve_garden.state == open. Or, if you want watering to continue while you're away, have R2 open valve_garden just before 06:00 and let R5 close it again once watering is done.

explanation: When sunlight makes the living room brighter than 800 lux, R1 closes the blinds. R2 sets it to 19 °C in eco mode whenever someone arrives between 17:00 and 19:00. If someone gets home between 18:00 and 19:00, R2 undoes R1's setting. If someone arrives just before 18:00, R1 then overrides the eco setting. Which temperature you end up with depends on who acted last.
evidence: R1 sets thermostat.setpoint := 23 and thermostat.mode := heat at time == 18:00
R2 sets thermostat.setpoint := 19 and thermostat.mode := eco when home_mode == home
R2's condition window [17:00, 19:00] contains R1's trigger time 18:00
Both rules act on the same device and settings (thermostat setpoint and mode) with different values
repair: Make the time windows not overlap. For example, limit R2 to arrivals between 17:00 and 17:59 so the 18:00 comfort setting in R1 always wins after that. Or add a condition to R2 so it doesn't run if R1 has already fired today.

explanation: The two triggers can't fire together because the room can't be above 24 °C and below 20 °C at once. The problem is that neither rule ever switches its device back off. After R3 puts the AC into cooling, the AC keeps cooling until the room drops below 20 °C. Then R4 turns on heating while the AC is still cooling, so the two devices fight each other, waste energy, and can keep swinging the temperature between the two limits.
evidence: R3 sets ac_living.mode to cool when temp_living > 24, and nothing ever sets it back.
R4 sets thermostat.mode to heat when temp_living < 20, and nothing ever sets it back.
Both devices change the same thing: the living room temperature (temp_living).
The AC's cooling can bring temp_living below 20, which fires R4 while the AC is still cooling. Heating can then push the room above 24, which fires R3 again.
repair: Have each rule switch the other device off before starting its own. R3 also sets thermostat.mode to off when it starts cooling, and R4 also sets ac_living.mode to off when it starts heating. Better still, also stop each device once the room is back in a comfortable range, for example AC off below 22 °C and heating off above 22 °C.

explanation: Both rules control the thermostat, but they run at different set times (18:00 and 08:00), so they never fire together. R1 turns on 23 °C heating in the evening and R5 switches to eco mode in the morning. Together they make a normal daily schedule, not opposing commands.
evidence: R1 fires only at time == 18:00 and sets thermostat.setpoint := 23 and thermostat.mode := heat.
R5 fires only at time == 08:00 and sets thermostat.mode := eco.
The two time triggers never happen at the same moment, so the actions can't clash.
Neither rule has conditions based on temperature or other conditions in the home, so one rule's action can't make the other fire or block it.
repair: none

explanation: When you leave home, R1 turns off the garage circuit breaker. The garage exhaust fan and the garage door opener are very likely powered by that circuit. If carbon monoxide is then detected (for example, a car left running or a faulty appliance), R2 tries to start the fan and open the door, but neither has power. The garage CO sensor may also lose power if it's wired to the same circuit. Your CO safety response would silently fail when nobody is home to notice.
evidence: R1 sets breaker_garage.power to off whenever home_mode becomes away.
R2 relies on fan_garage and garage_door in the garage, which are most likely powered by the garage circuit.
The rules have no conditions that keep them apart, so CO can be detected while the home is in away mode and the breaker is off.
R2 is a life-safety response for carbon monoxide, so if it fails, the gas can build up and spread into the house next to the garage.
repair: Don't cut power to the whole garage circuit in away mode. Either move the exhaust fan, garage door opener and CO sensor onto a circuit that always stays on, or change R1 so it only switches off the specific non-essential garage outlets. If that can't be done, add a rule: when co_garage == True, turn breaker_garage.power back on before R2's actions run, and send an alert to the owner.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door when carbon monoxide is detected so the gas can escape. R3 closes the same door whenever the home switches to away mode, and nothing stops it from running while CO is still present. If both happen at once, for example when you leave while a car is idling, the door could be shut and trap the CO inside. That defeats the safety ventilation.
evidence: R2 sets garage_door.position := open when co_garage == True
R3 sets garage_door.position := closed when home_mode == away
R3 has no conditions, so it does not check co_garage
Both rules control the same device (garage_door) and can be active at the same time
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only closes the garage door when co_garage == False. While CO is present, R3 should keep the door open and send a notification instead.

explanation: R4 starts EV charging when the car is parked in the garage, and the charger most likely runs on the garage circuit. R1 turns off the garage breaker whenever the home switches to away mode. If the house goes into away mode while the car is in the garage (for example, you leave on foot, by taxi or in a second car), the charger loses power and charging stops without warning. The car may not be charged when you need it. Neither rule mentions this power link, so it is a hidden physical dependency.

R4 action: ev_charger.charging := on when car_present == True (car in garage)

The car being present and the home being in away mode can both be true at once, because nothing in either rule rules this out
repair: Add a condition to R1 so the garage breaker only switches off when the EV charger is not charging (ev_charger.charging == off), or when car_present == False. Another option is to wire the EV charger to its own circuit that is not controlled by breaker_garage.

Neither rule undoes what the other does. Turning on the light doesn't change anything R4 depends on, and charging doesn't change anything R5 depends on. The rules don't mention any shared power supply or other physical link between the two devices, so they work well together.

explanation: At noon, R1 puts out food for the cat. If the feeder is in or near the kitchen, the cat will go there to eat. The kitchen motion sensor can pick up the cat, and if the home is in away mode, R2 treats it as an intruder and sounds the siren. Because R1 runs every day whether you're home or not, this false alarm can happen around noon on any day you're away.

R2 fires on motion_kitchen == True when home_mode == away and turns on alarm.siren.

In a loft apartment the kitchen is usually open to the living space, so the cat walking to or eating at the feeder is likely to be seen by the kitchen motion sensor.
repair: Keep the alarm active but make it ignore the cat. Use a pet-immune motion sensor, or point the kitchen sensor away from the feeder. You could also add a condition to R2 that skips kitchen motion for about 30 minutes after R1 dispenses, as long as no door or window sensor is triggered in that time.

explanation: R1 controls the cat feeder and R3 controls the kitchen camera. They act on different devices, so their actions can't contradict each other. At most, if the feeder is in the kitchen, the cat coming to eat could set off the motion sensor and start a recording. That would be harmless and is what the camera rule is for anyway.
evidence: R1 sets feeder.dispensing to on at 12:00 every day.
R3 sets camera_kitchen.recording to on when motion_kitchen becomes True.
The two rules control different devices (feeder and camera_kitchen).
Dispensing food doesn't change motion_kitchen or anything else R3 depends on, and recording doesn't affect R1's time trigger.

In an open-plan loft, the moving parts of the cleaning cycle, or the cat moving around because of it, can be picked up by the living room motion sensor. That would make R5 sound the siren with no intruder present. Whether this happens depends on whether the sensor can see the litter box, which the rules don't say.

explanation: At 10:00, R2 opens the living room window no matter what the weather is like. On a warm day, warm outside air comes in and pushes the room above 27 °C, which makes R1 switch the AC to cooling. The AC then tries to cool a room with an open window. That wastes energy and the room may never get cool enough. Also, if the AC is already cooling when the window opens at 10:00, the open window works against it.
evidence: R1 sets ac_living.mode to cool whenever temp_living > 27 C, with no conditions.

Also add a condition to R1 so it only starts cooling when window_living is closed. Optionally, send a notification asking someone to close the window instead.

explanation: R2 and R6 give opposite commands to the living room window. If the AC starts cooling before 10:00, R6 closes the window. Then at 10:00, R2 opens it again even though the AC is still cooling, and nothing closes it afterwards. If both rules fire at about 10:00, the window may end up open or closed depending on which runs last. Either way, the AC can end up cooling with the window open, which wastes energy.
evidence: R2 sets window_living.position := open at 10:00 with no conditions
R6 sets window_living.position := closed when ac_living.mode == cool
Both rules act on the same device (window_living) with opposite values
R2 does not check whether the AC is currently cooling, so both can apply at the same time
R6 fires only when the AC changes to cool, so it will not close the window again after R2 reopens it

explanation: The two rules control different devices, so they don't contradict each other directly. The risk comes from wiring that the rules don't mention. A home NAS usually sits in a closet and is plugged into a power strip there. If this NAS is powered from the closet strip, night mode (R2) cuts its power, and at 01:00 the backup (R1) either can't start or gets cut off partway, which can corrupt the backup or the NAS disks. This is likely because night mode is normally already on at 01:00.
evidence: R2 sets strip_closet.power to off when home_mode becomes night, with no conditions.
R1 sets nas.backup to running at 01:00 every night, with no conditions.
Night mode is normally already on at 01:00, so the strip is off when the backup is meant to run.
The rules don't say what the NAS is plugged into. A NAS on a closet power strip is a common setup, and in that case R2 cuts the power R1 needs.
Neither rule checks the other: R2 doesn't check whether a backup is running, and R1 doesn't check whether the strip has power.
repair: Check which outlet the NAS uses. If it is on the closet strip, move it to an outlet that is always on, or add a condition to R2 so the strip only turns off when nas.backup is not running. You could also have R1 turn the strip on (strip_closet.power := on) before it starts the backup.

explanation: Both rules control devices in the closet. If the closet cooling fan is plugged into the closet power strip, which is likely given where they are, R2 cuts the fan's power whenever the home goes into night mode. After that, R3 can still send 'fan on' when the closet goes above 35 °C, but the fan has no power and won't run. The closet could then overheat overnight without anyone noticing. This depends on how the fan is wired: the rules don't say whether it's on the strip. If it isn't, there's no conflict.
evidence: R2 turns off strip_closet.power when home_mode == night, with no conditions.
R3 relies on fan_closet.power := on when temp_closet > 35, and has no time or mode limit.
Both devices are in the closet, so the fan is likely powered through strip_closet. The rules don't say how it's wired.
Night mode and high closet temperature can happen at the same time, because nothing in the rules prevents it.
repair: Plug the closet fan into an outlet that is always on and not controlled by strip_closet. If you can't, add a condition to R2 so it only turns off the strip when temp_closet <= 35, and have R3 also turn the strip back on (strip_closet.power := on) before turning on the fan.

explanation: R1 and R3 don't conflict. They control different devices (the NAS and the closet fan), so they can't give opposite commands to the same device. If the NAS sits in the closet, the backup could warm it up and switch on the fan. That would be the fan doing its job, not one rule blocking or undoing the other.
evidence: R1 only sets nas.backup to running at 01:00.
R3 only sets fan_closet.power to on when temp_closet is above 35 C.
No device is controlled by both rules, and neither rule turns anything off.
Any heat from the backup would only cause R3 to cool the closet, which helps rather than conflicts.

explanation: R4 turns off the printer's smart plug in night mode, and R1 starts the NAS backup at 01:00. They control different devices with different actions. Nothing here says the NAS is powered through the printer plug, and turning off the printer doesn't change anything that R1 depends on. Both rules can run without affecting each other.
evidence: R4 acts only on plug_printer.power (off) when home_mode == night.

explanation: If the teenager comes home between 23:00 and 06:00, R1 unlocks the front door. That unlock then sets off R2, which locks the door again right away. explanation: Both rules control the driveway gate, but they run at different times: R3 closes it at 22:00 and R4 opens it at 07:00. They can never fire at the same moment, so together they form a normal daily routine (closed at night, open during the day) and don't conflict.

The two trigger times are different, so the rules never fire together
Neither rule changes anything that could trigger or block the other

explanation: R1 can't tell a crying baby from the white-noise speaker. It only checks whether the nursery is louder than 60 dB. Change R2 so that when humidity goes above 55 %, it turns the humidifier off first and only turns on the dehumidifier if humidity stays above 55 % while the humidifier is off. Also give R1 a humidity limit: only turn the humidifier on if humidity is below about 50 %, and turn it off when it reaches about 50 %.

explanation: R3 and R4 work together as an on/off pair with a gap between their thresholds. The fan turns on above 70% humidity and turns off below 50%. Humidity can't be above 70% and below 50% at the same moment, so the two rules never fire together. When the fan lowers humidity enough to set off R4, that's the intended result, not an unexpected side effect. The 20-point gap also stops the fan from rapidly switching on and off.
evidence: R3 trigger: humidity_bath > 70 → fan_bath.power := on

Neither rule affects the nursery humidifier, nursery dehumidifier or towel_heater

explanation: R2 turns the nursery dehumidifier on when humidity is above 55%, and R5 turns the same dehumidifier off at 20:00. If the nursery is humid at 20:00, R5 turns it off and undoes R2's mould protection. Once it's off, humidity can climb past 55% again, so R2 turns it back on during the night. That is exactly what R5 was meant to prevent. The two rules can keep switching the device on and off.

R5 sets dehumidifier_nursery.power := off at 20:00, with no humidity condition

repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs between 07:00 and 20:00, so R2 can't turn the dehumidifier back on at night. Add a morning rule: at 07:00, if humidity_nursery > 55, turn the dehumidifier on. Before choosing this, check how high the humidity actually gets overnight, because mould is still a risk.

explanation: The bedroom bulb is wired behind the bedroom wall switch. At night, R1 turns that switch off, which cuts the bulb's power. Nothing turns the switch back on, so in the morning R2's commands to turn the bulb on at 60% reach a bulb with no power, and the wake-up light doesn't come on.

repair: Change R2 so it first sets switch_bedroom.power := on, then turns on bulb_bedroom at 60% brightness. Another option is to change R1 so it turns off bulb_bedroom directly and leaves the relay switch powered.

bulb_corridor depends only on switch_corridor, and neither rule changes switch_corridor.

explanation: These two rules can give the thermostat opposite commands. R1 sets heating to 23 °C at 18:00. R2 sets eco mode at 19 °C when someone arrives home between 17:00 and 19:00, and 18:00 falls inside that window. If someone arrives between 18:00 and 19:00, R2 undoes R1's 23 °C setting. If someone arrives between 17:00 and 18:00, R1 replaces their eco setting at 18:00. Which setting you end up with depends only on when someone happens to get home.
evidence: R1 sets thermostat.setpoint := 23 and thermostat.mode := heat at 18:00, with no conditions
R2 sets thermostat.setpoint := 19 and thermostat.mode := eco when home_mode becomes home while the time is between 17:00 and 19:00
R1's 18:00 trigger falls inside R2's 17:00–19:00 window, so both rules can fire on the same evening
Both rules write different values to the same thermostat setpoint and mode (23/heat vs 19/eco)
repair: Decide which rule wins in the evening and change the times so they no longer overlap. For example, limit R2 to arrivals between 17:00 and 17:59 so R1's 18:00 comfort setting always applies afterwards. Or add a condition to R2 so it only runs if the setpoint has not already been set to 23 by R1.

explanation: R3 turns the AC to cooling, but nothing ever switches it back off. The AC keeps cooling the living room until it drops below 20 °C. That triggers R4, which turns on the heating, while the AC is still cooling. Neither rule turns the other device off, so the heating and the AC end up running at the same time and working against each other. Known effect: thermostat.mode = heat raises temp_living, so it can push the room above 24 °C and trigger R3 again.
Both devices are in the living_room and act on the same variable, temp_living.
repair: Make each rule turn off the opposing device: R3 should also set thermostat.mode := eco (or off), and R4 should also set ac_living.mode := off. You could also add rules that turn the AC off when temp_living falls below about 22 °C and turn the heating to eco when it rises above about 22 °C.

explanation: Both rules control the thermostat mode, but they run at different times: R1 at 18:00 (heat, 23 C) and R5 at 08:00 (eco). They never fire at the same moment, so this is an ordinary daily schedule: heating in the evening and eco during the day. Neither rule depends on the room temperature, so the heating from R1 can't set off or block R5.
evidence: R1 triggers only at time == 18:00 and sets thermostat.mode := heat, setpoint := 23
R5 triggers only at time == 08:00 and sets thermostat.mode := eco
The two trigger times are different and never overlap
Neither rule has a condition on temp_living or home_mode, so the heat effect on temp_living cannot trigger or block the other rule

explanation: When the home is in away mode, R1 switches off the garage circuit breaker. The garage exhaust fan is wired to that circuit. If carbon monoxide is then detected in the garage, R2 tells the fan to turn on, but it has no power, so the CO is not cleared. This is a safety problem because no one is home to notice.
evidence: R1: when home_mode == away, breaker_garage.power := off
R2: when co_garage == True, fan_garage.power := on (and garage_door.position := open)

Nothing stops CO from being detected while the home is in away mode, for example from a car left running or a fault, so both rules can apply together
repair: Change R2 so it first turns the garage breaker back on (breaker_garage.power := on) and then turns on the fan and opens the door. Also add a condition to R1 so it only cuts the breaker when co_garage == False. A longer-term option is to move the exhaust fan to a circuit that never gets switched off.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door to vent carbon monoxide, and R3 closes the same door when the home switches to away mode. If CO is still in the garage when the home goes to away mode (for example, right after someone drives out), R3 closes the door. That traps the CO inside and undoes R2's safety action.
evidence: R2 sets garage_door.position := open when co_garage == True
R3 sets garage_door.position := closed when home_mode == away
R3 has no conditions, so it fires even while co_garage is True
Both rules control the same device (garage_door) and its position state
repair: Add the condition co_garage == False to R3, so the door stays open for venting while CO is detected. Optionally, close the door automatically once co_garage goes back to False and home_mode is away.

explanation: The EV charger runs on the garage circuit. If the car is parked and charging when the home switches to away mode, R1 turns off the garage breaker and charging stops, which undoes R4. If the car arrives while the home is already in away mode, R4 tries to start charging, but the charger has no power. Either way, the car can be left uncharged without warning. The breaker also powers the garage exhaust fan, so turning it off removes ventilation.

R4: when car_present == True, ev_charger.charging := on

Known dependency: when breaker_garage.power is off, fan_garage.power becomes off
Neither rule has a condition that stops both from applying at once (for example, the car is parked while the household is away)
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only turns off the garage breaker when car_present == False and ev_charger.charging == off. Also have R1 check that co_garage == False so the exhaust fan is never left without power. A better long-term fix is to put the EV charger on its own circuit, separate from the garage breaker.

explanation: R4 and R5 are both triggered when the car parks in the garage, but they control different devices: R4 starts the EV charger and R5 turns on the garage light. Neither action works against the other. Neither action changes a sensor value that a rule depends on, and there is no known physical link between the charger and the light. Both rules can run together safely.

R5 sets light_garage.power to on when car_present == True
The two rules act on different devices (ev_charger and light_garage), so they cannot give opposite commands to the same device

Neither action changes car_present, home_mode or co_garage

explanation: At 12:00 the feeder puts out food (R1). The cat runs to it and sets off the kitchen motion sensor. If the home is in away mode at that time, R2 reads this motion as an intruder and sounds the siren, so you get a false alarm every day while you're out.
evidence: R1 turns feeder.dispensing on at 12:00 every day, with no conditions.
Known dependency: when feeder.dispensing is on, motion_kitchen becomes true because the cat runs to the feeder.
R2 fires on motion_kitchen == True when home_mode == away and turns alarm.siren on.
The feeder and the motion sensor are both in the kitchen.
Feeding at noon is likely to happen while the home is in away mode.
repair: Change R2 so it ignores kitchen motion for a short window after feeding (for example 11:59–12:15), or have it require a second check before sounding the siren, such as motion in the living room or a person detected on camera_kitchen. Keep the alarm active at all other times.

explanation: At 12:00 every day, R1 turns on the cat feeder. The cat runs to the food and sets off the kitchen motion sensor. That makes R3 start recording on the kitchen camera, even though no person entered the kitchen. You get a recording of the cat every day, which uses storage and can bury real security clips under false alerts.
evidence: R1: at 12:00, feeder.dispensing := on (no conditions)
Known dependency: when feeder.dispensing is on, motion_kitchen becomes true because the cat runs to the feeder
R3: when motion_kitchen == True, camera_kitchen.recording := on (no conditions)
The feeder and camera_kitchen are both in the kitchen
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only records when home_mode is away or night, and skip motion during a short window after the feeder runs (for example 12:00–12:15).

explanation: R4 starts the litter box cleaning cycle in the bathroom. R5 sounds the alarm when there is motion in the living room while the home is in away mode. The two rules control different devices, and the only known link in this home is that the feeder causes kitchen motion. That link doesn't involve the litter box or the living room motion sensor, so neither rule changes anything the other one depends on.
evidence: R4 only sets litter_box.cleaning to on. The litter box is in the bathroom.
R5 is triggered by motion_living, only fires when home_mode is away, and sets alarm.siren to on. The siren is in the living room.
The only known dependency is that feeder.dispensing being on makes motion_kitchen true. It doesn't involve the litter box, motion_living or the alarm.
No rule changes home_mode, and no two rules set the same device to different states.

explanation: Both rules start when the kitchen detects motion. When the home is in 'home' mode, both conditions are true, so R3 turns the kitchen camera's recording on while R6 turns it off at the same moment. Whichever rule runs last decides the result, so the camera may record when you expect privacy, or it may switch back and forth. When the cat feeder dispenses food, the cat runs to it and sets off the kitchen motion sensor, so this can happen even when no person is in the kitchen.
evidence: R3: trigger motion_kitchen == True, no conditions, action camera_kitchen.recording := on
R6: trigger motion_kitchen == True, condition home_mode == home, action camera_kitchen.recording := off
Both rules control the same device state, camera_kitchen.recording, and set it to opposite values
R3 has no condition, so it also fires when home_mode == home, the case where R6 fires
When feeder.dispensing is on, the cat triggers motion_kitchen, which starts both rules
repair: Add the condition home_mode != home (that is, away or night) to R3. The camera will then record kitchen motion only when the home is not in 'home' mode, and R6 alone will handle privacy in 'home' mode.

explanation: The CPAP machine is plugged into the bedside smart plug. R2 turns the CPAP on when the home goes into night mode, but at 23:30 R1 switches the bedside plug off to save energy. That cuts power to the CPAP while someone may be asleep and depending on it. The labels say the plug is for a phone charger, but the plug actually powers a medical breathing device.
evidence: R1 sets plug_bedside.power := off every day at 23:30, with no conditions
R2 sets cpap.power := on when home_mode == night
Known dependency: when plug_bedside.power is off, cpap.power becomes off (the CPAP is plugged into the bedside smart plug)
cpap is a medical_device (a CPAP breathing machine) in the bedroom, and it's used during sleep, which overlaps with 23:30
R1's description calls the plug a 'phone charger', so the rule doesn't account for the CPAP
repair: Never let R1 cut power to the CPAP. Either plug the CPAP into its own outlet that is always on, or add a condition to R1 so it only turns the plug off when home_mode != night and the CPAP is not in use. Simply removing R1 also works.

explanation: R3 unlocks the entrance door when a fall is detected so paramedics can get in. R4 locks the same door when the home switches to night mode. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other. If the home enters night mode during or after a fall, for example on a night-mode schedule while the person is still on the bathroom floor, R4 relocks the door and paramedics could be shut out.
evidence: R3 sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked when fall_detected == True, with no conditions
R4 sets lock_entrance.lock := locked when home_mode == night, with no conditions
Both rules control the same device: lock_entrance (the entrance door lock in the corridor)
fall_detected and home_mode are independent variables, so both triggers can be active at the same time
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only locks the door when fall_detected == False. That way, switching to night mode cannot relock the door while a fall emergency is active, and the door stays unlocked for paramedics until the fall alert is cleared.

explanation: R5 only turns off the reading lamp plug. The CPAP machine is plugged into the bedside plug, not the reading lamp plug. Turning off the reading lamp at 23:30 doesn't cut power to the CPAP, so R2 can still turn it on in night mode. The two rules control different devices, and neither one changes anything the other rule depends on.

R2 action: cpap.power := on, triggered by home_mode == night

No dependency is listed between plug_reading_lamp and the CPAP or home_mode

explanation: At 10:00, R2 opens the living room window. On warm days this lets hot outdoor air in, so the living room temperature can go above 27 °C. That makes R1 turn on the AC while the window is still open. The AC then cools against hot outside air, which wastes energy and doesn't cool the room well. Neither rule checks what the other device is doing.
evidence: R2 sets window_living.position := open at 10:00 with no conditions.
Known effect: when window_living.position is open, temp_living increases (hot outdoor air in summer).
R1 is triggered by temp_living > 27 and sets ac_living.mode := cool with no conditions.
Both devices are in the living room, and neither rule checks the state of the other device.
repair: Add the condition window_living.position == closed to R1, so the AC only cools when the window is shut. Also add the condition temp_living <= 27 and ac_living.mode == off to R2, so the window only opens for fresh air when the room isn't already hot and the AC isn't running.

explanation: At 14:00 R3 turns on the lawn sprinkler. The sprinkler sprays the rain sensor on the terrace, so the sensor reports rain when it isn't raining. That falsely triggers R4, which closes the bedroom skylight every day at watering time.
evidence: R3 sets sprinkler.watering := on at 14:00 with no conditions.
R4 is triggered by rain_sensor == True and closes skylight.position.
Known dependency: when sprinkler.watering is on, rain_sensor becomes true because the spray wets the terrace rain sensor.
The sprinkler is next to the terrace and the rain sensor is mounted on the terrace, so they are physically close.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only closes the skylight when sprinkler.watering is off. Or move the rain sensor out of the sprinkler's spray range so it only detects real rain.

explanation: R5 opens the bedroom window and R4 closes the skylight. These are two different devices, so neither rule undoes what the other does. Opening the window only lowers the bedroom CO2, which has no effect on the rain sensor. Closing the skylight doesn't change CO2 or rain either, so neither rule can make the other fire or stop it from firing.

Known effect: an open window_bedroom lowers co2_bedroom. This only pushes R5's own trigger back down and does not touch rain_sensor
The only known effect on rain_sensor comes from the sprinkler, and neither rule controls the sprinkler
There is no known physical or power link between the bedroom window and the skylight

explanation: R5 opens the bedroom window when CO2 is high, and R1 turns on the living room AC when it gets hot. They control different devices in different rooms. The bedroom window only affects bedroom CO2, which R1 doesn't use, and the AC only affects living room temperature, which R5 doesn't use. Neither rule can trigger or block the other.
evidence: R5 acts on window_bedroom.position (bedroom); R1 acts on ac_living.mode (living room) — different devices.

If the AC is already cooling at 10:00, R2 reopens the window and R6 won't fire again, so the AC keeps running with the window open. If both fire at the same moment, the window gets opposite commands.
evidence: R2 sets window_living.position := open at 10:00 with no conditions
R6 sets window_living.position := closed when ac_living.mode becomes cool

R6 is triggered by the AC switching to cool, so it does not fire again if R2 opens the window while the AC is already cooling

explanation: When the home goes into night mode, R2 turns off the closet power strip. The NAS is plugged into that strip, so it loses power. When R1 tries to start the backup at 01:00, the NAS is already off and the backup can't run. The closet cooling fan is on the same strip, so it would also be off during any backup, and backups heat the closet.
evidence: R2: when home_mode == night, strip_closet.power := off
R1: at 01:00, nas.backup := running

Physical dependency: when strip_closet.power is off, fan_closet.power becomes off (the cooling fan is plugged into the closet strip)

repair: Rewire the NAS and the closet cooling fan so they are powered from an always-on outlet, not the switched closet strip. Or add a condition to R2 so it only turns off the strip after the NAS backup is idle, such as after the backup finishes in the morning.

explanation: R2 turns off the closet power strip when the home goes into night mode. The cooling fan is plugged into that strip, so it loses power. If the closet then goes above 35 °C, R3 tells the fan to turn on, but the fan has no power and can't run, so the closet keeps heating up. A NAS backup job that starts before the strip shuts off can make the closet hot enough to trigger R3.

R3: temp_closet > 35 -> fan_closet.power := on

Dependency: when fan_closet.power is on, temp_closet decreases (the fan is the closet's cooling)
Dependency: when nas.backup is running, temp_closet increases

explanation: The nightly backup (R1) heats the closet, which may turn on the cooling fan (R3). The fan then cools the closet, so the two rules work together as intended. They control different devices, never give opposite commands, and neither one switches off the closet power strip that the NAS and fan are plugged into.

The rules act on different devices (nas vs. fan_closet) and never give opposite commands.

The NAS and cooling fan lose power only when strip_closet.power is off, and neither rule controls strip_closet.

explanation: If the teenager gets home between 23:00 and 06:00, R1 unlocks the front door. That unlock immediately sets off R2, which locks the door again. The two trigger times are different and never overlap

No known dependencies or effects are listed for this home

explanation: At 09:00, R1 closes the office shades. Closed shades block winter sun, so the office cools down. If it drops below 20 °C, R2 starts the radiator, which then has to make up for heat the shades blocked. That wastes energy and turns the heating on when you didn't expect it.
evidence: R1 sets shades_office.position := closed at 09:00 with no conditions
