Known dependency: when radiator_office.mode is heat, temp_office increases, so the radiator works against the heat loss caused by R1
repair: Add a condition to R1 so the shades close at 09:00 only if temp_office >= 21. That stops the shades from cooling the office below the 20 °C point that triggers the radiator.

explanation: R2 and R4 can never fire at the same time. The office can't be below 20 °C and above 24 °C at once. Turning on the heat will eventually warm the room enough for R4 to fire, but that is the intended result, not an unexpected side effect. Between 20 and 24 °C neither rule fires, which prevents rapid on/off switching

explanation: Both rules run when the home switches to away mode, and both aim to turn the desk heater off. R3 cuts power at the desk plug, which also turns the heater off because the heater is plugged into it. R5 then switches the heater itself off. explanation: Both rules run at exactly 09:00 and have no conditions, but R1 closes the office shades while R6 opens them. The shades end up in whichever position the last rule to run sets, which is unpredictable, and they may move back and forth. Closing them also blocks winter sun, so the office stays cooler.

R6 trigger: time == 09:00, no conditions, action shades_office.position := open

For example, only run R6 (open the shades for daylight) when temp_office is below a comfort threshold such as 20 °C, and only run R1 (close them for screen work) when temp_office is at or above that threshold. explanation: At 19:30, R2 turns on the white-noise speaker in the nursery. The baby monitor's microphone picks up that white noise, so the measured nursery sound level goes up. If it goes above 60 dB, R1 reads it as the baby crying and turns on the nursery lamp, which could wake the baby or keep them awake even though they aren't crying.
evidence: R2 sets white_noise.playing to on every day at 19:30, with no conditions.
Known dependency: when white_noise.playing is on, noise_nursery goes up because the baby monitor microphone picks up the white noise.
R1 turns nursery_lamp.power on whenever noise_nursery is above 60 dB, with no conditions.
R1 has no condition that rules out noise coming from the white-noise speaker, so R2's action can set off R1 even when the baby isn't crying.
repair: Make R1 account for the white noise. Either only let it fire when white_noise.playing is off, or raise its threshold while white noise is playing (for example, to the white-noise level plus a margin). A cry-detection sensor would also work better than raw decibel level.

explanation: When the TV turns on in the evening, R3 turns on the living-room soundbar. The soundbar shares a thin wall with the nursery, so the baby monitor picks up its sound and the nursery noise level goes up. If it goes above 60 dB, R1 mistakes the TV audio for the baby crying and turns on the nursery lamp. This can happen while the baby is asleep, and the light could wake them.
evidence: R3 sets soundbar.power := on when the TV turns on between 20:00 and 23:59, which is the baby's evening and bedtime.
Known dependency: when soundbar.power is on, noise_nursery increases (the soundbar shares a thin wall with the nursery).
R1 is triggered by noise_nursery > 60 dB and has no other conditions, so it can't tell crying apart from other noise.
R1 sets nursery_lamp.power := on, so the lamp can turn on in the nursery without anyone choosing it.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only fires when soundbar.power is off. Or replace the plain loudness threshold with a dedicated cry-detection signal from the baby monitor. You could also lower the soundbar volume or move it away from the nursery wall after 20:00.

explanation: R4 controls only the living room TV, and R2 controls only the nursery white-noise speaker. R2 makes the nursery louder, but neither rule uses the nursery noise level as a trigger or condition. No physical link between the TV and the speaker is listed. These rules can run together without interfering.

R2 acts only on white_noise.playing (on), triggered at 19:30.

No dependency links the TV to white_noise or to home_mode, and no rule changes home_mode.

explanation: When a frost warning comes in, R1 turns on the greenhouse heater. The heater warms the greenhouse, and once it passes 18 °C, R2 opens the roof vent. That lets the warm air out into the frosty night, so the heater keeps running while the vent dumps its heat. This wastes energy, and if the vent stays open, the plants could still get frost damage.
evidence: R1: frost_warning == True -> gh_heater.power := on
R2: temp_gh > 18 -> gh_vent.position := open
Dependency: when gh_heater.power is on, temp_gh increases
Dependency: when gh_vent.position is open, temp_gh decreases
R2 has no condition that stops it from running during a frost warning or while the heater is on
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only opens the vent when frost_warning == False and gh_heater.power == off. Another option is to make R2 open the vent at a higher temperature (for example 26 °C) during a frost warning.

explanation: The greenhouse heater is plugged into the outdoor smart plug. If a frost warning makes R1 turn the heater on, R3 will still switch the outdoor plug off at 22:00. That cuts power to the heater on a cold night, just when the plants need protection.
evidence: R1 turns on gh_heater.power when frost_warning == True
R3 turns off plug_outdoor.power every day at 22:00, with no conditions
Known dependency: when plug_outdoor.power is off, gh_heater.power becomes off (the heater is plugged into the outdoor plug)
Frost warnings often stay active overnight, so both rules can apply at the same time
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only turns off plug_outdoor at 22:00 when frost_warning == False. Another option is to move the greenhouse heater to a separate outlet that stays powered.

explanation: R4 only switches on the grow lights at 06:00, and R2 only opens the roof vent when the greenhouse is warmer than 18 C. The two rules control different devices. This home has no recorded link between the grow lights and the greenhouse temperature or the vent, so neither rule can cause the other to run or stop it from running.
evidence: R4 changes only grow_lights.power (to on) at 06:00.
R2 changes only gh_vent.position (to open) when temp_gh > 18.
No rule controls the same device as the other, so their actions cannot clash.

Opening the vent lowers temp_gh, but R4 runs on a clock time and doesn't depend on temperature.

explanation: Both rules control the roof vent but cannot fire together: R2 opens it only above 18 °C and R5 closes it only below 5 °C. An open vent cools the greenhouse, and if it drops below 5 °C, R5 closing the vent is the intended protection. The 13 °C gap between the settings stops the vent from switching open and closed over and over.
evidence: R2 trigger: temp_gh > 18 -> gh_vent.position := open
R5 trigger: temp_gh < 5 -> gh_vent.position := closed

explanation: The greenhouse heater gets its power from the outdoor smart plug. When R3 switches that plug off at 22:00, the heater turns off too. There is also a smaller problem: if the heater pushes the greenhouse above 18 °C, R2 opens the roof vent and lets the heat out, so the two rules end up working against each other.
evidence: R1 turns gh_heater.power on when frost_warning == True, and a frost warning usually applies through the night.

repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only turns off plug_outdoor at 22:00 when frost_warning == False. Or move the heater to a power source that isn't on a schedule. Optionally, add the condition gh_heater.power == off to R2 so the vent doesn't open while the heater is running.

explanation: R1 turns the greenhouse heater on when a frost warning comes in. R6 turns the same heater off every night at 22:00, even if the frost warning is still active. Frost warnings usually cover the night, so the heater can switch off at the coldest time. R1 only reacts when the warning first starts, so it won't turn the heater back on, and the plants could freeze.
evidence: R1 sets gh_heater.power to on when frost_warning becomes True, and it has no conditions.
R6 sets gh_heater.power to off at 22:00, and it has no conditions, so it doesn't check frost_warning.

The heater raises temp_gh (environmental dependency). Turning it off during frost lets the greenhouse cool down.
repair: Add a condition to R6 so it only turns the heater off at 22:00 when frost_warning is False. You could also add a rule that turns the heater on whenever frost_warning is True, at any time, so frost protection always comes first.

explanation: The hallway camera gets its power from the hallway smart plug. At 23:00, R1 turns that plug off, which also turns the camera off. If the home is in away mode, R2 expects the camera to be recording, so the front door goes unwatched from 23:00 onward while nobody is home.

explanation: Both rules control the front door lock at night, but they do opposite things. R3 locks the door when the home switches to night mode. R4 unlocks it whenever someone moves in the hallway between 22:00 and 06:00. Night mode usually starts in that same time window, so any hallway movement, like someone walking to the bathroom, a pet, or a guest, can undo the night-mode lock and leave the door unlocked overnight.

R4 sets lock_front.lock := unlocked when motion_hall == True during 22:00-06:00

motion_hall can also be triggered by people or pets who are not leaving
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only runs when home_mode != night. Or replace the automatic unlock with a notification that asks for manual confirmation, so night-mode locking always takes priority.

explanation: R5 only turns off the living room lamp at 23:00, and R2 only starts recording on the hallway camera when the home switches to away mode. They control different devices. Turning off the lamp doesn't change the home mode, motion, or the hallway plug that powers the camera, so neither rule can block or set off the other.
evidence: R5 acts only on lamp_living.power (off) at 23:00.
R2 acts only on camera_hall.recording (on) when home_mode == away.
The only known physical link is plug_hall.power -> camera_hall.power, and neither rule touches plug_hall.
lamp_living isn't tied to home_mode, motion_hall, or any camera-related device.

explanation: R1 turns off the hallway smart plug at 23:00 and R3 locks the front door when the home enters night mode. They control different devices, neither changes anything the other depends on, and the lock isn't powered through the plug, so they can run together safely. One side effect to know about: switching the plug off also turns off the hallway camera, which isn't part of either rule.
evidence: R1 only acts on plug_hall.power; R3 only acts on lock_front.lock - different devices, so no opposite commands.
R3 is triggered by home_mode == night, which R1 does not change (home_mode is set by the alarm panel).
The only known dependency links plug_hall to camera_hall power; there is no dependency between plug_hall and lock_front.
R3 does not use camera_hall or motion_hall, so the camera turning off does not affect R3.

explanation: R1 turns on the living room heater at 18:00, and nothing ever turns it off. The heater pushes the living room above 26 °C, which fires R2, so the fan comes on and the window opens while the heater is still running. The heater ends up heating cold outdoor air. That wastes energy and leaves the heater and the open window working against each other.
evidence: R1 sets heater_living.power := on at 18:00, with no conditions and no rule that turns it off

Neither rule checks the other device's state, so the heater and the open window can run at the same time

explanation: R3 turns on the bedroom heater, and that only warms the bedroom. R2 is triggered by the living room temperature and controls only the living room fan and window. The two rules share no devices, and nothing known links the bedroom heater to the living room temperature, so one rule can't set off or block the other.
evidence: R3 acts only on heater_bedroom.power, which is in the bedroom.
The known effect of heater_bedroom is that temp_bedroom increases; no effect on temp_living is listed.
R2 is triggered by temp_living > 26 and acts on vent_living and window_living, both in the living room.
R2's open window lowers temp_living, and R3 does not depend on temp_living in any way.
The two rules never act on the same device.

explanation: When R2 opens the living room window, cold air lowers the temperature, which can set off R4 and turn on the heater. No rule ever closes the window or turns off the heater, so the heater can run with the window open, wasting energy. Because nothing stops the heater, the room can go back above 26 °C, so the two rules keep undoing each other.

Add matching "off" rules so the heater and fan stop once the room is comfortable again (e.g. heater off above 21 °C; window closed and fan off below 24 °C).

explanation: Both rules run at exactly 18:00. When the home is in away mode, R1 turns the living room heater on and R5 turns it off at the same moment. Which one wins depends on the order they happen to run in, so the heater could end up running in an empty house.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 18:00, no conditions, action heater_living.power := on
R5 trigger: time == 18:00, condition home_mode == away, action heater_living.power := off
home_mode can be 'away', so both rules can fire at the same moment
heater_living.power has the states on/off, so the two actions contradict each other
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so it only turns the heater on when someone is home. The two rules then never fire together, and R5 becomes unnecessary.

explanation: On weekdays at 10:00, R1 starts the robot vacuum in the living room. The moving vacuum sets off the living room motion sensor, so R2 thinks someone is home and unlocks the entrance door. This can happen when nobody is home, which leaves the house unlocked.

The vacuum is in the living_room.

R2 is triggered by motion_living == True and sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked, with no conditions.
Weekday mid-morning is a typical time for the house to be empty (home_mode = away).
repair: Add conditions to R2 so it only unlocks when home_mode == home and vacuum.mode == docked. That way, motion caused by the vacuum (or picked up while the house is in away mode) can never unlock the entrance door.

explanation: At 10:00, R1 starts the robot vacuum in the living room. The living room motion sensor picks up the moving vacuum. If the home is in away mode, which is likely on a weekday morning, R3 treats that motion as an intruder and sounds the siren. The result is a false alarm.

The vacuum is in the living_room.

R3 fires on motion_living == True when home_mode == away and sets alarm.siren := on.
No rule stops the vacuum from running while the home is in away mode, so both rules can be active at the same time.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only sounds the siren when vacuum.mode == docked. Better still, have it check a second sensor too, such as the entrance door or bedroom motion. That way the vacuum alone can't set off the alarm, and the alarm still works when the vacuum is docked.

explanation: R1 starts the robot vacuum and R4 turns on the entrance light. They control different devices, so their actions can't clash. When the vacuum moves around, it sets off the living room motion sensor, but R4 only reacts to the bedroom motion sensor, so the vacuum won't turn on the light by accident. Neither rule cuts power to or blocks the other.
evidence: R1 acts only on vacuum.mode (cleaning); R4 acts only on light_entrance.power (on) – the devices are different.
Known dependency: vacuum cleaning makes motion_living true, but R4 is triggered by motion_bedroom, not motion_living.
The vacuum is in the living_room and the motion sensor that triggers R4 is in the bedroom.
No physical or power dependency is listed between the vacuum and the entrance light.

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door when smoke is detected, and R2 locks it when the home switches to away mode. Both can fire close together. For example, if away mode starts while smoke is present, R2 locks the door during a fire, which blocks the escape route R1 opened. If smoke is detected while you're away, R1 leaves the empty apartment unlocked.
evidence: R1 action: lock_door.lock := unlocked when smoke_kitchen == True
R2 action: lock_door.lock := locked when home_mode == away

explanation: R1 turns off the air handler when the kitchen smoke detector goes off, so smoke isn't spread through the apartment. R4 turns the air handler on at 08:00 every day and doesn't check for anything else. If a smoke event is still going on at 08:00, R4 switches the air handler back on and undoes R1's safety action.

R4 sets hvac.power to on at time == 08:00 and has no conditions
Both rules control the same device (hvac.power) and set it to opposite values
Nothing stops R4 from running while smoke_kitchen is still True
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only turns the air handler on when smoke_kitchen == False. R1's smoke response stays exactly as it is.

explanation: R3 turns on the kitchen range hood when the oven turns on. R2 locks the apartment door when the home switches to away mode. The two rules control different devices, and neither one's action changes anything the other rule depends on. The hood clearing kitchen smoke has no effect on the door lock or the household mode.
evidence: R3 only controls hood.power, and R2 only controls lock_door.lock, so they never act on the same device.
R3 is triggered by oven.power, and R2 is triggered by home_mode. Neither rule's action changes the other rule's trigger.
The only known dependency (hood on → smoke_kitchen false) affects smoke_kitchen, which neither rule uses as a trigger or condition.
Neither rule has extra conditions that the other rule's action could block.

explanation: The Wi-Fi router gets its power from the office smart plug. At 00:30, R1 turns that plug off, which also turns off the router. You could be away and miss visitors or alerts at the door, and the garden camera also stops uploading to the cloud.

evidence: R4 acts only on plug_desk_lamp.power := off

The two rules act on different devices and don't change any shared context variable

The router depends on plug_office.power, not plug_desk_lamp.power (router is plugged into the office smart plug).
Doorbell notifications only turn off when router.power is off, and neither rule affects the router or plug_office.

explanation: The aquarium heater and the aquarium pump are both plugged into the living room power strip. In night mode, R1 turns that strip off, so the heater and the pump both lose power. The heater warming the water until R4 switches it off is what you want, not an unexpected side effect.

Once the water cools after the heater goes off at night, R2 turns it back on, which goes against R5's goal of a quiet room.
