explanation: When you're away, R1 closes the main water valve. The garden irrigation gets its water through that valve. So when R2 turns on watering at 06:00, the controller reports watering as on, but no water reaches the garden. Your garden won't get watered while you're away, and the system will still show watering as active.
evidence: R1 sets valve_main.state to closed whenever home_mode becomes away, with no other conditions.
R2 sets irrigation.watering and irrigation.flow to on every day at 06:00, with no conditions, so it also runs while the home is in away mode.
Known physical dependency: when valve_main.state is closed, irrigation.flow becomes off, because the irrigation line is supplied through the main water valve.
Both rules can be active together: the home can stay in away mode overnight and through 06:00.
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R2 so it doesn't try to water while the main valve is closed. You can also skip watering when soil_moisture is already high. If the garden needs watering while you're away, have a plumber connect the irrigation to the separate garden valve (valve_garden) so it no longer depends on the main valve. Keep R1 closing the main valve so the leak protection stays in place.

explanation: R2 turns garden watering on at 06:00 no matter how wet the soil is, and R4 turns the same watering off when the soil is above 60%. If the soil is already above 60% at 06:00, the two rules give opposite commands at the same moment. Depending on how R4 is checked, you get one of two results. Either the watering flips on and off, or it keeps running on wet soil because the 'above 60%' trigger already fired earlier and doesn't fire again. Also, R4 only turns 'watering' off and leaves irrigation 'flow' on.
evidence: R2: at 06:00 sets irrigation.watering := on (and irrigation.flow := on) with no conditions
R4: when soil_moisture > 60 sets irrigation.watering := off
Both rules control the same state, irrigation.watering, with opposite values
R2 never checks soil_moisture, so it can start watering when the soil is already above 60%
Known effect: when irrigation.watering is on, soil_moisture increases, so R2's action pushes moisture toward R4's threshold
R4 does not reset irrigation.flow, which R2 set to on
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only starts watering when soil_moisture <= 60. Also make R4 set irrigation.flow := off together with irrigation.watering := off.

explanation: R5 closes the garden valve on the outdoor tap line, and R2 turns on the garden sprinklers. These are different devices. In this home, the sprinkler line gets its water through the main water valve, not the outdoor tap valve. So closing the garden valve in away mode doesn't stop the 06:00 watering, and the two rules don't affect each other in any other way.
evidence: R5 only sets valve_garden.state to closed when home_mode becomes away.
R2 only sets irrigation.watering and irrigation.flow to on at 06:00.
valve_garden is described as a separate valve on the outdoor tap line.
The only listed physical dependency for irrigation flow is valve_main.state == closed, which makes irrigation.flow off. Neither rule touches valve_main.
The listed environmental effect (watering raises soil_moisture) doesn't trigger or block either rule.
repair: none

explanation: On a bright day, R1 closes the living room blinds to cut glare. Closed blinds block daylight, so the light level can drop below 150 lux. That triggers R2, which turns the ceiling lights on in the middle of the day. Neither rule reopens the blinds, so the lights can stay on all day and waste energy.
evidence: R1: when lux_living > 800, blinds_living.position := closed
R2: when lux_living < 150, lights_living.power := on
Known effect: when blinds_living.position is closed, lux_living decreases (closed blinds block daylight)
Both rules run with no conditions, so R2 can fire right after R1 closes the blinds
Known effect: when lights_living.power is on, lux_living increases, so the lights feed back into the same sensor that R1 and R2 both use
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only fires when blinds_living.position is open (or only after sunset). Alternatively, have R2 first reopen the blinds partly instead of switching on the lights when the blinds were closed by R1.

explanation: R3 opens the living room blinds at 07:30 and R4 closes them at 22:00. These are two separate times, so the rules never fire together and never give opposite commands at once. Closing the blinds lowers the light level in the living room, but no other rule here reacts to that light level, so nothing is set off by accident. This is a normal daily open/close schedule.
evidence: R3 trigger: time == 07:30 sets blinds_living.position := open
R4 trigger: time == 22:00 sets blinds_living.position := closed
The two times are different and never overlap, so the opposite actions can't happen at the same moment
Closed blinds_living lowers lux_living, but neither R3 nor R4 depends on lux_living or any other context variable
repair: none

explanation: R1 and R5 don't conflict because they work in different rooms. R1 closes the living room blinds, which only makes the living room darker. R5 turns on the study desk light based on the study's light level. Neither rule changes anything the other rule depends on.
evidence: R1 controls blinds_living.position, and R5 controls lights_study.power. These are different devices.
R1 is triggered by lux_living, and R5 is triggered by lux_study. These are separate sensors in separate rooms.
Closing blinds_living only lowers lux_living. No known dependency links it to lux_study.
The only known effect on lux_study comes from blinds_study, and neither rule touches that device.
lights_study has no listed effect on lux_living.
repair: none

explanation: R3 opens the living room blinds at 07:30, and R1 closes the same blinds when the room goes above 800 lux. On a bright morning, opening the blinds lets in daylight, the light level passes 800 lux, and R1 closes the blinds right away. The two rules give the same device opposite commands, and the first rule's effect triggers the second.
evidence: R3 sets blinds_living.position := open at 07:30 with no conditions
R1 sets blinds_living.position := closed whenever lux_living > 800 with no conditions
Both rules act on the same device (blinds_living) with opposite states (open vs. closed)
Known dependency: closed blinds_living block daylight and lower lux_living, so opening them raises lux_living and can trigger R1
repair: Make the priority explicit: have R1 fire only when lux_living stays above 800 for about 10 minutes, or only during the hours when glare is a real problem (e.g. after 10:00), so it doesn't immediately reverse the scheduled 07:30 opening.

explanation: R1 turns on the nursery humidifier at 20:00, and nothing ever turns it off, so the nursery keeps getting more humid. Once humidity goes above 55 %, R2 turns on the dehumidifier. Both machines then run at the same time and work against each other all night. This wastes energy, makes noise in the baby's room and undoes what R1 was set up to do.
evidence: R1: at 20:00 humidifier_nursery.power := on, with no condition and no rule that turns it off
Known effect: when humidifier_nursery is on, humidity_nursery increases
R2 is triggered by humidity_nursery > 55 and sets dehumidifier_nursery.power := on
Known effect: when dehumidifier_nursery is on, humidity_nursery decreases, which works against the humidifier
Neither rule turns the other device off, so both can stay on at the same time
repair: Add an action to R2 that turns humidifier_nursery off whenever the dehumidifier turns on. Also add a condition to R1 so it only turns the humidifier on when humidity_nursery is below a target, for example 50 %. That way the two devices never run at the same time.

explanation: R3 and R4 work together as one control loop with a gap between the on and off levels. The fan turns on above 70% humidity and off below 50%. These two triggers can never be true at the same moment, so the rules can't send opposite commands to the fan at once. The fan does lower the humidity, which eventually makes R4 turn it off, but that is the intended result, not a conflict.
evidence: R3 fires only when humidity_bath > 70, and R4 fires only when humidity_bath < 50. Both cannot be true at the same time.
Between 50% and 70%, neither rule fires, so the fan doesn't keep switching on and off.
Known dependency: when fan_bath.power is on, humidity_bath decreases. This leads to R4 switching the fan off, which is the intended result of R3.
The two rules only control fan_bath. They don't affect the nursery humidifier, the nursery dehumidifier or the towel rail.
repair: none

explanation: R1 only turns on the nursery humidifier, and R3 only turns on the bathroom extractor fan. The two rules control different devices in different rooms. The humidifier raises nursery humidity, and nothing listed for this home links that to bathroom humidity, so R1 can't make R3 fire or stop it. The fan lowers bathroom humidity, which R1 doesn't depend on.
evidence: R1 acts on humidifier_nursery.power, and R3 acts on fan_bath.power, which are different devices.
humidifier_nursery affects only humidity_nursery, and R3 is triggered by humidity_bath.
fan_bath affects only humidity_bath, and R1 is triggered by time (20:00) and has no conditions.
No dependency is listed between the nursery and bathroom humidity, and no shared power dependency is listed.
repair: none

explanation: R5 turns the nursery dehumidifier off at 20:00 so it doesn't disturb sleep, but R2 turns it back on whenever nursery humidity is above 55%, at any time. If the nursery is humid at night, the two rules give the dehumidifier opposite commands and it may keep switching on and off. Turning it off also lets humidity rise, which makes R2 more likely to switch it back on.
evidence: R2 sets dehumidifier_nursery.power := on when humidity_nursery > 55, with no time condition.
R5 sets dehumidifier_nursery.power := off at 20:00, with no humidity condition.
Both rules control the same device state (dehumidifier_nursery.power) with opposite values.
Known dependency: when dehumidifier_nursery is on, humidity_nursery decreases, so turning it off lets humidity rise and can cause R2 to fire again.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs between 07:00 and 20:00. If night-time mould protection is still needed, add a separate rule for the night hours with a higher limit, for example humidity_nursery > 65%.

explanation: At night, R1 turns off the bedroom wall switch, and that cuts power to the bedroom bulb. If the wake-up alarm rings while the switch is still off, R2 can't turn the bulb on or fade it to 60 %, so the wake-up light won't work. Neither rule mentions this dependency.
evidence: R1: when home_mode == night, switch_bedroom.power := off
R2: when alarm_clock == True, bulb_bedroom.power := on; bulb_bedroom.brightness := 60
Known dependency: when switch_bedroom.power is off, bulb_bedroom.power becomes off (the bulb is wired behind the bedroom wall switch relay)
No rule turns switch_bedroom back on before the alarm, so the relay can still be off when R2 runs
repair: Change R2 so it first sets switch_bedroom.power := on, waits a few seconds for the bulb to start up, and then sets bulb_bedroom.power := on and brightness := 60.

explanation: R3 turns the corridor bulb off only at the moment the home switches into night mode, and R4 turns it on at 06:30. They fire at different times, so the result is a normal off-at-bedtime, on-in-the-morning cycle rather than a clash. Neither rule changes anything the other depends on, and neither touches the corridor wall switch that powers the bulb.
evidence: R3 is triggered by the event home_mode == night and sets bulb_corridor.power := off
R4 is triggered by time == 06:30 and sets bulb_corridor.power := on
The two triggers are separate events that happen at different times, so the actions run one after the other rather than together
Neither action changes home_mode or the time, so neither rule causes or blocks the other
No rule changes switch_corridor.power, so the wiring dependency between the corridor switch and bulb is not affected
repair: none

explanation: R1 cuts power to the bedroom wall switch, which also turns off the bedroom bulb. R4 turns on the corridor bulb, which is wired behind a different switch (the corridor switch). The two rules control different devices and different power circuits. Neither rule changes anything the other one depends on, so they can't conflict.
evidence: R1 acts only on switch_bedroom.power (off).
R4 acts only on bulb_corridor.power (on).
switch_bedroom only cuts power to bulb_bedroom, not bulb_corridor.
bulb_corridor depends on switch_corridor, and neither rule controls switch_corridor.
Neither rule changes home_mode or the time, so neither one can trigger or block the other.
repair: none

explanation: R1 sets the thermostat to 23 °C heat at 18:00, and R2 sets it to 19 °C eco when someone arrives home between 17:00 and 19:00. These times overlap. If someone gets home after 18:00, R2 undoes R1's comfort setting. If someone got home before 18:00, R1 overrides the eco setting R2 just chose. Which setting you end up with depends only on which rule ran last.
evidence: R1 actions: thermostat.setpoint := 23; thermostat.mode := heat at time == 18:00
R2 actions: thermostat.setpoint := 19; thermostat.mode := eco when home_mode == home and time in [17:00, 19:00]
18:00 falls inside R2's 17:00-19:00 window, so both rules can fire on the same evening
Both rules write different values to the same thermostat states (setpoint 23 vs 19, mode heat vs eco)
repair: Make the two rules not overlap: shorten R2's window to 17:00-17:59 so it only applies before the 18:00 comfort setting. Alternatively, add a condition to R2 so it does nothing when time >= 18:00 and the thermostat is already in heat at 23 °C.

explanation: R3 turns the air conditioner to cooling when it's warmer than 24 °C. Nothing ever switches it off again, so it keeps cooling until the room drops below 20 °C. That fires R4, which turns on the heating, and R4 also never switches the heating off. You can end up with the air conditioner cooling and the radiators heating the same room at the same time. That wastes energy, and if the heating pushes the room back above 24 °C, R3 fires again and the cycle repeats.
evidence: R3 sets ac_living.mode := cool when temp_living > 24 and never sets it back to off.
R4 sets thermostat.mode := heat when temp_living < 20 and never sets it back to off or eco.
Known effect: when ac_living.mode is cool, temp_living decreases, so it can fall below 20 and fire R4.
Known effect: when thermostat.mode is heat, temp_living increases, so it can rise above 24 and fire R3 again.
Both devices are in the living_room and act on the same variable, temp_living.
repair: Make each rule turn the opposite device off. R3 becomes 'ac_living.mode := cool AND thermostat.mode := eco (or off)', and R4 becomes 'thermostat.mode := heat AND ac_living.mode := off'. Optionally, add rules that stop cooling at about 22 °C and stop heating at about 22 °C, so the room settles inside the 20–24 °C range.

explanation: R1 and R5 both control the thermostat, but at different times. R1 turns on heating at 23 C at 18:00, and R5 switches to eco mode at 08:00. Since they never run at the same moment, together they make a normal day/evening heating schedule rather than a conflict. Neither rule depends on the room temperature, so the heat raised by R1 can't set off or block R5.
evidence: R1 fires only at time == 18:00 and sets thermostat.mode := heat, setpoint := 23
R5 fires only at time == 08:00 and sets thermostat.mode := eco
The two triggers are fixed, separate times, so the rules never fire together
Neither rule has a condition on temp_living or home_mode, so heating's effect on temp_living can't trigger or block the other rule
Neither rule uses ac_living, and there's no power or physical dependency between the devices
repair: none

explanation: When the home goes into away mode, R1 turns off the garage circuit breaker. The garage exhaust fan is on that circuit, so it loses power too. If carbon monoxide is detected in the garage while you're away, R2 tries to turn on the fan, but the fan has no power and can't clear the gas. This weakens a safety response, and nothing in the rules shows that the fan is unavailable.
evidence: R1 sets breaker_garage.power to off when home_mode becomes away.
R2 sets fan_garage.power to on when co_garage is True, in any home mode.
Known dependency: when breaker_garage.power is off, fan_garage.power becomes off because the exhaust fan is on the garage circuit.
Carbon monoxide can build up in the garage while the home is in away mode, for example from a car that is present (car_present).
repair: Add a first action to R2 that sets breaker_garage.power to on before it turns on fan_garage. A longer-term fix is to move the exhaust fan to a circuit that R1 doesn't switch off.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door to let carbon monoxide out, and R3 closes the same door when the home switches to away mode. Neither rule checks what the other one is doing. So if the home goes into away mode while CO is in the garage (for example, the household leaves while a car is still running), R3 can close the door and trap the CO inside. The order in which the rules fire decides which one wins, and that is a safety risk.
evidence: R2 action: garage_door.position := open when co_garage == True
R3 action: garage_door.position := closed when home_mode == away
Neither rule has a condition, so both can be active at the same time
co_garage and home_mode are independent variables, so CO can be detected while the home is in away mode
garage_door has only one position state (open/closed), so the two actions directly contradict each other
repair: Add the condition co_garage == False to R3 so the door only closes for away mode when no CO is detected. Optionally, also have R3 close the door once co_garage returns to False while the home is still in away mode.

explanation: R4 starts EV charging when the car is parked in the garage. The EV charger runs on the garage circuit, so when the home switches to away mode, R1 turns off the garage breaker and charging stops. Neither rule mentions this link. For example, if you park the car to charge and then leave on foot or on a trip, the car stays uncharged.
evidence: R4 sets ev_charger.charging to on when car_present == True
R1 sets breaker_garage.power to off when home_mode == away
Known dependency: when breaker_garage.power is off, ev_charger.charging becomes off (the EV charger is on the garage circuit)
No condition stops both rules from applying at once: the car can be in the garage while the home is in away mode
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only turns off the garage breaker when car_present == False and ev_charger.charging == off. Another option is to put the EV charger on its own circuit, separate from the garage breaker.

explanation: Both rules start when the car is parked in the garage, but they control different devices. R4 turns on the EV charger and R5 turns on the garage light. Neither rule changes anything the other relies on, and no known physical link connects the charger and the light. Both rules can run together without problems.
evidence: R4 and R5 share the same trigger (car_present == True) and neither has any conditions.
R4 only sets ev_charger.charging to on, and R5 only sets light_garage.power to on, so they act on different devices.
Neither action changes car_present, home_mode or co_garage.
The only known dependencies involve breaker_garage, which cuts power to the EV charger and the fan. Neither rule switches the breaker, and the light is not listed as depending on it.
repair: none

explanation: At noon, R1 turns on the cat feeder. The cat runs to the bowl, and the kitchen motion sensor picks it up. If the home is in away mode, that motion sets off R2 and the siren sounds even though no one has broken in. Since the feeder runs every day, this false alarm can happen whenever you're away at noon.
evidence: R1 turns on feeder.dispensing every day at 12:00, with no other conditions.
The feeder is in the kitchen.
Known dependency: when feeder.dispensing is on, motion_kitchen becomes true (the cat runs to the feeder).
R2 turns on alarm.siren when motion_kitchen becomes true and home_mode == away.
The automatic feeder exists so the cat gets fed while no one is home, so away mode at 12:00 is likely.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so kitchen motion doesn't sound the siren in a short window after the feeder runs (for example, 12:00–12:15), or make R2 use a pet-immune motion sensor or a second check like a door/entry sensor. Keep the alarm working at all other times.

explanation: At noon, R1 turns on the cat feeder. The cat then runs to the feeder, and the kitchen motion sensor detects it. That motion triggers R3, so the kitchen camera starts recording every day at feeding time even though no person is in the kitchen. This creates false recordings and may set off any alerts linked to the camera.
evidence: R1 sets feeder.dispensing := on at 12:00 with no conditions.
Known dependency: when feeder.dispensing is on, motion_kitchen becomes true because the cat runs to the feeder.
R3 is triggered by motion_kitchen == True and sets camera_kitchen.recording := on with no conditions.
The feeder and camera_kitchen are both in the kitchen.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it ignores kitchen motion during the feeding window (for example, 12:00–12:15). Another option is to make R3 record only when home_mode is 'away' or 'night', with the feeding window still excluded. Either way, the camera will still record intruders.

explanation: R4 runs the litter box cleaning cycle every day at 12:00. R5 sounds the living-room siren when it detects motion while the home is in away mode. The two rules control different devices. Running the litter box doesn't change living-room motion or the home mode, so it can't set off the siren. The only known link in this home is between the feeder and the kitchen motion sensor, and neither rule uses those.
evidence: R4 controls only litter_box.cleaning (bathroom); R5 controls only alarm.siren (living room).
R5 is triggered by motion_living and requires home_mode == away; R4 doesn't change either one.
The only known dependency in this home is that feeder.dispensing sets motion_kitchen to true. Neither rule uses the feeder or motion_kitchen.
No known dependency links litter_box.cleaning to motion_living.
repair: none

explanation: Both rules start when the kitchen detects motion. When the home is in 'home' mode, R3 turns the kitchen camera's recording on and R6 turns it off at the same moment. Which one wins depends on which rule runs last, so the camera may record when you wanted privacy, or stop when you wanted it on. The cat feeder can also set off kitchen motion, so the same clash can happen with nobody in the kitchen.
evidence: R3 trigger: motion_kitchen == True, no conditions, action camera_kitchen.recording := on
R6 trigger: motion_kitchen == True, condition home_mode == home, action camera_kitchen.recording := off
R6's condition is not ruled out by R3, so when home_mode == home both rules fire on the same event
Known dependency: feeder.dispensing on makes motion_kitchen true, which is another way to trigger both rules
repair: Add the condition home_mode != home to R3, so it only records in away or night mode and the two rules can no longer fire at the same time.

explanation: The CPAP machine is plugged into the bedside smart plug, but R1 treats that plug as only a phone charger. At 23:30 every night, R1 turns the plug off, and that cuts power to the CPAP. This can happen after R2 has already switched the CPAP on for night mode, so the machine could stop while someone is asleep and depending on it. Nothing turns the CPAP back on afterward, because R2 only runs at the moment the home switches to night mode.
evidence: R1 turns plug_bedside.power off at 23:30 every day, with no conditions.
Known dependency: when plug_bedside.power is off, cpap.power becomes off, because the CPAP is plugged into the bedside smart plug.
R2 turns cpap.power on when home_mode switches to night, so the CPAP is expected to stay running overnight.
Night mode usually starts before 23:30, so R1 would cut CPAP power after R2 has turned it on.
cpap is a medical breathing device in the bedroom.
repair: Take the bedside plug out of R1's energy-saving schedule. Either plug the phone charger into a separate plug and point R1 at that one, or add a condition to R1 so it never switches off plug_bedside while the CPAP is plugged in or home_mode is night.

explanation: R3 unlocks the entrance door when a fall is detected so paramedics can get in. R4 locks the same door when the home switches to night mode. Nothing stops both from firing close together, for example a fall in the bathroom in the evening just before the scheduled night mode. In that case R4 would lock the door again and could keep paramedics out during an emergency.
evidence: R3 sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked when fall_detected == True
R4 sets lock_entrance.lock := locked when home_mode == night
Both rules act on the same device state (lock_entrance.lock) with opposite values
Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other: R3 works in any mode and R4 does not check fall_detected
Fall detection and the switch to night mode are independent, so they can happen around the same time
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only locks the door when fall_detected == False. Also have an active fall alert block automatic re-locking until a person clears the alert.

explanation: R5 turns off the reading lamp plug at 23:30, and R2 turns the CPAP machine on when the home goes into night mode. The CPAP gets its power from the bedside plug, not the reading lamp plug. So R5 can't cut power to the CPAP, and neither rule changes anything the other one depends on.
evidence: R5 only acts on plug_reading_lamp.power (sets it to off).
R2 only acts on cpap.power (sets it to on).
The only known physical dependency links plug_bedside to cpap, not plug_reading_lamp.
Neither action changes home_mode or the 23:30 time trigger, so neither rule affects when the other one fires.
repair: none

explanation: At 10:00, R2 opens the living room window. In summer, hot outdoor air comes in and warms the room. Once it goes above 27 °C, R1 turns on the AC, which then cools the room while the window is still open. The two rules work against each other: the AC fights the open window, wasting energy and possibly never getting the room cool.
evidence: R2 sets window_living.position := open every day at 10:00 with no conditions.
Known effect: when window_living is open, temp_living increases (hot outdoor air in summer).
R1 fires when temp_living > 27 and sets ac_living.mode := cool with no check on the window.
Known effect: when ac_living is cool, temp_living decreases, so the AC and the open window push the temperature in opposite directions.
Both devices and the temperature variable are in the living_room.
repair: Add the condition "window_living.position == closed" to R1, and have R1 also set window_living.position := closed before cooling. Alternatively, only let R2 open the window when temp_living < 27 and ac_living.mode == off.

explanation: At 14:00, R3 turns on the lawn sprinkler. Its spray wets the rain sensor on the terrace, so the sensor reports rain. That makes R4 close the bedroom skylight on a dry day. The skylight stays closed for no reason, which cuts off bedroom ventilation.
evidence: R3 sets sprinkler.watering := on every day at 14:00 with no conditions.
Known dependency: when sprinkler.watering is on, rain_sensor becomes true because the spray wets the terrace rain sensor.
R4 is triggered by rain_sensor == True and sets skylight.position := closed.
The sprinkler is in the garden next to the terrace, where the rain sensor is mounted.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only fires when sprinkler.watering is off, so false rain readings during watering are ignored. Alternatively, move the rain sensor out of the sprinkler's spray area.

explanation: R5 opens the bedroom window and R4 closes the bedroom skylight. These are two separate devices, so the rules never give opposite commands to the same device. Opening the window only lowers bedroom CO2, which doesn't affect the rain sensor, and closing the skylight has no known effect on CO2. Neither rule can cause the other to run or stop it from running.
evidence: R5 acts on window_bedroom.position (open). R4 acts on skylight.position (closed). These are different devices.
Known effect: when window_bedroom is open, co2_bedroom decreases. This only affects R5's own trigger, not rain_sensor.
No known dependency links skylight.position to co2_bedroom or rain_sensor.
rain_sensor is only affected by the sprinkler, which neither rule controls.
repair: none

explanation: R5 opens the bedroom window to lower bedroom CO2, and R1 turns on the living room AC to cool the living room. They control different devices in different rooms. Neither action changes the variable that triggers the other rule. The known effect that heats the living room comes from the living room window, which neither rule moves. These rules can safely run together.
evidence: R5 only sets window_bedroom.position to open; R1 only sets ac_living.mode to cool, so the two rules never control the same device.
Opening window_bedroom only lowers co2_bedroom, which is in the bedroom, and has no listed effect on temp_living.
Setting ac_living to cool only lowers temp_living and has no listed effect on co2_bedroom.
The effect that raises temp_living comes from window_living opening, and neither R5 nor R1 moves window_living.
No rule controls the sprinkler, skylight or window_living, and no power or physical link connects the bedroom window to the living room AC.
repair: none

explanation: R2 opens the living room window at 10:00 whatever the AC is doing. R6 closes the same window only at the moment the AC switches to cooling. If the AC is already cooling at 10:00, R2 opens the window and R6 doesn't fire again, so the AC cools against an open window. If the AC starts cooling at about 10:00, the window gets 'open' and 'closed' commands almost at once and ends up in whichever state arrives last.
evidence: R2 sets window_living.position := open at time == 10:00 with no conditions
R6 sets window_living.position := closed when ac_living.mode becomes cool, with no conditions
Both rules control the same device state: window_living.position
R2 does not check the AC state, so it can fire while ac_living.mode == cool
Known effect: when window_living is open, temp_living increases, working against the AC, which lowers temp_living
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only opens the window when ac_living.mode == off (don't open the window while the AC is cooling).

explanation: When the home switches to night mode, R2 turns off the closet power strip. The NAS is plugged into that strip, so it loses power. At 01:00 the home is usually in night mode, so R1's backup either can't start or gets cut off partway through. The closet cooling fan is on the same strip, so it would also be off during any backup that did run.
evidence: R2: when home_mode == night, strip_closet.power := off
R1: at 01:00, nas.backup := running
When strip_closet.power is off, nas.power becomes off (the NAS is plugged into the closet strip)
When strip_closet.power is off, fan_closet.power becomes off (the cooling fan is plugged into the closet strip)
When nas.backup is running, temp_closet increases; the fan is what cools the closet
Night mode usually covers 01:00, so both rules apply at the same time
repair: Move the NAS and the closet fan to an outlet that is always on, not on the switched closet strip. If that isn't possible, add a condition to R2 so it only turns the strip off when nas.backup is idle, and schedule the strip to turn off after the backup finishes.

explanation: The closet cooling fan is plugged into the closet power strip. When night mode turns the strip off (R2), the fan loses power too. After that, R3 can't cool the closet even if it gets hotter than 35 °C, because its 'fan on' command does nothing. This could also leave the closet hot right after a backup, since the fan stops at the moment the strip is cut.
evidence: R2 sets strip_closet.power := off when home_mode == night
R3 sets fan_closet.power := on when temp_closet > 35
Known dependency: when strip_closet.power is off, fan_closet.power becomes off (the fan is plugged into the closet strip)
Known dependency: when strip_closet.power is off, nas.power becomes off
Known effect: nas.backup running increases temp_closet; fan on decreases temp_closet
repair: Plug the cooling fan into its own outlet or smart plug that is not on the closet strip, so R2 doesn't cut power to the fan. If you can't rewire it, add a condition to R2 so it only turns the strip off when temp_closet <= 35 and nas.backup is idle.

explanation: R1 starts the nightly NAS backup and R3 turns on the closet fan when the closet gets hotter than 35 °C. The backup heats the closet, which can make R3 turn the fan on, but that is exactly what R3 is for: the fan cools the closet while the backup runs. The two rules control different devices, and neither one turns off the closet power strip, so they work together rather than against each other.
evidence: R1 only sets nas.backup := running; R3 only sets fan_closet.power := on.
Neither rule acts on strip_closet, so the power-strip dependency is never used.
A running nas.backup raises temp_closet, which can make R3 turn the fan on. This is the intended cooling response.
A running fan_closet lowers temp_closet, which offsets the backup's heat rather than working against R1.
repair: none

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R4 turns off the printer's smart plug in the office, and R1 starts the NAS backup in the closet. The printer plug doesn't power the NAS or the closet fan, and none of the listed dependencies link the two, so neither rule can block or set off the other.
evidence: R4 only acts on plug_printer.power (office smart plug).
R1 only acts on nas.backup (closet NAS).
The NAS and closet fan are powered by strip_closet, not plug_printer.
No known dependency links plug_printer to nas, fan_closet, or temp_closet.
Neither rule's trigger (home_mode, time) is changed by the other rule's action.
repair: none

explanation: If your teenager gets home between 23:00 and 06:00, R1 unlocks the front door. That unlock then triggers R2, which locks the door again straight away. The two rules give opposite commands to the same lock. The teen could be locked out, or the lock could switch back and forth while they're at the door.
evidence: R1 sets lock_front.lock to unlocked when teen_phone_home becomes True, and it has no time condition.
R2 is triggered by lock_front.lock == unlocked and sets it to locked during 23:00–06:00.
R1's unlock action is exactly what triggers R2, so both rules fire on the same device whenever the teen arrives during that window.
Both rules control the same state, lock_front.lock, with opposite values (unlocked vs. locked).
repair: Change R2 so it relocks the door a few minutes after any unlock during 23:00–06:00 (for example, only if the door has stayed unlocked for 5 minutes), instead of relocking it instantly. The teen gets in, and the door still locks itself again at night.

explanation: R3 closes the driveway gate at 22:00 and R4 opens it at 07:00. Both rules control the same gate, but they run at different times and can never fire together. Together they make a normal daily schedule: the gate is closed overnight and open during the day.
evidence: R3 trigger: time == 22:00, action: gate.position := closed
R4 trigger: time == 07:00, action: gate.position := open
The two triggers are at different times, so the rules never fire at the same moment
Neither rule has conditions or changes any environment variable that the other rule uses
Known dependencies in this home: none
repair: none

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R5 only turns on the porch light when someone presses the doorbell. R1 only unlocks the front door when the teenager's phone arrives home. They control different devices, neither changes anything the other rule reacts to, and this home has no known links between the light and the lock.
evidence: R5 changes only porch_light.power (sets it to on); R1 changes only lock_front.lock (sets it to unlocked).
Each rule controls a different device, so they can't send opposite commands to the same device.
R5 is triggered by doorbell_pressed and R1 by teen_phone_home. Neither rule changes the other's trigger.
The home lists no known dependencies between devices (Known dependencies: none), so there is no physical conflict.
repair: none

explanation: Every day at 09:00, R1 closes the office shades. In winter, closed shades block sunlight from warming the office, so the room gets colder. Once it drops below 20 °C, R2 turns on the radiator. As a result, the shade rule ends up starting the heating, and the radiator burns energy to replace the free solar heat the shades just blocked.
evidence: R1: at 09:00 shades_office.position := closed, with no conditions
Known effect: when shades_office.position is closed, temp_office decreases (closed shades block winter solar gains)
R2 is triggered by temp_office < 20 and sets radiator_office.mode := heat, with no conditions
Known effect: when radiator_office.mode is heat, temp_office increases. The radiator is making up for heat lost because of R1
Neither rule has a condition (such as season, home_mode, or outdoor/solar conditions) that stops this chain
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it closes the shades only when temp_office is at least 21 °C, or lower the shades only partway to cut screen glare while still letting in winter sun. That way the shade rule no longer drives the office below R2's 20 °C threshold. R2 stays in place as a comfort backstop.

explanation: R2 and R4 can never fire for the same temperature, because the office can't be below 20 °C and above 24 °C at once. Together they act like a normal thermostat: the radiator turns on to heat below 20 °C and turns off above 24 °C. The 4 °C gap between them stops the radiator from switching back and forth. Heating the room until R4 turns the radiator off is the intended result, not a conflict.
evidence: R2 trigger: temp_office < 20 sets radiator_office.mode := heat
R4 trigger: temp_office > 24 sets radiator_office.mode := off
The trigger ranges (<20 and >24) don't overlap, so the rules can never fire at the same time
Known effect: radiator_office.mode = heat raises temp_office, which eventually triggers R4 to switch the radiator off, as intended
Neither rule touches the shades, the desk heater or the smart plug, so no physical dependency is involved
repair: none

explanation: Both rules start when the home switches to away mode, and both turn the desk heater off. R3 does it by cutting power at the desk plug, which also switches off the heater. R5 switches the heater off directly. Because both rules want the same result, they don't contradict each other, and neither changes the temperature or anything else another rule depends on.
evidence: R3 and R5 share the same trigger: home_mode == away.
R3 sets plug_office_heater.power := off; R5 sets desk_heater.power := off.
Physical dependency: when plug_office_heater.power is off, desk_heater.power becomes off. This gives the same result R5 sets directly.
Neither rule sets any device to on or heat, and neither affects temp_office or home_mode.
repair: none

explanation: Both rules run at exactly 09:00 and neither has any condition, so they always fire together. R1 closes the office shades and R6 opens them. Which one wins depends on execution order, so the shades may end up in a random position or move back and forth.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 09:00, no conditions, action shades_office.position := closed
R6 trigger: time == 09:00, no conditions, action shades_office.position := open
shades_office.position has the mutually exclusive states open and closed
Closed shades lower temp_office (blocking winter solar gains), so the result also affects office temperature
repair: Make the two rules exclusive with a condition. For example, run R1 (close for screen work) only when the office is in use for screen work or when home_mode == home. Run R6 (open for daylight) only otherwise. Another option is to move R6 to a different time, such as opening the shades after the screen-work block ends.

explanation: At 19:30, R2 turns on the white-noise speaker in the nursery. The baby monitor's microphone picks up the white noise, so the measured sound level in the nursery goes up. If it goes above 60 dB, R1 thinks the baby is crying and turns on the nursery lamp even though the baby may be quiet. That could wake the baby at bedtime and make the crying alert unreliable.
evidence: R2 sets white_noise.playing to on at 19:30 every day, with no conditions.
Known dependency: when white_noise.playing is on, noise_nursery increases, because the baby monitor microphone picks up the white noise.
R1 fires whenever noise_nursery is above 60 dB and has no conditions, so it cannot tell crying from white noise.
R1 turns on nursery_lamp, the light in the same room where the white noise is meant to help the baby sleep.
repair: Set the white-noise speaker's volume so the monitor reads well below 60 dB. Then add a condition to R1 so that while white_noise.playing is on, it only fires above a higher threshold (for example, the white-noise baseline plus 10 dB, such as noise_nursery > 70). The white noise alone will then no longer turn on the lamp.

explanation: When the TV is turned on in the evening, R3 turns on the soundbar. The soundbar shares a thin wall with the nursery, so the baby monitor picks up its sound. If the level goes above 60 dB, R1 thinks the baby is crying and turns on the nursery lamp, which could wake a sleeping baby.
evidence: R3 sets soundbar.power to on when the TV turns on between 20:00 and 23:59
Known dependency: when soundbar.power is on, noise_nursery increases (the soundbar shares a thin wall with the nursery)
R1 is triggered when noise_nursery > 60 and has no conditions, so it can't tell the soundbar apart from a crying baby
R1 turns on nursery_lamp.power, and 20:00 to 23:59 is a time when the baby is likely asleep
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only fires when soundbar.power is off. Alternatively, raise R1's threshold while the soundbar is on, or move the soundbar away from the shared wall or turn its volume down after 20:00.

explanation: R4 only turns off the living-room TV, and R2 only turns on the nursery white-noise speaker. They control different devices, so their actions can't clash. White noise does raise the nursery sound level, but neither rule checks that level. The TV has no listed link to the speaker or to the nursery.
evidence: R4 acts only on tv.power (off) when home_mode becomes night.
R2 acts only on white_noise.playing (on) at 19:30.
white_noise.playing=on raises noise_nursery, but neither rule uses noise_nursery as a trigger or condition.
There is no listed dependency between the TV and the white-noise speaker, home_mode, or noise_nursery.
repair: none

explanation: When there is a frost warning, R1 turns on the greenhouse heater. Once the heater pushes the greenhouse above 18 °C, R2 opens the roof vent. The open vent lets warm air out on a frosty night, which works against the heater. Neither rule turns the heater off or closes the vent, so the heater keeps running while heat escapes. This wastes energy, and the vent may be left open in freezing weather.
evidence: R1: frost_warning == True -> gh_heater.power := on
R2: temp_gh > 18 -> gh_vent.position := open
Dependency: when gh_heater.power is on, temp_gh increases (the heater can push temp_gh above 18 °C and set off R2)
Dependency: when gh_vent.position is open, temp_gh decreases (the open vent works against the heater)
Neither rule turns the heater off or closes the vent, so both can stay active at the same time during a frost warning
repair: Add a condition to R2 so the vent only opens when frost_warning == False. If you need venting during a frost warning, use a higher threshold, such as temp_gh > 25, and turn the heater off before the vent opens.

explanation: The greenhouse heater gets its power from the outdoor smart plug. R1 turns the heater on when there's a frost warning, but R3 switches the outdoor plug off every night at 22:00. That cuts power to the heater, so on a frost night the greenhouse can go unheated through the coldest hours.
evidence: R1 sets gh_heater.power to on when frost_warning == True
R3 sets plug_outdoor.power to off at 22:00 with no conditions
Known dependency: when plug_outdoor.power is off, gh_heater.power becomes off (the heater is plugged into the outdoor plug)
Frost warnings are often still active at 22:00, so both rules can apply at the same time
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only turns off the outdoor plug when frost_warning == False. Another option is to move the greenhouse heater to an outlet that isn't switched off at night.

explanation: R4 only turns on the grow lights at 06:00, and R2 only opens the roof vent when the greenhouse is warmer than 18 °C. They control different devices. No dependency in this home links the grow lights to the vent or to the greenhouse temperature, so neither rule can block the other or set it off by accident.
evidence: R4 acts only on grow_lights.power (on) at a fixed time, 06:00.
R2 acts only on gh_vent.position (open) when temp_gh > 18.
The two rules control different devices, so their actions can't contradict each other.
The only things known to change temp_gh are gh_heater (raises it) and gh_vent (lowers it). No dependency says grow_lights affect temp_gh.
The only physical dependency is plug_outdoor → gh_heater, and neither rule uses either device.
repair: none

explanation: R2 opens the roof vent above 18 °C and R5 closes it below 5 °C. Both can't be true at once, so the rules never fire together. The 5–18 °C gap keeps the vent from flipping open and shut. If the open vent cooled the greenhouse below 5 °C, R5 closing it is the frost protection working as intended, not a conflict.
evidence: R2 trigger: temp_gh > 18 -> gh_vent.position := open
R5 trigger: temp_gh < 5 -> gh_vent.position := closed
The trigger ranges (>18 and <5) can't both be true, so the actions never compete
Known effect: an open vent lowers temp_gh. Getting from 18 °C down to 5 °C means crossing the 5–18 °C gap, where neither rule fires
Closing the vent doesn't actively raise temp_gh above 18, so R2 isn't set off again and there's no loop
repair: none

explanation: R1 turns on the greenhouse heater when there is a frost warning. But the heater is plugged into the outdoor plug, so when R3 switches that plug off at 22:00 the heater loses power and the plants have no frost protection overnight. There is also a smaller issue: the heater warms the greenhouse above 18 °C, which makes R2 open the roof vent and let the heat out while the frost warning is still active.
evidence: R1: frost_warning == True -> gh_heater.power := on
R3: at 22:00 -> plug_outdoor.power := off
Physical dependency: when plug_outdoor.power is off, gh_heater.power becomes off (heater is plugged into the outdoor plug)
Frost warnings typically cover the night, so they can still be active at 22:00
Secondary: gh_heater on increases temp_gh; R2 opens gh_vent when temp_gh > 18; an open vent lowers temp_gh
repair: Add the condition "frost_warning == False" to R3 so the outdoor plug, and with it the heater, stays powered during a frost warning. Optionally add the same condition to R2 so the vent doesn't open during a frost warning.

explanation: Frost warnings often start in the evening and last overnight. If one is issued before 22:00, R1 turns the greenhouse heater on, but R6 turns it off at 22:00 even though the warning is still active. R1 only fires when a warning is first issued, so it won't turn the heater back on. That leaves the greenhouse unheated during the coldest part of the night.
evidence: R1 turns gh_heater.power on when frost_warning becomes True, with no time limit.
R6 turns gh_heater.power off at 22:00 with no conditions, so it doesn't check the frost warning.
Both rules control the same device (gh_heater.power) and set it to opposite states.
A frost warning can still be active at 22:00, so both rules can apply on the same night.
When gh_heater is on, temp_gh increases, so turning it off removes the greenhouse's frost protection.
repair: Add a condition to R6 so it only turns off the heater when frost_warning == False. You could also add a rule that turns the heater on whenever a frost warning is active, so the heater comes back on if it gets switched off.

explanation: The hallway camera gets its power from the hallway smart plug. Every night at 23:00, R1 turns that plug off, which also turns off the camera. If the home is in away mode, R2 expects the camera to be recording, but with no power it records nothing. The front door goes unwatched from 23:00 onward while nobody is home.
evidence: R1 turns plug_hall.power off at 23:00 every day, with no conditions.
Known physical dependency: when plug_hall.power is off, camera_hall.power becomes off, because the camera is powered through the hallway smart plug.
R2 sets camera_hall.recording to on when home_mode is away, and needs the camera to have power.
Nothing stops R1 from running while home_mode is away, so both situations can happen at the same time.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only turns off the hallway plug when home_mode is not away. Alternatively, plug the camera into a socket that is always on, so the energy-saving rule can't cut its power.

explanation: R3 locks the front door when the home goes into night mode. R4 unlocks the same door whenever the hallway sensor detects motion between 22:00 and 06:00. Night mode is usually on during those hours, so both rules can fire at the same time. Any movement in the hallway, such as walking to the bathroom or a pet, would unlock the door and undo the night lock, leaving the apartment unlocked overnight.
evidence: R3 sets lock_front.lock := locked when home_mode == night
R4 sets lock_front.lock := unlocked when motion_hall == True during 22:00-06:00
Both rules control the same device state, lock_front.lock, with opposite values
R4 has no condition on home_mode, so it can fire while night mode is on
The 22:00-06:00 window for R4 overlaps the hours when night mode is normally on
lock_front and motion_hall are both in the hallway, so normal movement near the door can trigger R4
repair: Add the condition home_mode != night to R4 so motion can't unlock the door while night mode is on. Alternatively, replace R4's motion trigger with a deliberate action, such as an inside button or an unlock from the app, so the door only unlocks when someone actually wants to leave.

explanation: I found no conflict between these two rules. R5 only turns off the living room lamp at 23:00. R2 only starts recording on the hallway camera when the home switches to away mode. They control different devices, and neither one changes anything the other rule depends on, such as the home mode or the hallway plug that powers the camera.
evidence: R5 changes only lamp_living.power (sets it to off).
R2 changes only camera_hall.recording (sets it to on), triggered by home_mode == away.
The only known dependency is that turning off plug_hall turns off camera_hall. Neither rule changes plug_hall.
Turning off the lamp does not change home_mode or motion_hall, so it cannot set off or block R2.
repair: none

explanation: R1 turns off the hallway smart plug at 23:00, and R3 locks the front door when the home switches to night mode. They control different devices, their actions don't contradict each other, and neither changes anything the other rule depends on. R1 does also turn off the hallway camera through the plug, but R3 doesn't use the camera, so the two rules don't conflict.
evidence: R1 acts only on plug_hall.power (off at 23:00).
R3 acts only on lock_front.lock (locked when home_mode == night).
The only known dependency links plug_hall to camera_hall power, not to lock_front or home_mode.
Neither rule changes home_mode or motion_hall, so neither can cause or block the other's trigger.
repair: none

explanation: R1 turns on the living room heater at 18:00, and nothing turns it off. As the heater warms the room past 26 °C, R2 turns on the fan and opens the window. Cold outdoor air then comes in while the heater keeps running, so the two rules work against each other and waste energy. The room may also cycle between warming up and cooling down.
evidence: R1 sets heater_living.power := on at 18:00 and has no rule that turns it off.
Known effect: when heater_living.power is on, temp_living increases.
R2 fires when temp_living > 26 and sets window_living.position := open and vent_living.power := on.
Known effect: when window_living.position is open, temp_living decreases (cold outdoor air in heating season).
Nothing in R2 turns the heater off, so the heater and the open window run at the same time.
repair: Change R2 so it first turns off heater_living (heater_living.power := off) when temp_living > 26, and only opens the window and runs the fan if the room is still above 26 °C after the heater is off. Also add an upper limit to R1, such as only heating while temp_living < 24.

explanation: R3 turns on the bedroom heater, which only warms the bedroom. R2 runs when the living room gets warmer than 26 C. These rules control different devices, and nothing in this home connects the bedroom heater to the living room temperature. Neither rule can set off or block the other.
evidence: R3 only controls heater_bedroom.power, and R2 only controls vent_living.power and window_living.position, so they share no device.
heater_bedroom.power = on raises temp_bedroom, not temp_living.
R2 is triggered by temp_living > 26, which no action in R3 changes.
No known dependency links the bedroom heater to the living room temperature, ventilation fan or window.
repair: none

explanation: When the living room goes above 26 °C, R2 opens the window, and no rule ever closes it. During the heating season the open window keeps cooling the room until it drops below 19 °C. Then R4 turns on the heater while the window is still open, which wastes energy. The heater is never turned off either, so it can push the room back above 26 °C and start the cycle again.
evidence: R2 sets window_living.position := open when temp_living > 26, and no rule closes it again.
Known effect: when window_living is open, temp_living decreases (cold outdoor air in the heating season).
R4 turns heater_living on when temp_living < 19, with no condition about the window.
Known effect: when heater_living is on, temp_living increases, and no rule turns the heater off, so the room can heat back above 26 °C and fire R2 again.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only runs when window_living.position is closed. Also add a companion rule: when temp_living drops below about 22 °C, close window_living and turn off vent_living.

explanation: Both rules run at exactly 18:00 and act on the living room heater. When the home is in away mode, R1 turns the heater on while R5 turns it off. So the heater's final state depends on which rule happens to run last, and the heater could be left running in an empty house.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 18:00, no conditions, action heater_living.power := on
R5 trigger: time == 18:00, condition home_mode == away, action heater_living.power := off
home_mode can be 'away', so both rules can fire at the same moment
on and off are incompatible states of heater_living.power
When heater_living is on, temp_living rises, so an unintended 'on' heats an empty house
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so it only turns the heater on when someone is home. The two rules then never apply at the same time, and R5 reliably keeps the heater off in away mode.

explanation: At 10:00 on weekdays, R1 starts the robot vacuum in the living room. The moving vacuum sets off the living room motion sensor, so R2 thinks someone is home and unlocks the front door. This can happen when nobody is home, which leaves the house unlocked.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays, with no conditions.
The vacuum is in the living_room.
Known dependency: when vacuum.mode is cleaning, motion_living becomes true because the motion sensor detects the moving vacuum.
R2 is triggered by motion_living == True, has no conditions, and sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked.
Weekday mid-morning is a time when the household is often away, and R2 does not check home_mode or presence.
repair: Add conditions to R2 so it only unlocks when vacuum.mode == docked and home_mode == home. Better still, use a reliable presence signal instead of living room motion to decide when to unlock the door.

explanation: R1 starts the robot vacuum at 10:00 regardless of whether anyone is home. The living room motion sensor picks up the moving vacuum, so if the house is in away mode, R3 treats it as an intruder and sounds the siren. This causes a false alarm whenever the vacuum runs while you're out, which is a common time to schedule cleaning.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 with no conditions
Known dependency: when vacuum.mode is cleaning, motion_living becomes true (the vacuum is detected by the living room PIR sensor)
R3 triggers on motion_living == True with condition home_mode == away and sets alarm.siren := on
The vacuum is in the living_room, the same room as the motion_living sensor
Nothing stops home_mode from being away at 10:00 on a weekday
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only sounds the siren when vacuum.mode == docked, or ignore living room motion while the vacuum is cleaning. That way the alarm still works whenever the vacuum isn't running.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. When the vacuum runs (R1), it sets off the living room motion sensor. R4 only reacts to the bedroom motion sensor, so the vacuum can't turn on the entrance light. The rules also control different devices (the vacuum and the entrance light), so their actions can't clash.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00.
Known effect: vacuum.mode == cleaning makes motion_living true, not motion_bedroom.
R4 is triggered only by motion_bedroom == True.
The vacuum is in the living_room, and R4's trigger sensor is in the bedroom.
R1 acts on vacuum and R4 acts on light_entrance. These are different devices, and neither has a stated power or physical link to the other.
repair: none

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door so people can get out when the kitchen smoke detector goes off. R2 locks the same door when the home switches to away mode. Neither rule checks the other's situation. If the home switches to away while smoke is still detected, R2 relocks the door that R1 unlocked for the escape route. If both fire at about the same time, the door could end up either locked or unlocked depending on which runs last.
evidence: R1 sets lock_door.lock := unlocked when smoke_kitchen == True, with no conditions
R2 sets lock_door.lock := locked when home_mode == away, with no conditions
Both rules act on the same device (lock_door, the apartment door lock) and set opposite states
home_mode and smoke_kitchen are separate variables, so both rules can fire in the same situation (for example, an oven left on when the occupants leave)
repair: Add the condition smoke_kitchen == False to R2, so the door only locks in away mode when no smoke is detected. Give R1's unlock priority over any lock command while smoke is present.

explanation: R1 turns the air handler off when the kitchen smoke detector goes off, so smoke isn't spread through the apartment. R4 turns the same air handler on at 08:00 and doesn't check for smoke. If smoke is still there at 08:00, R4 switches the air handler back on and undoes R1's safety action.
evidence: R1 sets hvac.power := off when smoke_kitchen == True
R4 sets hvac.power := on at time == 08:00 with no conditions
R4 does not check smoke_kitchen, so it can fire while smoke is still detected
Both rules control the same device state (hvac.power) with opposite values
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only turns on the air handler when smoke_kitchen == False. If smoke is detected at 08:00, the air handler stays off.

explanation: R3 turns on the range hood when the oven is switched on. R2 locks the apartment door when the home switches to away mode. The two rules control different devices, and neither one changes anything the other rule depends on. When the hood runs it clears kitchen smoke, but no rule here reacts to smoke, so this doesn't cause a conflict.
evidence: R3 acts only on hood.power; R2 acts only on lock_door.lock — no shared device.
R3's trigger is oven.power; R2's trigger is home_mode — neither rule's action changes the other's trigger.
The only known dependency (hood on -> smoke_kitchen false) affects a variable that neither rule uses.
repair: none

explanation: At 00:30, R1 turns off the office plug. The Wi-Fi router is plugged into that plug, so it shuts down too. Without Wi-Fi, the garden camera can't upload to the cloud, which R2 turned on for night mode. The doorbell also stops sending notifications. Your overnight camera footage won't be backed up to the cloud, even though the rules don't show any link between them.
evidence: R1 sets plug_office.power to off every day at 00:30, with no conditions.
R2 sets camera_garden.cloud_upload and camera_garden.recording to on when home_mode is night, which covers 00:30.
The router is plugged into the office smart plug: when plug_office.power is off, router.power becomes off.
The garden camera uploads over Wi-Fi: when router.power is off, camera_garden.cloud_upload becomes off.
Doorbell notifications use Wi-Fi: when router.power is off, doorbell.notifications becomes off.
repair: Plug the router into an always-on wall socket instead of the office smart plug, so R1 only cuts standby power to the desk devices. If you can't move it, add the condition "home_mode != night" to R1.

explanation: At 00:30, R1 turns off the office plug. The Wi-Fi router is plugged into that plug, so the router loses power too. Without Wi-Fi, the doorbell can't send the notifications that R3 turns on when you're away, so you won't get doorbell alerts from 00:30 onward. The garden camera also stops uploading to the cloud.
evidence: R1 sets plug_office.power to off every day at 00:30, with no conditions.
Known dependency: when plug_office.power is off, router.power becomes off (the router is plugged into the office smart plug).
Known dependency: when router.power is off, doorbell.notifications becomes off (notifications are sent over Wi-Fi).
R3 sets doorbell.notifications to on when home_mode is away, and R1 has no condition that stops it in away mode.
Known dependency: when router.power is off, camera_garden.cloud_upload becomes off.
repair: Plug the router into a regular outlet that is always on, not the office smart plug. Then R1 only cuts standby power to the desk equipment. If you can't move the router, add a condition to R1 so it runs only when home_mode is not away.

explanation: R4 only turns off the desk lamp plug at 00:30. R2 turns on the garden camera's cloud upload and recording in night mode. The router that the camera needs for uploads is on the separate office plug, which R4 never touches. So the two rules don't affect each other.
evidence: R4 acts only on plug_desk_lamp.power := off
R2 acts only on camera_garden.cloud_upload and camera_garden.recording
The router depends on plug_office, not plug_desk_lamp
No known dependency links plug_desk_lamp to any other device or to home_mode
repair: none

explanation: R4 only turns off the desk lamp plug at 00:30, and R3 only turns on doorbell notifications when the home goes into away mode. The desk lamp plug has no known link to the router or the doorbell. The plug that powers the router is a different one (plug_office), so R4 can't cut Wi-Fi or silence doorbell notifications.
evidence: R4 acts only on plug_desk_lamp.power; R3 acts only on doorbell.notifications.
The router is powered by plug_office, not plug_desk_lamp.
No known dependency links plug_desk_lamp to router or doorbell.
Neither action changes home_mode, the variable that triggers R3.
