explanation: In night mode, R1 turns off the living room power strip. The aquarium heater and the filter/oxygen pump are both plugged into that strip, so they lose power too. If the water then drops below 24 C, R2 will try to turn the heater on, but it can't work without power. The fish could end up in cold water with no filtering or oxygen all night.
evidence: R1 sets strip_living.power to off when home_mode == night, with no conditions
R2 sets aquarium_heater.power to on when water_temp < 24
The aquarium heater is plugged into strip_living, so when the strip is off, aquarium_heater.power becomes off
The aquarium pump is plugged into strip_living, so when the strip is off, aquarium_pump.power becomes off
The heater is the only listed thing that raises water_temp, so with no power the water can't be kept above 24 C
repair: Plug the aquarium heater and pump into an outlet that is always on, not into strip_living. Or change R1 so it only turns off the TV smart plug (plug_tv), which still cuts the TV's standby power, and leave the strip that feeds the aquarium on.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R3 turns off the TV smart plug, which only cuts power to the TV. The aquarium heater that R2 turns on is plugged into the living room power strip, not the TV plug. The rules control different devices and don't change each other's triggers.
evidence: R3 sets plug_tv.power to off, and the only dependency on plug_tv is tv.power becoming off.
The aquarium heater gets its power from strip_living, not plug_tv. No rule here changes strip_living.
R2's trigger is water_temp, and R3's action doesn't affect it. R2's action raises water_temp, which doesn't affect home_mode.
repair: none

explanation: R2 turns the aquarium heater on below 24 °C and R4 turns it off above 28 °C. These conditions can never be true at the same time, so the rules can't fire together. When R2's heating eventually sets off R4, that's the intended thermostat behavior that keeps the water between 24 °C and 28 °C, not a conflict.
evidence: R2 trigger: water_temp < 24 -> aquarium_heater.power := on
R4 trigger: water_temp > 28 -> aquarium_heater.power := off
The trigger ranges (<24 and >28) don't overlap, so the rules can't fire at the same time
When aquarium_heater.power is on, water_temp increases, so heating eventually triggers R4, which is the intended thermostat behavior
Neither rule acts on strip_living, so there is no physical power dependency between them
repair: none

explanation: R5 and R2 give opposite commands to the same aquarium heater (off and on), and nothing stops them from firing at the same time. At night, R5 turns the heater off. The water then cools, and once it drops below 24 °C, R2 turns the heater back on. If night mode starts while the water is already cold, one rule turns the heater off and the other turns it on. The heater may switch back and forth, and the fish could be left without heat.
evidence: R5 sets aquarium_heater.power := off when home_mode == night, with no conditions.
R2 sets aquarium_heater.power := on when water_temp < 24, with no conditions.
Neither rule's conditions exclude the other: the water can be below 24 °C at night.
Known effect: the heater raises water_temp, so turning it off lets the water cool and can trigger R2.
repair: Add a condition to R5 so it only turns the heater off when water_temp >= 25 °C. Keep R2 as it is, so the heater always comes back on when the water drops below 24 °C, including at night.

explanation: When the home is in away mode, R1 closes the main water valve. The garden irrigation gets its water through that same valve. At 06:00, R2 still turns watering and flow on, but no water can reach the sprinklers. The controller will show it is watering when it isn't, and the garden won't get watered while you're away.
evidence: R1 sets valve_main.state to closed when home_mode == away.
R2 sets irrigation.watering and irrigation.flow to on every day at 06:00, with no conditions.
Known physical dependency: when valve_main.state is closed, irrigation.flow becomes off, because the irrigation line is supplied through the main water valve.
Nothing stops R2 from running while home_mode is away, so the 06:00 schedule overlaps with the valve being closed.
repair: Keep R1 as it is, since the main shut-off protects the house against leaks. Add the condition home_mode != away to R2 so the schedule doesn't run while the house water is shut off, and send a notification that watering was skipped. If the garden must be watered while you're away, have a plumber supply the irrigation line through the separate garden valve (valve_garden) instead of the main valve.

explanation: At 06:00, R2 starts watering. Watering raises soil moisture, and once it goes above 60% R4 turns watering off. R2 never checks the soil, so on days when moisture is already above 60% it still starts watering, and R4 may not fire because moisture never crosses the 60% line. The garden could then keep watering wet soil. Also, R4 turns off only 'watering' and leaves 'flow' on, so the controller can end up in a mismatched state.
evidence: R2: at 06:00 sets irrigation.watering := on and irrigation.flow := on, with no conditions
R4: when soil_moisture > 60, sets irrigation.watering := off (flow is not changed)
Known effect: when irrigation.watering is on, soil_moisture increases
R4's trigger is a threshold crossing, so it may not fire if moisture is already above 60% when R2 starts watering
repair: Add the condition 'soil_moisture <= 60' to R2 so it only waters dry soil, and have R4 also set irrigation.flow := off so the controller ends up fully off.

explanation: R5 closes the outdoor tap valve (valve_garden) and R2 turns on the garden sprinklers (irrigation). They control different devices. The only listed dependency that can stop sprinkler flow involves the main water valve (valve_main), not the outdoor tap valve. Neither rule changes a variable that starts or blocks the other, so they can run together safely.
evidence: R5 acts only on valve_garden.state (closed); R2 acts only on irrigation.watering and irrigation.flow.
valve_garden is described as a separate valve on the outdoor tap line.
The only physical dependency stopping irrigation flow is valve_main.state == closed, which neither rule touches.
R2's watering raises soil_moisture, but R5 is triggered only by home_mode, which is unaffected.
repair: none

explanation: On a bright day, R1 closes the living room blinds to cut glare. Closed blinds block daylight, so the light level can drop below 150 lux, which sets off R2 and turns the ceiling lights on in the middle of the day. Nothing reopens the blinds, so the room stays artificially lit while the sun is out. This wastes energy and isn't what either rule is meant to do.
evidence: R1 sets blinds_living.position to closed when lux_living > 800.
Known dependency: when blinds_living.position is closed, lux_living decreases (closed blinds block daylight).
R2 turns lights_living on when lux_living < 150, with no other conditions.
Neither rule reopens the blinds or checks whether the blinds are closed, so the lights can stay on in daytime.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only turns on the lights when blinds_living.position is open (or only after sunset). Another option is to have R2 open the blinds partly before it turns the lights on.

explanation: R3 opens the living room blinds at 07:30 and R4 closes them at 22:00. They control the same blinds, but at two different times that can never fire together, so they make a normal daily schedule. Closing the blinds does lower the living room light level (lux_living), but neither rule depends on that value, so it doesn't affect the other rule.
evidence: R3 triggers only at time == 07:30 and sets blinds_living.position := open
R4 triggers only at time == 22:00 and sets blinds_living.position := closed
The two trigger times are different, so the rules never fire at the same moment
Neither rule has conditions that depend on lux_living, so the effect of closing the blinds on light level doesn't change whether either rule fires
repair: none

explanation: R1 and R5 don't conflict. R1 closes the living room blinds when that room gets too bright, and R5 turns on the study desk light when the study gets too dark. They control different devices in different rooms. Closing the living room blinds only lowers the living room light level and doesn't affect the study reading that R5 uses.
evidence: R1 only acts on blinds_living.position; R5 only acts on lights_study.power, so no device is shared.
R1 is triggered by lux_living, and R5 is triggered by lux_study.
Closing blinds_living affects only lux_living, according to the known dependencies.
No known dependency links blinds_living or lights_study to lux_study or lux_living in a way that would trigger the other rule.
No power or physical dependency connects the devices involved.
repair: none

explanation: Both rules control the living room blinds and give opposite commands: R3 opens them and R1 closes them. Neither rule has a condition that keeps them apart. On a bright morning, R3 opens the blinds at 07:30 and lets daylight in. If the room then goes above 800 lux, R1 closes them right away. The blinds would open and then shut again, so the 07:30 opening doesn't stick.
evidence: R3 sets blinds_living.position := open at 07:30, with no conditions.
R1 sets blinds_living.position := closed when lux_living > 800, with no conditions.
Both rules act on the same device state (blinds_living.position) and set it to opposite values (open vs. closed).
Nothing in either rule (no time window or lux check) stops both from firing on a bright morning.
Opening the blinds lets daylight into the living room, which can push lux_living above 800 and trigger R1. (The home's dependency list only states the reverse: closed blinds lower lux_living.)
repair: Set an explicit priority between the rules. One option is to make R3 open the blinds only partway, or only if it isn't sunny, and let R1's glare protection win when lux_living is above 800. Another is to add a condition to R1 so it doesn't fire for a short period (for example 15 minutes) after R3 opens the blinds, and then closes them only if the room is still above 800 lux.

explanation: At 20:00, R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which raises the humidity in the nursery. Once it goes above 55%, R2 turns on the dehumidifier while the humidifier is still running. The two machines then work against each other all night. This wastes energy and the room never settles at a steady humidity for the baby.
evidence: R1 turns on humidifier_nursery at 20:00 with no humidity limit and no off action.
When humidifier_nursery is on, humidity_nursery goes up.
R2 turns on dehumidifier_nursery when humidity_nursery is above 55, with no other conditions.
When dehumidifier_nursery is on, humidity_nursery goes down, which works directly against the humidifier.
Neither rule turns the other device off, so both can run at the same time.
repair: Have R2 also turn humidifier_nursery off (or add a 'humidifier_nursery.power == off' condition to R2). Also add a condition to R1 so it only turns the humidifier on when humidity_nursery is below a lower threshold, such as 45%. This leaves a gap between the two thresholds, so the devices never run together.

explanation: R3 and R4 work as a matched on/off pair. The fan turns on above 70% humidity and off below 50%. Humidity can't be above 70% and below 50% at once, so the two rules never fire together. The gap between 50% and 70% also stops the fan from switching on and off over and over. The fan lowering humidity until R4 turns it off is how the pair is meant to work, so this isn't a conflict.
evidence: R3 trigger: humidity_bath > 70 → fan_bath.power := on
R4 trigger: humidity_bath < 50 → fan_bath.power := off
The triggers can't both be true at once (>70 vs <50)
There's a 20-point gap (50–70%) where neither rule fires, so the fan doesn't rapidly switch on and off
When fan_bath.power is on, humidity_bath decreases. This leads to R4 turning the fan off, which is the intended result
No other rule acts on fan_bath or humidity_bath. The nursery devices and the towel_heater aren't connected to these rules
repair: none

explanation: R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which only raises humidity in the nursery. R3 depends only on bathroom humidity and controls the bathroom fan. The two rules control different devices, and no known dependency links nursery humidity to bathroom humidity, so neither rule can trigger or block the other.
evidence: R1 acts on humidifier_nursery.power; R3 acts on fan_bath.power, which are different devices.
The humidifier only increases humidity_nursery; R3 is triggered by humidity_bath.
The fan only decreases humidity_bath, which R1 does not use (R1 is triggered by time).
No dependency between the nursery and bathroom humidity, or any shared power dependency, is listed for this home.
repair: none

explanation: R2 turns the nursery dehumidifier on whenever humidity goes above 55 %, and R5 turns it off at 20:00. Neither rule has a time window or humidity condition that keeps the other from running. If the nursery is humid in the evening, R5 switches the dehumidifier off. As humidity rises again, R2 switches it back on during the night. The device keeps flipping between on and off, and you end up with either a noisy nursery or a risk of mould.
evidence: R2: trigger humidity_nursery > 55, no conditions, action dehumidifier_nursery.power := on
R5: trigger time == 20:00, no conditions, action dehumidifier_nursery.power := off
Both rules control the same state, dehumidifier_nursery.power, with opposite values
When dehumidifier_nursery.power is on, humidity_nursery decreases; once it is off, humidity can rise above 55 % again and set off R2 after 20:00
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs from 07:00 to 20:00, matching your quiet hours. For overnight mould protection, set a separate, higher night threshold (for example, above 65 %) or use a quiet or low-fan mode if the dehumidifier has one.

explanation: At night, R1 turns off the bedroom wall switch. That cuts power to the bedroom bulb, because the bulb is wired behind that switch's relay. When the wake-up alarm rings in the morning, R2 tells the bulb to turn on at 60 %. The bulb has no power, so it can't respond, and nothing in R2 turns the switch back on. As a result, the wake-up light silently fails.
evidence: R1: when home_mode == night, switch_bedroom.power := off
Known dependency: when switch_bedroom.power is off, bulb_bedroom.power becomes off (the bulb is wired behind the bedroom wall switch relay)
R2: when alarm_clock == True, bulb_bedroom.power := on and brightness := 60, with no action on switch_bedroom
The alarm usually rings while the home is still in night mode, so the switch is still off when R2 runs
repair: Add switch_bedroom.power := on as the first action of R2, before it turns on the bulb and sets the brightness. Another option is to change R1 so it turns off bulb_bedroom (the bulb itself) instead of cutting power at the wall switch.

explanation: R3 turns the corridor bulb off when the home switches into night mode, and R4 turns it back on at 06:30. They act on the same bulb but at different moments, so they never give opposite commands at the same time. Together they make a normal evening-off, morning-on routine.
evidence: R3 is triggered by the event home_mode == night and sets bulb_corridor.power to off
R4 is triggered by time == 06:30 and sets bulb_corridor.power to on
The two triggers are separate events that are not expected to happen at the same moment
Neither rule acts on switch_corridor, so the wiring that cuts power to the corridor bulb is not involved
repair: none

explanation: R1 and R4 control different devices in different rooms. R1 turns off the bedroom wall switch, which also turns off the bedroom bulb. R4 turns on the corridor bulb, which depends only on the corridor switch, and neither rule changes that switch. Neither rule changes anything the other rule uses to start, so they don't affect each other.
evidence: R1 acts only on switch_bedroom.power (off), triggered by home_mode == night
R4 acts only on bulb_corridor.power (on), triggered by time == 06:30
switch_bedroom only cuts power to bulb_bedroom, not bulb_corridor
bulb_corridor depends on switch_corridor, which neither rule changes
Neither action changes home_mode or the time, so neither rule can trigger or block the other
repair: none

explanation: Both rules control the same thermostat, and their time windows overlap. R1 sets the thermostat to 23 C in heat mode at 18:00. R2 sets it to 19 C in eco mode when someone arrives home between 17:00 and 19:00. If someone gets home around 18:00, or arrives between 18:00 and 19:00 after R1 has run, the two rules give opposite settings. The thermostat ends up with whichever rule ran last.
evidence: R1 fires at 18:00 and sets thermostat.setpoint := 23 and thermostat.mode := heat
R2 fires when home_mode changes to home and time is in [17:00, 19:00], and sets thermostat.setpoint := 19 and thermostat.mode := eco
18:00 falls inside R2's 17:00-19:00 window, so both rules can act on the thermostat in the same period
The thermostat's mode can only be one of heat, eco or off at a time, and the setpoint can only hold one value (23 or 19)
repair: Make the windows stop overlapping, and pick which rule wins if they still meet. For example, limit R2 to arrivals between 17:00 and 17:59. Or add a condition to R2 that it only runs when the thermostat isn't already in heat mode at 23 C, so the 18:00 comfort setting stays in place.

explanation: The two rules have different triggers (above 24 °C and below 20 °C), but neither rule turns anything off. Once R3 sets the AC to cool, it keeps cooling and can bring the room below 20 °C. That fires R4, which turns on the heating while the AC is still cooling. The two devices then work against each other: the heating can push the room back above 24 °C, which keeps the AC cooling, and energy is wasted in a loop.
evidence: R3 sets ac_living.mode := cool when temp_living > 24 and never turns it off
R4 sets thermostat.mode := heat when temp_living < 20 and never turns it off
Known effect: when ac_living.mode is cool, temp_living decreases, which can drop it below 20 and fire R4
Known effect: when thermostat.mode is heat, temp_living increases, which can push it above 24 and fire R3 again
Both devices are in the living_room and affect the same variable, temp_living
repair: Make each rule turn off the opposite device: add thermostat.mode := eco (or off) to R3 and ac_living.mode := off to R4. Also stop each device when the room reaches a comfortable temperature, for example turn the AC off at or below 22 °C and the heating off at or above 21 °C.

explanation: R1 and R5 both change the thermostat mode, but they run at different times. R1 switches to heat at 18:00 and R5 switches to eco at 08:00, so they never fire together. Together they make a normal daily schedule (warm in the evening, energy-saving during the day), not a conflict. Neither rule reacts to temperature or another context variable, so the heating effect on temp_living can't set off or block the other rule.
evidence: R1 fires only at time == 18:00 and sets thermostat.mode := heat, setpoint := 23
R5 fires only at time == 08:00 and sets thermostat.mode := eco
The two triggers are fixed, separate times, so the actions never happen at the same moment
Neither rule has a trigger or condition based on temp_living, so the heating effect (thermostat heat raises temp_living) can't cause either rule to fire unexpectedly
Neither rule controls ac_living, so there is no heating vs. cooling clash
repair: none

explanation: When the home is in away mode, R1 turns off the garage circuit breaker. The exhaust fan runs on that circuit. If carbon monoxide is then detected in the garage, R2 tries to turn the fan on, but the fan has no power, so it can't clear the gas. Your CO safety response silently fails exactly when no one is home to notice.
evidence: R1: home_mode == away -> breaker_garage.power := off
R2: co_garage == True -> fan_garage.power := on; garage_door.position := open
Known dependency: when breaker_garage.power is off, fan_garage.power becomes off (the exhaust fan is on the garage circuit)
Neither rule has conditions, so CO can be detected while the home is in away mode and the breaker is off
Both the breaker and the fan are in the garage, the same space the CO detector monitors
repair: Change R2 so its first action is breaker_garage.power := on, before it turns on the fan and opens the door. Also add the condition co_garage == False to R1, so the breaker is never cut while CO is present. A sturdier long-term fix is to move the exhaust fan onto its own circuit that is always powered.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door to vent carbon monoxide, and R3 closes the same door when the home switches to away mode. Neither rule checks the other's situation. If CO is still present when the household leaves, for example after a car was left running, R3 can shut the door, trap the CO in the garage and undo the safety response from R2.
evidence: R2 sets garage_door.position := open when co_garage == True
R3 sets garage_door.position := closed when home_mode == away
R3 has no condition on co_garage, and R2 has no condition on home_mode, so both can fire while CO is present
garage_door is one device with one position state (open or closed), so these actions are directly opposed
car_present shows a car can be in the garage, which is a likely source of CO
repair: Add the condition co_garage == False to R3, so the door only closes for away mode when no CO is detected. Optionally, have R3 run again once CO clears while the home is still in away mode.

explanation: R4 starts charging the EV when the car is parked in the garage. The EV charger runs on the garage circuit, so when the home switches to away mode, R1 turns off the garage breaker and the charger loses power. This can happen if the car is parked and the household then leaves by other means, or if the car is parked while the home is already in away mode. In both cases R4's charging is cut off without warning, and the car may stay uncharged.
evidence: R1: home_mode == away -> breaker_garage.power := off
R4: car_present == True -> ev_charger.charging := on
Known dependency: when breaker_garage.power is off, ev_charger.charging becomes off (the EV charger is on the garage circuit)
Nothing in R1 checks car_present or ev_charger.charging, so both rules can apply while the car is in the garage
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only turns off the garage breaker when car_present == False or ev_charger.charging == off. Another option is to put the EV charger on its own circuit, separate from the breaker that R1 switches off.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. When the car arrives, both rules fire and each one turns on a different device: R4 starts the EV charger and R5 turns on the garage light. Neither action changes anything that triggers or blocks the other rule. The home has no known physical link between the charger and the light.
evidence: R4 sets ev_charger.charging to on, and R5 sets light_garage.power to on. These are different devices, and neither rule turns anything off.
Both rules share the same trigger (car_present == True), and neither action changes car_present or any other context variable.
The only known dependencies are breaker_garage → ev_charger and breaker_garage → fan_garage. Neither rule controls the breaker, and no dependency links the charger and the light.
repair: none

explanation: At noon R1 runs the cat feeder in the kitchen. The cat runs over to eat, and the kitchen motion sensor picks it up. If the home is in away mode at that moment, R2 reads this motion as an intruder and sounds the siren. The result is a false alarm almost every day you're out at lunchtime.
evidence: R1 turns feeder.dispensing on at 12:00 every day, with no conditions.
The feeder is in the kitchen, the same room as the motion_kitchen sensor.
Known dependency: when feeder.dispensing is on, motion_kitchen becomes true because the cat runs to the feeder.
R2 is triggered by motion_kitchen == True and turns alarm.siren on when home_mode == away.
People are often away at noon, so away mode and the feeding time can easily overlap.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so kitchen motion is ignored during feeding time, for example from 11:55 to 12:15, or while feeder.dispensing is on. A sturdier fix is to use a pet-immune motion sensor, or to require the kitchen camera to confirm a person before the siren sounds. The alarm stays fully active at all other times.

explanation: When R1 feeds the cat at 12:00, the cat runs to the feeder and sets off the kitchen motion sensor. That motion triggers R3, so the kitchen camera starts recording every day at noon. It records the cat eating rather than a real event, which leads to unwanted recordings and possibly false security alerts.
evidence: R1 sets feeder.dispensing := on at 12:00 with no conditions.
Known dependency: when feeder.dispensing is on, motion_kitchen becomes true because the cat runs to the feeder.
R3 is triggered by motion_kitchen == True and sets camera_kitchen.recording := on with no conditions.
The feeder and the kitchen camera are both in the kitchen.
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it ignores kitchen motion from 12:00 to about 12:10, or switch R3 to people-only detection, so the cat eating doesn't start a recording. The camera still records at all other times.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R4 runs the bathroom litter box's cleaning cycle at noon. R5 sounds the living room siren when it detects motion while the home is in away mode. They control different devices. Running the litter box doesn't change living room motion or the home mode, so R4 can't cause R5 to fire or stop it from firing.
evidence: R4 only sets litter_box.cleaning (bathroom); R5 only sets alarm.siren (living room) — no shared device.
R5 is triggered by motion_living and needs home_mode == away; R4's action doesn't change either one.
The only recorded side effect in this home is that the feeder dispensing food triggers motion_kitchen. Neither rule uses the feeder or the kitchen motion sensor.
No physical or power link is recorded between the litter box and the alarm siren.
repair: none

explanation: Both rules start when motion is detected in the kitchen. When the home is in 'home' mode, R3 turns the kitchen camera's recording on and R6 turns it off at the same moment. Whether the camera ends up recording depends on which rule runs last. This could also happen when no one is in the kitchen, because the cat feeder dispensing food draws the cat to it and sets off the motion sensor.
evidence: R3: trigger motion_kitchen == True, no conditions, action camera_kitchen.recording := on
R6: trigger motion_kitchen == True, condition home_mode == home, action camera_kitchen.recording := off
R3 has no conditions, so it also fires whenever R6's condition (home_mode == home) is true
Both rules set the same device state (camera_kitchen.recording) to opposite values
Known dependency: feeder.dispensing on sets motion_kitchen to true, which can trigger both rules together
repair: Add the condition home_mode != home (that is, away or night) to R3. Then the camera only records when the household isn't in home mode, and R6 handles privacy in home mode without the two rules competing.

explanation: The CPAP machine is plugged into the bedside smart plug, not just the phone charger. When R1 turns that plug off at 23:30, the CPAP loses power, usually after night mode has already switched it on through R2. The CPAP could shut off while someone is asleep and using it, which is a health risk, and R2 won't turn it back on because night mode doesn't change again.
evidence: R1 turns off plug_bedside every day at 23:30, with no conditions.
R2 sets cpap.power to on when home_mode changes to night.
Known dependency: when plug_bedside.power is off, cpap.power becomes off, because the CPAP is plugged into the bedside smart plug.
R1 calls the plug a 'phone charger', so whoever wrote it didn't know the CPAP depends on that plug.
The CPAP is a medical device in the bedroom, so losing its power at night is a safety problem.
repair: Don't let R1 cut power to the CPAP. Either plug the CPAP straight into a regular wall outlet and keep only the phone charger on plug_bedside, or add a condition to R1 so it only switches off when cpap.power is off and home_mode is not night.

explanation: R3 unlocks the entrance door when a fall is detected so paramedics can get in. R4 locks the same door whenever the home switches to night mode. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other. So if a fall happens in the evening and night mode turns on afterwards, R4 locks the door again and paramedics can't get in.
evidence: R3 sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked when fall_detected == True, with no conditions.
R4 sets lock_entrance.lock := locked when home_mode == night, with no conditions.
Both rules act on the same device state (lock_entrance.lock) with opposite values.
fall_detected and home_mode are independent variables, so a fall can happen before or during the switch to night mode.
The bathroom fall radar is an emergency trigger, so re-locking the door affects safety.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only locks the door when fall_detected == False (no active fall emergency). This keeps the door unlocked for paramedics until the fall alert is cleared.

explanation: R5 only turns off the reading lamp plug. The CPAP machine is powered by a different plug, the bedside plug. R2 turns the CPAP on in night mode, and nothing in R5 cuts its power or changes the home mode. These two rules can run together safely.
evidence: R5 action: plug_reading_lamp.power := off (it does not touch plug_bedside)
The only listed power link is that cpap.power turns off when plug_bedside.power is off
No dependency links plug_reading_lamp to cpap
R5 does not change home_mode, which is what triggers R2
repair: none

explanation: At 10:00, R2 opens the living room window. On warm days, hot outdoor air comes in and pushes the living room temperature up. Once it goes above 27 °C, R1 turns on the AC while the window is still open. The AC then cools air that keeps leaking outside, which wastes energy, and the two rules work against each other.
evidence: R2 sets window_living.position to open at 10:00 with no conditions.
Known effect: when window_living is open, temp_living increases (hot outdoor air in summer).
R1 fires when temp_living > 27 and sets ac_living.mode to cool, with no check on the window.
Known effect: when ac_living is cool, temp_living decreases, so the AC and the open window push the temperature in opposite directions.
Neither rule closes the window or stops the AC, so both stay in effect together.
repair: Add the condition window_living.position == closed to R1, and have R1 close the window before it starts cooling. Also add the condition temp_living < 27 to R2, so the window only opens for fresh air when it won't overheat the room.

explanation: Every day at 14:00, R3 turns on the lawn sprinkler. Its spray wets the rain sensor on the terrace, so the sensor reports rain when it isn't raining. That false reading fires R4, which closes the bedroom skylight even though the weather is dry.
evidence: R3 sets sprinkler.watering := on every day at 14:00 with no conditions.
Known dependency: when sprinkler.watering is on, rain_sensor becomes true because the spray wets the terrace rain sensor.
R4 is triggered by rain_sensor == True and sets skylight.position := closed.
The sprinkler is next to the terrace, and the rain sensor is mounted on the terrace.
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only closes the skylight when sprinkler.watering is off. A better fix is to move the rain sensor out of the sprinkler's spray area, so it only detects real rain.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R5 opens the bedroom window, and R4 closes the bedroom skylight, which is a separate device. Opening the window only lowers bedroom CO2, which doesn't affect the rain sensor that triggers R4. Closing the skylight has no listed effect on CO2 or on the window.
evidence: R5 acts on window_bedroom.position (open); R4 acts on skylight.position (closed). These are different devices.
The only listed effect of window_bedroom being open is that co2_bedroom decreases. This only affects R5's own trigger, not R4's trigger (rain_sensor).
The home lists no effect of the skylight on co2_bedroom or on window_bedroom.
The sprinkler can set off rain_sensor, but neither rule controls the sprinkler, so neither rule can trigger the other.
repair: none

explanation: R5 opens the bedroom window when bedroom CO2 is high, and R1 turns on cooling for the living room AC when that room is hot. The two rules control different devices in different rooms. Opening the bedroom window only lowers bedroom CO2, which is the variable that triggers R5, and the AC only lowers the living room temperature, which is the variable that triggers R1. Neither rule can trigger the other, block the other, or pull the same device in opposite directions.
evidence: R5 acts only on window_bedroom.position (bedroom); R1 acts only on ac_living.mode (living room).
The only listed effect of window_bedroom being open is that co2_bedroom goes down, and only R5 reacts to that variable.
The only listed effect of ac_living cooling is that temp_living goes down, and only R1 reacts to that variable.
The dependency that raises temp_living involves window_living, not window_bedroom, and no rule here opens window_living.
Neither rule turns off power or depends on a device that the other rule controls.
repair: none

explanation: R2 opens the living room window at 10:00 no matter what the AC is doing, while R6 closes the same window when the AC starts cooling. If the AC is already cooling at 10:00, R2 opens the window and R6 won't close it again, so the window stays open while the AC runs. If the AC starts cooling just before 10:00, R2 reopens the window R6 just closed.
evidence: R2 sets window_living.position := open at 10:00 with no conditions
R6 sets window_living.position := closed when ac_living.mode becomes cool
Both rules act on the same device (window_living) with opposite values
R6 only fires when the AC switches to cool, so it can't undo R2 if the AC was already cooling
Known effects: an open window_living raises temp_living, while ac_living in cool mode lowers it
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only opens the window when ac_living.mode == off.

explanation: When the home goes into night mode, R2 turns off the closet power strip. The NAS is plugged into that strip, so it loses power too. If night mode is on at 01:00, R1 tries to start the backup on a NAS that has no power, and the backup fails. The cooling fan is on the same strip, so if the NAS did get power back during a backup, the closet would heat up with no fan running.
evidence: R2 sets strip_closet.power := off when home_mode == night
R1 sets nas.backup := running at 01:00, a time when the home is normally in night mode
Known dependency: when strip_closet.power is off, nas.power becomes off (the NAS is plugged into the closet strip)
Known dependency: when strip_closet.power is off, fan_closet.power becomes off (the cooling fan is on the same strip)
Known effect: a running backup raises temp_closet, and only the fan lowers it
repair: Plug the NAS and the cooling fan into an outlet that R2 doesn't switch off. Or add a condition to R2 so it only turns off the strip when nas.backup == idle, and have it wait until the backup finishes.

explanation: The cooling fan is plugged into the closet power strip. When night mode starts, R2 turns the strip off, which also cuts power to the fan. If the closet then gets hotter than 35 °C, R3 will try to turn on the fan, but the fan has no power, so the closet can't be cooled. If R3 turns the fan on first, R2 will still shut it off when night mode begins.
evidence: R2: when home_mode == night, set strip_closet.power to off
R3: when temp_closet > 35, set fan_closet.power to on
Known dependency: when strip_closet.power is off, fan_closet.power becomes off (the cooling fan is plugged into the closet strip)
Known effect: when fan_closet.power is on, temp_closet decreases, so the fan is the closet's only listed way to cool down
repair: Plug the cooling fan into an outlet that is always on, or into its own smart plug, instead of the closet strip, so R2 cannot cut its power. Another option is to add a condition to R2 so it only turns the strip off when temp_closet is 35 °C or lower.

explanation: The nightly backup (R1) warms the closet, which may make the cooling-fan rule (R3) turn on. That is the fan's intended job, so the two rules work together rather than against each other. They control different devices and never give opposite commands, and neither rule switches off the closet power strip that both the NAS and the fan use.
evidence: R1 sets nas.backup := running at 01:00; R3 sets fan_closet.power := on when temp_closet > 35.
When nas.backup is running, temp_closet increases, so R1 can cause R3 to fire.
When fan_closet.power is on, temp_closet decreases, which counters the heat from the backup and doesn't interfere with it.
Neither rule acts on strip_closet, so the physical dependency (strip off turns off the NAS and the fan) is never triggered.
repair: none

explanation: R4 turns off the printer plug in the office when the home switches to night mode. R1 starts the NAS backup in the closet at 01:00. The printer plug has no known physical or environmental link to the NAS, the closet power strip, the closet fan or the closet temperature. Neither rule changes anything the other depends on, and they don't control the same device.
evidence: R4 only sets plug_printer.power to off. plug_printer is a smart plug in the office.
R1 only sets nas.backup to running. The NAS is in the closet.
The NAS and the closet fan are powered through strip_closet, not plug_printer.
No known dependency links plug_printer to nas, fan_closet, strip_closet or temp_closet.
Neither rule's trigger (home_mode or time) is changed by the other rule's action.
repair: none

explanation: If the teenager gets home between 23:00 and 06:00, R1 unlocks the front door. That unlock then triggers R2, which locks the door again right away. The two rules give opposite commands to the same lock, so the teenager can end up locked out, or the door may switch between locked and unlocked over and over.
evidence: R1 sets lock_front.lock to unlocked when teen_phone_home becomes True, and it has no time condition.
R2 fires whenever lock_front.lock becomes unlocked between 23:00 and 06:00 and sets it to locked.
Both rules control the same device state (lock_front.lock) with opposite values.
The teenager can arrive home late at night, so both rules can fire together.
repair: Decide which rule wins at night. One option is to add a condition to R1 so it only unlocks outside 23:00–06:00; at night it could turn on the porch light and send a notification instead. Another option is to let R2 wait a short grace period (for example 2 minutes) after an unlock from R1, then relock the door, so the teenager can get in and the door still ends up locked.

explanation: Both rules control the driveway gate, but they run at different times. R3 closes it at 22:00 and R4 opens it at 07:00, so they can never fire at the same moment. Together they make a normal daily routine: the gate is closed overnight and open during the day.
evidence: R3 is triggered only at time == 22:00 and sets gate.position := closed
R4 is triggered only at time == 07:00 and sets gate.position := open
The two triggers are separate points in time that never overlap
Neither rule has conditions or changes any environment variable that another rule depends on
This home has no known physical dependencies
repair: none

explanation: These two rules control different devices. R5 turns on the porch light and R1 unlocks the front door. Neither action changes the doorbell or the phone-geofence signal that starts the other rule, and no physical links between the devices are listed for this home. Both rules can run together without getting in each other's way.
evidence: R5 acts only on porch_light.power (sets it to on)
R1 acts only on lock_front.lock (sets it to unlocked)
No rule acts on the same device as the other, so there are no opposite commands
R5 is started by doorbell_pressed and R1 by teen_phone_home. Neither rule's action changes either of these signals
Known dependencies and effects in this home: none
repair: none

explanation: Closing the office shades at 09:00 (R1) blocks the winter sun, so the office gets colder. If it drops below 20 °C, R2 turns on the radiator. The radiator then heats the room to make up for warmth the shades kept out. This wastes energy, and it happens because of R1 even though R1 never mentions heating.
evidence: R1 sets shades_office.position := closed every day at 09:00 with no conditions.
Known effect: when shades_office.position is closed, temp_office decreases (closed shades block winter solar gains).
R2 is triggered by temp_office < 20 and sets radiator_office.mode := heat.
Known effect: when radiator_office.mode is heat, temp_office increases. The radiator replaces the heat the closed shades blocked.
Both rules are in the same room (office) and have no conditions, so nothing stops this chain.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only closes the shades when temp_office >= 21 °C. If you need less glare on cold days, tilt the slats partly instead of fully closing them, so the office keeps its solar heat and doesn't trigger R2's radiator.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R2 turns the office radiator on below 20 °C, and R4 turns it off above 24 °C. The office can't be both colder than 20 °C and warmer than 24 °C, so the rules never fire at the same time. When the radiator heats the room, R4 will eventually turn it off. That's the expected thermostat behaviour, and the 20–24 °C gap between the two settings stops the radiator from switching on and off too often.
evidence: R2 trigger: temp_office < 20 sets radiator_office.mode := heat
R4 trigger: temp_office > 24 sets radiator_office.mode := off
The trigger ranges (<20 and >24) never overlap, so the two commands can't be active at the same moment
Known effect: radiator_office heat increases temp_office, which eventually leads to R4 turning the radiator off. That's the intended result.
The 4 °C gap between the two settings stops the radiator from switching on and off too often
Neither rule acts on the shades, the desk heater or the smart plug
repair: none

explanation: Both rules start when the home switches to away mode, and both turn things off: R3 turns off the desk plug and R5 turns off the desk heater. The heater is plugged into that desk plug, so turning off the plug also turns off the heater. Both rules lead to the same result (heater off), so they work together. Neither rule turns anything back on or changes the office temperature in a way that would set off another rule.
evidence: R3 and R5 share the same trigger: home_mode == away.
R3 sets plug_office_heater.power := off; R5 sets desk_heater.power := off. Neither rule sets a device to on.
Known physical dependency: when plug_office_heater.power is off, desk_heater.power becomes off, which is the same state R5 sets.
Neither rule acts on the shades or radiator, which are the devices that affect temp_office, and no rule is triggered by temp_office.
repair: none

explanation: Both rules run at exactly 09:00 every day with no conditions, but R1 closes the office shades and R6 opens them. Whichever rule runs last decides where the shades end up, so the result is unpredictable and the shades may move back and forth. Closed shades also block winter sun, so the office may get cooler if R1 wins.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 09:00, no conditions, action shades_office.position := closed
R6 trigger: time == 09:00, no conditions, action shades_office.position := open
Both actions target the same device state (shades_office.position) with opposite values
Known effect: when shades_office.position is closed, temp_office decreases (blocks winter solar gains)
repair: Make the two rules mutually exclusive. For example, have R1 (close for screen work) run only when home_mode == home and someone is working at the desk, and have R6 (open for daylight) run only when that condition is false. Another option is to move one rule to a different time, such as opening at 09:00 and closing at 10:00.

explanation: At 19:30, R2 starts the white-noise speaker in the nursery. The baby monitor's microphone picks up the white noise, so the measured nursery sound level goes up. If it goes above 60 dB, R1 thinks the baby is crying and turns on the nursery lamp, which could wake the baby when no one is crying.
evidence: R2 sets white_noise.playing to on at 19:30 every day, with no conditions.
Known dependency: when white_noise.playing is on, noise_nursery increases because the baby monitor microphone picks up the white noise.
R1 fires whenever noise_nursery > 60 and has no condition about the white-noise speaker.
R1 turns on nursery_lamp, which is located in the same room.
repair: Make R1 tell crying apart from white noise. While white_noise.playing is on, raise R1's threshold above the white-noise level (for example, more than 10 dB above it), or require the sound to stay loud for a set time, such as 10 seconds. Another option is to set the white-noise volume low enough that it alone stays well under 60 dB on the monitor.

explanation: When the TV comes on in the evening, R3 turns on the soundbar. The soundbar is on the other side of a thin wall from the nursery, so the baby monitor picks up its sound. If that pushes the reading above 60 dB, R1 thinks the baby is crying and turns on the nursery lamp. The baby isn't crying, and the light could wake them up.
evidence: R3 sets soundbar.power := on when the TV turns on between 20:00 and 23:59, which is the baby's evening and sleep time.
Known dependency: when soundbar.power is on, noise_nursery increases (the soundbar shares a thin wall with the nursery).
R1 fires on noise_nursery > 60 with no other conditions, so it can't tell soundbar noise from a crying baby.
R1's action (nursery_lamp.power := on) is a real change in the nursery that the owner didn't intend for TV sound.
repair: Make R1 more careful: only turn on the lamp when noise_nursery > 60 and the soundbar is off. Another option is to raise the threshold or require the noise to last a while when the soundbar is on. You could also move the soundbar or cap its volume after 20:00 so it doesn't push the nursery reading over 60 dB.

explanation: R4 only turns off the living-room TV and R2 only turns on the nursery white-noise speaker, so the two rules control different devices. The white noise raises the nursery noise level, but neither rule depends on that level. The TV has no known connection to the white-noise speaker or to nursery noise. The two rules can run together safely.
evidence: R4 action: tv.power := off; R2 action: white_noise.playing := on, so the rules act on different devices
white_noise.playing on increases noise_nursery, but neither R4 nor R2 uses noise_nursery as a trigger or condition
Neither rule changes home_mode, so R2 can't set off R4
No known dependency links the TV to the white-noise speaker or to nursery noise
repair: none

explanation: During a frost warning, R1 turns on the greenhouse heater, which warms the greenhouse. When the temperature goes above 18 °C, R2 opens the roof vent. The open vent lets the warm air out while the heater keeps running, so the two rules work against each other. This wastes energy and can let the plants get cold on a frosty night.
evidence: R1: frost_warning == True -> gh_heater.power := on
R2: temp_gh > 18 -> gh_vent.position := open
Dependency: when gh_heater.power is on, temp_gh increases
Dependency: when gh_vent.position is open, temp_gh decreases
R2 has no condition that stops it from firing during a frost warning
repair: Add the condition frost_warning == False to R2, so the roof vent doesn't open automatically during a frost warning. Alternatively, use a higher vent temperature (for example 26 °C) while frost_warning is True.

explanation: The greenhouse heater is plugged into the outdoor smart plug. If a frost warning turns the heater on (R1), the 22:00 rule that turns off the outdoor plug (R3) also cuts the heater's power. That leaves the greenhouse unheated during a frost night. Neither rule mentions the other device, so this hidden power link is what causes the conflict.
evidence: R1 sets gh_heater.power := on when frost_warning == True
R3 sets plug_outdoor.power := off at 22:00 with no conditions
Known physical dependency: when plug_outdoor.power is off, gh_heater.power becomes off (the heater is plugged into the outdoor plug)
Frost warnings usually stay active overnight, so both rules can apply at 22:00
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only turns off the outdoor plug when frost_warning == False (or when gh_heater is off). This keeps the heater powered while a frost warning is active.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R4 only turns on the grow lights at 06:00, and R2 only opens the roof vent when the greenhouse is warmer than 18 °C. They control different devices. This home has no recorded link between the grow lights and the greenhouse temperature, the vent, or power, so neither rule can block the other or make it fire unexpectedly.
evidence: R4 acts only on grow_lights.power (sets it to on); R2 acts only on gh_vent.position (sets it to open). They control different devices.
R4 is triggered by time (06:00); R2 is triggered by temp_gh > 18.
The known dependencies link only gh_heater and gh_vent to temp_gh, and plug_outdoor to gh_heater. None involves grow_lights.
Opening the vent lowers temp_gh, but no rule here depends on a low temperature, and R4 doesn't use temperature at all.
repair: none

explanation: R2 and R5 do opposite things to the roof vent, but they can never run at the same time. R2 opens the vent only above 18 °C and R5 closes it only below 5 °C, and the temperature can't be in both ranges at once. The open vent does cool the greenhouse and could eventually let R5 close it, but that is the intended behaviour. The vent won't keep switching back and forth either: it opens again only once the temperature climbs back above 18 °C, so the 5–18 °C gap prevents rapid switching.
evidence: R2 trigger: temp_gh > 18 -> gh_vent.position := open
R5 trigger: temp_gh < 5 -> gh_vent.position := closed
The trigger ranges (>18 and <5) don't overlap, so the two commands can't fire together
Dependency: an open vent lowers temp_gh. Cooling below 5 °C makes R5 close the vent, which is consistent with what both rules aim for
The 13 °C gap between the thresholds stops the vent from opening and closing over and over
repair: none

explanation: The greenhouse heater is plugged into the outdoor smart plug. If a frost warning turns the heater on (R1), the 22:00 power-saving rule (R3) switches off that plug and the heater goes off with it. That leaves the greenhouse unheated overnight, when frost is most likely. A second, smaller problem: heating can push the temperature above 18 °C, which makes R2 open the roof vent and let the heat out.
evidence: R1 sets gh_heater.power := on when frost_warning == True
R3 sets plug_outdoor.power := off every day at 22:00, with no conditions
Physical dependency: when plug_outdoor.power is off, gh_heater.power becomes off (the heater is plugged into the outdoor plug)
A frost warning can be active at 22:00, because frost warnings usually cover the night
Side issue: the heater raises temp_gh, and once temp_gh is above 18 °C, R2 opens gh_vent, which lowers temp_gh
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only turns off the outdoor plug when frost_warning == False. If R3 also controls other devices, move the greenhouse heater to a separate outlet that R3 doesn't switch off.

explanation: R1 turns the greenhouse heater on when a frost warning is issued, and R6 turns the same heater off at 22:00 every night. Nothing stops R6 from running while the frost warning is still active. Frost is most likely overnight, so the heater can be switched off right when the plants need it. R1 won't switch it back on, because it only runs when a new warning is issued.
evidence: R1 sets gh_heater.power := on when frost_warning == True, with no conditions
R6 sets gh_heater.power := off at 22:00, with no conditions
Both rules control the same device state (gh_heater.power) in opposite directions
frost_warning can still be True at 22:00 (for example, a warning issued in the afternoon), so both rules apply at the same time
When gh_heater is on, temp_gh increases, so turning it off during frost lets the greenhouse get colder
repair: Add a condition to R6 so it only turns the heater off when frost_warning == False. Optionally, add a rule that turns the heater back on if a frost warning is active after 22:00.
